title: WERBUNG - Auf Kasse: Medizinische Hauskrankenpflege
content:
Nach einer OP oder bei notwendiger Wundpflege kann die medizinische Hauskrankenpflege für daheim verordnet werden. Das erspart mühsame Ambulanzbesuche.
Zuckerkrank! Das war ein Riesenschock für die 89-jährige Herta M., als der Hausarzt bei ihr „Diabetes mellitus“ diagnostizierte. Und dann auch noch eine akute Überzuckerung im Dezember 2024.
Glück im Unglück: Obwohl Herta M. auch bei laufender Behandlung im Spital ihr diabetischer Fuß noch zu schaffen machte, konnte sie bereits nach wenigen Tagen wieder nach Hause. Der entlassende Arzt hatte ihr nämlich eine „Medizinische Hauskrankenpflege“ verordnet. Herta M. hat zuvor noch nie von dieser – für sie kostenlosen – Leistung gehört. Noch bevor sie das Krankenhaus verließ, organisierte das Entlassungsmanagement bereits ganz unbürokratisch die medizinische Hauskrankenpflege der FSW-Pflege- und Betreuungsdienste für sie.
Medizinisch-pflegerische Versorgung im eigenen Zuhause
„Ich war so erleichtert, wieder nach Hause zu können. Am liebsten bin ich einfach in meinen eigenen vier Wänden“, sagt sie. Gleichzeitig beschäftigte Herta M. die Sorge um ihre Wunde: „Ich hatte Angst, dass sich etwas entzündet oder ich etwas falsch mache.“
Diese Sorge war rasch beseitigt: Bereits am Tag nach der Entlassung kam eine diplomierte Pflegefachkraft zu ihr nach Hause. Ihr Fuß, bei dem durch den ständig erhöhten Blutzuckerspiegel die Nerven- und Blutgefäße geschädigt waren, konnte so einfach in ihrer Wohnung in Simmering professionell behandelt werden: ohne mühsame Fahrten in die Ambulanz und lange Wartezeiten! Dreimal pro Woche wurde ihre Wunde professionell versorgt und der Heilungsverlauf kontrolliert.
Rasch merkte die Seniorin, dass sich die schmerzhaften und schlecht abheilenden Wunden dank der medizinisch-pflegerischen Versorgung besserten. Das spürte sie auch durch mehr Lebensqualität und Beweglichkeit.
„Es war ein gutes Gefühl zu wissen, dass jemand kommt, auf den ich mich verlassen kann und dass ich mit meinen Sorgen nicht allein bin“, erinnert sich die Seniorin.
Medizinische Hauskrankenpflege – wie bekomme ich sie?
Wenn der Arzt – so wie bei Herta M. – einen Bedarf für Pflegeleistungen erkennt, kann er medizinische Hauskrankenpflege verordnen. Hinter der medizinischen Hauskrankenpflege steht ein Team speziell geschulter Pflegeexpert:innen. Sie übernehmen die Versorgung komplexer Wunden, Stoma-, Fistel- oder Katheterpflege, sorgen für die Verabreichung von speziellen Injektionen bzw. Infusionen oder künstlicher Ernährung. So erhalten Patient:innen nach einem Krankenhausaufenthalt – oder sogar stattdessen – eine medizinisch-pflegerisch hochwertige Versorgung direkt zu Hause.
Die Anordnung gilt zunächst für maximal 28 Kalendertage und ist bei Bedarf nach chefärztlicher Bewilligung verlängerbar. Die Kosten dafür trägt der jeweilige Sozialversicherungsträger.
Einfach medizinische Hauskrankenpflege vereinbaren
Wer in Wien wohnt und eine solche Anordnung erhalten hat, meldet sich am besten direkt bei der Mobilen Hauskrankenpflege des FSW (werktags von 7:30 – 15:30 Uhr unter 01/24 5 24 – 30 300) und vereinbart einen persönlichen Besuchstermin daheim. Dann kommt die professionelle Pflegekraft zum vereinbarten Zeitpunkt vorbei und übernimmt die notwendige Versorgung. Das erspart langwierige Arzt- oder Ambulanzbesuche bzw. stationäre Aufenthalte und gibt den Betroffenen die Sicherheit, zu Hause bestens versorgt zu sein.

title: Julie Gobert créée un groupe dédié aux parents solos pour briser la solitude et trouver de l’entraide à Mons : “Ce n’est pas toujours facile à vivre”
content:
Julie Gobert créée un groupe dédié aux parents solos pour briser la solitude et trouver de l'entraide à Mons : "Ce n'est pas toujours facile à vivre"
Garder les enfants, retrouver un logement, profiter d'un événement, recréer du lien, ce sont les objectifs affichés du groupe "Parents solo Mons"
- Publié le 19-09-2026 à 16h01
Être parent solo, c'est parfois devoir tout gérer seul : les enfants, les imprévus, les finances, mais aussi les moments où l'on aurait simplement besoin de souffler. Dans la Cité du Doudou, Julie Gobert a décidé de créer un espace pour permettre à ces parents de se retrouver et de s'entraider. Baptisé "Parents Solo Mons", son groupe Facebook compte déjà 145 membres, quelques semaines seulement après son lancement.
Montoise et maman solo de deux garçons de 6 et 13 ans, Julie Gobert connaissait déjà le groupe "Parents Solo Belgique". "C'est un groupe hypersolidaire, il y a beaucoup de publications chaque jour, que ce soit sur la garde des enfants, les pensions alimentaires, le mal-être… Il y a énormément de témoignages et de solidarité", souligne-t-elle. "C'est aussi une façon de partager des événements qui pourraient intéresser les membres."
Mais le groupe national couvre toute la Belgique. "Il faut donc parfois parcourir de nombreux kilomètres pour participer à une activité." D'où l'idée de créer une déclinaison montoise, davantage ancrée localement. "Le but, c'est de rassembler, de faire de nouvelles rencontres et de pouvoir aussi se rencontrer dans la réalité sans avoir à traverser la Belgique. La proximité, dans ce genre de situation, cela peut aussi être une force et une aide précieuse."
S'entraider aussi dans les moments difficiles
Depuis la création du groupe, les demandes d'adhésion arrivent quotidiennement. Sorties, bons plans, garde d'enfants, repassage ou encore événements, chacun peut partager ses besoins ou ses propositions. Pour Julie Gobert, cette entraide peut également prendre une dimension plus concrète lorsque la situation devient compliquée. Elle pense notamment aux parents qui se séparent et doivent rapidement trouver un logement.
"Quand on devient solo, c'est très difficile. Moi-même, au début, je partageais encore la maison familiale et j'avais besoin de trouver un autre logement, ne serait-ce que temporairement, pour pouvoir souffler, avoir ma propre chambre. Mais trouver rapidement, et dans un contexte financier qui est lui aussi changeant n'est pas simple." Elle imagine dès lors des formes d'entraide comme de petites colocations entre parents solos. "Ce serait une situation transitoire, le temps de se retourner, de vendre la maison ou de retrouver un logement après la séparation."
Elle-même se dit prête à aller dans ce sens : "J'ai une chambre que je peux mettre à disposition d'un parent solo qui se retrouverait dans une situation compliquée." Au-delà des difficultés matérielles, c'est surtout le lien social que Julie Gobert souhaite recréer. "Nous vivons dans une société de surcommunication et pourtant, nous n'avons jamais été aussi seuls, surtout lorsque notre situation amoureuse chance. Personnellement, si je n'avais pas eu mes amis pour me sortir et me faire bouger, je ne sais pas où j'en serais."
À 42 ans, l'éducatrice spécialisée est par ailleurs actuellement à la recherche d'un nouveau défi professionnel, notamment dans les domaines de l'assistance commerciale ou administrative. Une nouvelle étape dans un parcours où l'envie de créer du lien et d'aider les autres reste bien présente. Le groupe "Parents Solo Mons" est ouvert aux parents solos de la région. L'objectif de Julie Gobert est désormais de continuer à le faire grandir, mais surtout de transformer les échanges virtuels en véritables rencontres.

title: À Molenbaix, l’art contemporain s’invite dans les rues et les champs et attire des visiteurs de toute la Wallonie
content:
À Molenbaix, l'art contemporain s'invite dans les rues et les champs et attire des visiteurs de toute la Wallonie
Il reste deux semaines pour découvrir "Butor", la première biennale d'art contemporain en campagne. Dix-neuf artistes, entre champs et hameaux.
- Publié le 19-09-2026 à 12h01
Le centre du village et le hameau de Butor voient passer de nombreux visiteurs, depuis quelques semaines. Ils viennent de différents coins de Wallonie, mais aussi des Flandres et de France.
"Butor" et douceur
Marcher de la ferme d'Ecavée au centre du village permet de découvrir un sentier singulier, en céramique gravée de mots. "De Molenbeek à Molenbaix", "Ce chemin est celui de tous" ... Citadins et ruraux se souviennent de venelles, sentes, petites voies, ruelles, chemins de pavés et de liens. Les enfants apprécient particulièrement cette oeuvre de Various Artists, un collectif également auteur d'un totem et de quelques interventions insolites.
"C'est ma petite-fille !" annonce fièrement Christian Collie quand des visiteurs s'approchent du terrain de foot. Léa - en miroir - est peinte par Charlotte Beaudry sur bois chantourné, aux couleurs du club. La jeune footballeuse de quinze ans joue à présent à Avelgem, elle est de plus, vu son talent, reprise dans la sélection nationale des Jeunes à Mons. Son grand-père, qui évolua au Racing de Tournai, fait partie du comité de foot de Molenbaix.
Un pas plus loin, Raphaël De Coster a créé une "zone de rupture potentielle", en utilisant un cordeau. Ligne droites et penchées, tendues vers la cime d'une structure qui puise son énergie dans un geste géométrique résolu. Chemin du centre, Lise Duclaux a placé des affiches porteuses de slogans courts, limpides : "Nous ne sommes que les autres". L'église Saint-Ghislain abrite des recherches picturales de Charlotte Beaudry, un autel à sainte Rita (Jacques Charlier) et une étonnante sculpture de Maaerten Vanden Eynde : un tronc d'arbre scié, posé sur une ancienne balance en fonte. L'oeuvre interroge l'équilibre, la fragilité, la pesanteur.
Lieux et liens
"C'est un choc, ce jaillissement !", s'exclame Frédérique, venue de Lasne à la rencontre de l'exposition. Devant "La terre saigne", fontaine de Laurence Dervaux, elle évoque son réflexe de "juguler la plaie", "voir arriver une ambulance" "une énorme puissance suggestive" . "Des visiteurs parlent ici autant de vie que de mort, songeant aux guerres comme aux souffrances infligées à la planète", souligne Caroline, l'une des guides de l'exposition.
Des groupes et duos se croisent, échangeant leurs impressions à propos du parcours, de la campagne, des nombreuses haltes proposées. Aucun artiste n'est oublié dans les conversations, les précisions et questions. Les interventions en extérieur comme en intérieur ouvrent des perspectives, déclenchent la surprise, l'admiration, la réflexion collective. Et cette certitude d'être au coeur d'une approche que l'on dit contemporaine : l'intégration au paysage, à la nature, l'assurance d'une discrétion privilégiée, la présence du symbole et de la beauté.
"Butor", au départ de la ferme d'Ecavée à Molenbaix, du jeudi au dimanche, de 10h30 à 18h. Possibilité de visites guidées. Jusqu'au 4 octobre.

title: Liège : la bibliothèque d’Angleur se pare de nouvelles couleurs grâce à de nouvelles fresques
content:
Liège : la bibliothèque d'Angleur se pare de nouvelles couleurs grâce à de nouvelles fresques
À Angleur, les habitants ont mis la main à la mosaïque. La bibliothèque s'offre un nouveau décor après près d'un an de travail collectif.
- Publié le 19-09-2026 à 19h00
À Angleur, les murs de la bibliothèque ont désormais un nouveau visage. Des fresques en mosaïque, réalisées collectivement par des habitants, des élèves et des enfants participant aux stages de la Ville de Liège, ont été inaugurées, il y a quelques jours. Un projet participatif qui aura mobilisé le quartier pendant plusieurs mois.
Entre octobre 2025 et août 2026, habitants d'Angleur et de Liège, élèves de l'école fondamentale communale Andréa Jadoulle et enfants des stages de la Ville de Liège ont mis la main à la pâte pour donner naissance à ces œuvres. Leur objectif : apporter de la couleur aux abords de la bibliothèque, tout en associant directement les habitants à la transformation de leur quartier.
Le projet a été porté par le Centre culturel Ourthe et Meuse, en partenariat avec la bibliothèque d'Angleur, l'école Andréa Jadoulle et les différents participants. Il a également bénéficié du soutien des services culturels et techniques de la Ville de Liège.
Près d'un an de travail collectif
Au fil des mois, les participants ont travaillé à la réalisation des mosaïques, dans une démarche mêlant différentes générations. L'inauguration a permis de découvrir le résultat de ce travail et de réunir habitants, partenaires et participants autour d'un moment festif.
La cérémonie a notamment été animée par le groupe vocal Polyfunny, dirigé par Marie Zinnen. Les échanges entre les participants ont prolongé cette dimension conviviale, au cœur d'un projet qui entendait autant embellir les lieux que favoriser les rencontres.
Ces nouvelles fresques viennent aussi renforcer la place de la bibliothèque comme lieu de culture et de vie dans le quartier.
Une nouvelle édition dès octobre
L'initiative s'inscrit dans la continuité des "Journées mosaïque", lancées à la suite des inondations de juillet 2021. Le projet vise depuis lors à créer du lien entre les habitants tout en intervenant directement dans l'espace public.
L'histoire ne s'arrête d'ailleurs pas avec cette inauguration. Une nouvelle édition des Journées mosaïque est annoncée dès le mois d'octobre. Ouverte à toutes et tous, elle permettra à nouveau aux habitants de participer à la création d'œuvres collectives appelées à prendre place dans l'espace public angleurois.
Les fresques constituent ainsi un nouveau repère dans le quartier, fruit d'un travail associant habitants, école, acteurs culturels et services publics

title: 'I'm forever grateful for my girl's donated heart'
content:
'I'm forever grateful for my girl's donated heart'
- Published
Ahead of Organ Donation Week, two mothers whose children were involved in transplants share their stories from either side of the experience.
Seven-year-old Evie is thriving.
She is doing well at school, enjoys playing with friends and is keen to give everything a go, her mother Chloe Green says.
But for her daughter to be doing so well today, another family had to go through the unimaginable pain of losing their child.
When she was three years old, Evie needed a new heart.
The toddler from Middlesbrough spent 16 months in hospital in Newcastle being kept alive by a Berlin Heart, a mechanical pump which she had to be permanently attached to.
Evie featured in a project by Consett-based photographer Debbie Todd, taking before and after pictures of children awaiting life-saving organs.
Sadly, Debbie says, not all the children got their "after" picture.
Evie's wait was so long she ended up having three "before" photos taken, images treasured by Chloe as showing the journey her daughter had to undertake.
Chloe, 31, and her husband David, 38, would swap places by her hospital bedside, juggling looking after her with work and caring for their other child, Evie's brother Theo, who is a year older than his sister.
Chloe says she tried to stay optimistic, focusing on "small wins all the time", but her mindset changed when Evie had to be attached to the machine.
"I was watching her dying," Chloe says. "Suddenly my priority was 'we need a new heart'."
She understood what that meant for any potential donor.
"I did feel I was in a moral quandary," Chloe says. "It comes with a lot of guilt.
"Of course you are not wanting someone else to die, but the doctors said we could only think of what we needed for Evie's treatment plan, you have to have that boundary."
They were waiting for another family to do an "amazing thing", Chloe says, and the appreciation never fades.
"Whenever I reflect back or see Evie hitting a milestone, I think of that [donor] child," she says.
"I almost feel like they are part of our family, they are coming along with us."
The donated heart was a "perfect match" for Evie and has "done so much for her", Chloe says.
She acknowledges that may not fully comfort the donor's family but might give them some peace to know.
Chloe does not know who the donor was but has written a letter to their family, there for them to read should they ever choose to.
"If I could speak to the donor's family, I would just be forever thanking them," Chloe says.
"We would love to share everything about Evie's life if they were willing to, but of course it has to be their choice.
"It would just be constant gratitude. I am forever grateful to them."
Anna-Louise Bates knows what it is like to receive such a letter.
In 2015, her husband Stuart and seven-year-old son Fraser were killed when they were hit by a car near their home in Talbot Green in south Wales.
Because he died at the scene, Stuart, who had signed the organ registry and wanted to be a donor, was unable to be one.
But Fraser's heart, lungs, liver and kidneys were given to three other children and an adult, with his heart going to a young twin boy from Hartlepool called Roman.
"I won't forget the first letter I ever received from his mum," Anna-Louise says. "How the loss of my boy had allowed hers to grow.
"To know Fraser lives on has given me so much hope, it was like they didn't die in vain.
"Life is a gift and the biggest gift you can give is life."
She said milestones such as Fraser's recent 18th birthday were "incredibly difficult", but hearing of Roman enjoying life and having "10 years' worth of memories and love" gave "some comfort".
Anna-Louise founded Believe Organ Donor Support, to encourage people to think about organ donation and discuss it with their loved ones.
At Stuart's insistence, she and her husband had the "icky" conversation just two weeks before the crash, and Anna-Louise is so grateful they did.
It meant in that "24 hours of hell", the questions around organ donation were the "only time I didn't have to think", she says.
Knowing her husband's wishes and how her son was meant she felt confident to agree to donate, with the lives Fraser saved "a testament to the big heart he had".
She has in the years since thought about it from the recipient's point of view, she says, about how a parent might feel knowing a "young child passed away for you to have that organ".
"The way I reconcile that is I am just pleased Fraser's gift has allowed a child to live on," she says.
"He gave the greatest gift and especially because this was so close to Christmas, he gave the gift of life that he could no longer be part of."
She says she is not telling everyone they have to be a donor, but is encouraging people to "have those conversations" and register their preference on the organ donation registry so their loved ones know their wishes.
Anna-Louise has spoken to many children since and found they were "really open" to organ donation and more willing to discuss it than their adult parents, she says.
According to the NHS, some 408 people died last year while on the UK transplant waiting list, with Anna-Louise saying just 1% of people end up being eligible to be a donor.
Since 2015 in Wales, 2020 in England and 2021 in Scotland, authorities have operated an opt-out service, external, where adults are presumed to be donors unless they declare otherwise on the NHS Organ Donation Register.
But families will still be consulted and can object.
The system does not apply to people under 18 and decisions regarding children are made by their families, although anyone of any age can add themselves to the register.
Chloe in Middlesbrough is also asking people to think about it in advance, what would they do if the unthinkable happened?
"You do not want to think about your child dying, I understand that" she says.
"But look at the children doing well, what can come from thinking about it and making that decision to donate.
"I totally respect people's choices.
"It's just about thinking and talking about it."

title: 'I thought it would make the team special' - a papal blessing with a difference
content:
'I thought it would make the team special' - a papal blessing with a difference
- Published
Wearing a special jersey on the day of the big game, sitting in the exact same seat match after match, or maybe donning some lucky underpants.
These are just some of the rituals sports fans believe can help their team win.
But 10-year-old Eoghan decided it was time to step up his fan game.
For him, the best chance to ensure success would be to wear his Tyrone GAA colours while meeting Pope Leo XIV.
"I was wearing the jersey because I thought it would make Tyrone special."
Eoghan, along with his older sister Áine and mum Edel Quinn, met the Pope in August after a friend arranged tickets to one of his weekly public audiences.
Áine says they did not realise how close they were going to be to the pontiff until they arrived at St Peter's Basilica in Vatican City.
"They led us up to the very front, we were gobsmacked."
The Castlederg family were even more surprised when they found out they would have a chance to chat with Pope Leo.
Eoghan says he shook his hand first, then Áine's and then their mum's.
"He was looking at the jersey wondering where it was from."
Áine says the Pope then acknowledged how far they had travelled.
Eoghan thinks the Pope may have recognised the jersey, as this was not the first time he came into contact with one.
In November 2025, Aidan Gallagher tossed a Tyrone jersey with 'Leo 14' written on the back of it to the pontiff outside the Vatican.
And the Tyrone connection did not stop once the meeting was over.
After receiving a blessing from the Pope and rosary beads from one of the guards, Áine says they were escorted down an aisle where hundreds of people were watching them from behind barricades.
From out of nowhere, someone in the crowd shouted "up Tyrone!".
"I could not believe it walking down seeing all those different faces and then someone says up Tyrone."
Besides the excitement of meeting the Pope, it was also an emotional day for the siblings, as Edel has Multiple Sclerosis
"Our faith is important to us, we always went to mass every Saturday or Sunday and my mum has MS, so the trip was very special for her," says Áine.
The family still cannot not believe it really happened.
Eoghan says his friends have all been asking him: "How do you shake hands with the Pope?"
While Áine says people have grabbing the hand the pontiff shook: "Being just two ordinary people from Castlederg, sitting inches from the Pope and meeting him, it was surreal."

title: Wie dank Budgetpolitik mehr Weiblichkeit in Wien einzog
content: Ein Spaziergang mit Symbolcharakter: Vizebürgermeisterin Barbara Novak, Frauenstadträtin Elke Hanel-Torsch (beide SPÖ) und Neos-Abgeordnete Maria In der Maur-Könne waren kürzlich gemeinsam in der Donaustadt anzutreffen. Dabei wurde die Frage erörtert, wie geschlechtsneutral die Stadtentwicklung wirklich ist. Und was insbesondere für Frauen schon getan wurde.Das Budget spielt dabei eine große Rolle. Grundsätzlich wurde 2009 in der Verfassung „Gender Budgeting“ verankert – Bund, Länder und Gemeinden müssen bei der Haushaltsführung die tatsächliche Gleichstellung von Frauen und Männern anstreben und das auch ausweisen. Wien war allerdings früher dran und veröffentlicht seit 2006 die Bemühungen im Budgetvoranschlag. „Da waren wir wieder einmal First Mover“, sagt Hanel-Torsch.Im letztjährigen Budgetvoranschlag nahm das Kapitel immerhin 59 Seiten ein – also mehr als ein Zehntel des rund 500-seitigen Berichts. Was sich genau hinter „Gender Budgeting“ verbirgt, wurde anhand von fünf Stationen erläutert.Ausbau der KinderbetreuungGestartet wurde beim Bildungscampus in der Attemsgasse. „Care-Arbeit ist immer noch hauptsächlich Frauensache“, so In der Maur-Könne. Darum sei es so wichtig, Betreuungsmöglichkeiten auszubauen, um Müttern zu ermöglichen, arbeiten gehen zu können. „Ich bin selbst Mutter von zwei Töchtern, die jetzt in den 20ern sind. Ich hätte vieles nicht machen können, wenn das Bildungsangebot nicht da gewesen wäre.“ Die Anzahl der Kinderbetreuungseinrichtungen wie Kindergärten oder Horte haben sich seit dem Doppelbudget 2005/2006 von 1.863 bis 2024/2025 auf 2.685 gesteigert. Im selben Zeitraum ist die Beschäftigungsquote von Frauen von 64,1 Prozent auf 71,4 Prozent gestiegen.Geförderter Wohnraumöffentliche Parks Nächster Stopp: Der Kirschblütenpark. Hier wurde bei der Gestaltung auf breite, für Kinderwägen geeignete Wege geachtet, auf ausreichend Toilettenanlagen und auch Trinkbrunnen – alles, was Kinderbetreuung erleichtert. Hier wird besonders deutlich, dass von den Maßnahmen zwar besonders Frauen profitieren, aber sie eben auch Männern zu Gute kommen. Wohnbauten, wie man sie in der Donaustadt oft sieht, sind auch wesentlich. „Geförderter Wohnbau ist seit 100 Jahren Grundvoraussetzung für alleinstehende Frauen“, so Hanel-Torsch. Und Novak verweist darauf, dass es nicht darum gehe, dass sich Architekten mit innovativen Grundrissen selbst verewigen, sondern um Wohnräume, die man mit günstigeren Standardmöbeln einrichten kann.Förderung von Unternehmertum Als Nächstes bleiben die Politikerinnen bei einem Geschäft für Baby-und Kindermode stehen. Auch Förderungen von Gründerinnen ist ein Teil des „Gender Budgeting“. Bei Einzelunternehmen lag der Frauenanteil im Jahr 2007 noch bei 32,7 Prozent. 2025 lag er bereits bei 45,1 Prozent. Laut Wirtschaftsagentur beträgt der Frauenanteil bei Erstgesprächen für Unternehmensgründungen bei 51,29 Prozent.Sportmöglichkeiten und Gesundheitsversorgung Weiter geht es zum Eissportzentrum Steffl Arena. „Zur Teilhabe gehört auch Sport dazu“, sagt Hanel-Torsch. Essenziell sei dabei die Förderung. Verwiesen wird auch auf die ehemalige SPÖ-Sportstadträtin Grete Laska, die 2006 federführend vorangetrieben hatte, dass Umziehcontainer für Läuferinnen auf der Prater Hauptallee aufgestellt wurden. In der Gesundheitsversorgung gibt es noch Luft nach oben, bei Gynäkologen gibt es einen Mangel. Die Stadt Wien hat allerdings angekündigt, in den kommenden Jahren jährlich zwei Frauengesundheitszentren auszuschreiben. Insgesamt sind bis 2030 neun Einheiten vorgesehen.Aus- und Weiterbildung ermöglichen Das Donauzentrum stehe sinnbildlich für Jobs, Lehrlingsausbildung und Weiterbildung, sagt Novak. Beim waff, dem Wiener Arbeitnehmer*innen Förderungsfonds, sind 65,5 Prozent aller Teilnehmer bei Angeboten zur beruflichen Weiterentwicklung weiblich. Die vergangenes Jahr ins Leben gerufene Frauenarbeitsstiftung, die Frauen ohne abgeschlossene Berufsausbildung ab 25 Jahren beim (Wieder-)Einstieg ins Arbeitsleben helfen soll, wird nächstes Jahr fortgeführt und die Investitionssumme von 1,7 Millionen Euro weiter aufgestockt, stellt Novak in Aussicht. Gleich beim Donauzentrum ist die U1-Station Kagran. Auch die Wiener Linien seien für Frauen ein wichtiger Faktor, weil sie weniger oft ein Auto besitzen als Männer.Dass beim Spaziergang alles in Gehweite ist, ist übrigens mehr als Symbolik. Die in Wien angestrebte „Stadt der kurzen Wege“ ist besonders für Frauen wichtig, weil diese im Bemühen, den Alltag zu jonglieren, „möglichst alles gleichzeitig an einem Ort machen wollen“, wie Novak sagt.

title: Three-Day Methadone Bridge Therapy Keeps People in Opioid Treatment, Study Finds
content:
Methadone remains one of the most effective medications available for opioid use disorder, yet in the United States it is locked behind a regulatory architecture that few other medicines must navigate. Federal law restricts methadone treatment for addiction to specially licensed opioid treatment programs, or OTPs, which are scarce in many regions, often maintain long waitlists, and typically limit intake to narrow windows during the business week. For a person in opioid withdrawal who arrives at a clinic on a Friday afternoon, those structural barriers can mean the difference between starting treatment and returning to the illicit drug supply. A new study from researchers at the University of California, San Francisco and the San Francisco Department of Public Health examines whether a legally sanctioned workaround, the so-called three-day methadone rule, can convert a fleeting moment of readiness into durable treatment engagement.
The three-day rule is a provision of federal regulation that permits practitioners who are not affiliated with an OTP to administer methadone to a patient for the purpose of relieving acute withdrawal symptoms while arranging referral to a licensed program. The allowance is capped at three days, and it cannot be renewed within the same month. In practice, it has historically been used sparingly, because clinicians have worried about safety and because the short window seems ill-suited to overcoming the administrative delays that often accompany OTP enrollment. The new research, published in the journal Addiction Science & Clinical Practice, offers a detailed real-world test of the approach as implemented at the San Francisco General Hospital Bridge Clinic, a low-threshold service designed to meet patients where they are.
The study team, led by Sarah Rosenwohl-Mack of UCSF’s Department of Family and Community Medicine, conducted a retrospective case series covering every patient who initiated methadone under the three-day rule at the Bridge Clinic between June 2024 and July 2025. The setting is notable for an unusual piece of geography: the hospital also houses an opioid treatment program in the same building. When that program could not complete an intake, for example because a patient arrived outside scheduled intake hours or the program was at capacity, staff could refer the person down to the Bridge Clinic, where a dose of methadone could be started immediately under the three-day provision. This bidirectional referral pathway became the study’s central variable.
The researchers tracked two primary outcomes. The first was linkage to an OTP within seven days of receiving the initial Bridge Clinic dose, a window that extends beyond the three-day medication allowance and therefore captures whether the bridge actually carried patients to permanent care. The second was retention in OTP treatment at 30 days, a marker of early stability that addiction medicine researchers view as a meaningful predictor of longer-term benefit. Because methadone carries its own risks, particularly when combined with other sedatives, the team also built in a safety monitoring framework that reviewed urine drug screens, emergency department visits, hospitalizations within seven days, and Medical Examiner overdose reports.
The results are striking for a population that conventional systems routinely lose. Among 166 unique patients who received at least one dose of three-day methadone at the Bridge Clinic, 63 percent, or 104 individuals, successfully linked to an opioid treatment program within seven days. Of those who linked, 62 percent, or 64 patients, were still retained in treatment at the 30-day mark. In a field where attrition between first contact and enrollment has long been considered one of the most stubborn leaks in the continuum of care, the finding suggests that a short bridge of medication can hold a substantial fraction of patients long enough for the formal system to catch up with them.
The most consequential finding, however, concerned the direction of the referral. Using multivariable logistic regression to adjust for other factors, the researchers found that patients who arrived at the Bridge Clinic by referral from the co-located OTP had 3.1-fold higher odds of remaining in treatment at 30 days compared with patients who came through other routes. The interpretation is not that the referral itself dispensed a pharmacological benefit, but that the pathway reflects a coordinated system in which the OTP and the Bridge Clinic function as two doors into the same building of care. A patient handed off from the OTP arrives with an established clinical relationship, a documented treatment plan, and a clear route back, whereas a patient walking in cold must navigate enrollment largely on their own after the three-day window closes.
On the safety side, the record was clean in ways that will reassure clinicians who have hesitated to use the three-day rule. The study identified no methadone-related emergency department visits, no hospitalizations, and no deaths within 30 days of receiving methadone at the Bridge Clinic. The urine drug screen review, designed to flag unexpected results such as methadone positivity in patients not prescribed it or the absence of non-prescribed opioids suggesting diversion, surfaced only one notable case: a single patient who, on closer chart review, turned out to have already been enrolled in methadone treatment elsewhere before receiving a dose at the Bridge Clinic. That finding points to a practical quality-control challenge, ensuring that bridge dosing does not duplicate existing treatment, but it does not undermine the overall safety signal.
The technical logic of the intervention deserves attention. Methadone is a long-acting full mu-opioid receptor agonist with a half-life that supports once-daily dosing, which is precisely why it smooths the cycle of withdrawal and craving that drives much of the daily chaos in untreated opioid use disorder. When a patient presents in withdrawal, the clinical task is to provide enough of the medication to relieve symptoms without accumulating toxicity, which is why Bridge Clinic protocols begin with conservative doses and titrate carefully. The three-day rule fits neatly into this pharmacology: three days of supervised dosing is enough to stabilize a patient physiologically and to interrupt the withdrawal-driven urgency that otherwise pushes people back to fentanyl and other illicit opioids, while the referral machinery works in parallel to secure a permanent slot at an OTP.
The San Francisco team acknowledges intellectual debts in the paper, crediting the Faster Paths Emergency Opioid Withdrawal Protocol at Boston Medical Center, whose published approach informed the local protocol. That lineage matters because it illustrates how low-threshold models are spreading through a kind of open-source clinical adaptation, with programs borrowing and refining each other’s protocols rather than waiting for multi-year trials. The study itself was deemed exempt by the UCSF Institutional Review Board and used retrospectively collected anonymized data, a design that trades the rigor of randomization for the realism of observing how an intervention performs inside the ordinary friction of a public hospital.
The implications reach well beyond one clinic. Opioid treatment programs remain the only legal channel for methadone maintenance in the United States, and their geographic maldistribution means that many counties have no OTP at all. The three-day rule cannot substitute for structural reform, but the study demonstrates that when a low-threshold bridge service and a licensed OTP are deliberately networked, the rule becomes a functional handoff mechanism rather than a rarely used legal footnote. The 3.1-fold retention advantage associated with OTP referral suggests that the return on investment lies in building those connections, ensuring that every bridge dose is paired with a warm pathway back into licensed care. For a lethal epidemic that has proven resistant to conventional outreach, the message is deceptively simple: meet people in withdrawal with medication the same day, and engineer the system so that the door they entered stays open behind them.

title: Projekt "Eko hrana u školama" širi se na vrtiće u Zagrebu
content:
Eko hrana stiže u vrtiće u Zagrebu. Tomašević: Postavljamo standarde
U POVODU Europskog dana ekološke proizvodnje zagrebački gradonačelnik Tomislav Tomašević predstavio je, u Dječjem vrtiću Trnsko, objektu na Kajzerici, novu fazu projekta "Eko hrana u školama", koji se ove jeseni, uz osnovne škole, proširuje i na vrtiće te će obuhvatiti oko 21.000 djece.
Pilot-projekt "Eko hrana u školama", koji Grad Zagreb provodi treću godinu zaredom, od ove školske, odnosno pedagoške godine, proširuje se i na gradske dječje vrtiće. "Zagreb je prvi i jedini hrvatski grad koji je putem javne nabave sustavno uveo ekološku hranu u škole, a sada i u vrtiće.
U novoj školskoj godini ekološke namirnice bit će dostupne u 32 škole, odnosno u gotovo trećini svih gradskih škola, koje pohađa oko 16.000 učenika. Projekt se istodobno širi i na devet gradskih vrtića s približno 5000 djece. Ukupno će tako ekološkom hranom biti obuhvaćeno oko 21.000 djece", istaknuo je Tomašević.
"Ponosni smo što kao Grad možemo postavljati standarde za koje vjerujem da će slijediti i drugi hrvatski gradovi, ali i državna uprava", poručio je gradonačelnik na konferenciji za novinare. Istaknuo je da mu je to jedan od najdražih gradskih projekata jer donosi trostruku korist.
"Prva i najvažnija korist je za djecu, koje dobivaju kvalitetniju i zdraviju hranu poznatog podrijetla. Druga korist je za domaće proizvođače, kojima osiguravamo tržište, više od 90 posto hrane obuhvaćene ovim programom dolazi iz domaće proizvodnje.
Treća korist je za okoliš, jer ekološka poljoprivreda manje opterećuje tlo, a kraći put hrane do škola i vrtića znači manje emisija iz prijevoza", istaknuo je Tomašević. Od prvih isporuka ekoloških jabuka u studenome 2024. godine projekt je znatno proširen te danas obuhvaća nabavu 49 različitih ekoloških proizvoda.
Na jelovnicima su voće, povrće, jaja, med...
Na jelovnicima se tako nalaze svježe voće i povrće, jaja, med, maslinovo ulje, kruh, voćni namazi i proizvodi od žitarica. Istaknuto je da je za jačanje nabave ekološke hrane od 2024. do ove godine osigurano 1,2 milijuna eura, a za razdoblje od 2027. do 2029. planirano je dodatnih 2 milijuna eura.
"Sve je više škola i vrtića koji žele biti uključeni, a posebno me veseli što o tome pitaju i roditelji. To pokazuje da prepoznaju vrijednost kvalitetnije i zdravije prehrane za djecu", poručio je Tomašević. Grad Zagreb planira nastaviti širiti projekt kako bi se u narednim godinama svim zainteresiranim školama, vrtićima i proizvođačima omogućilo uključivanje u nabavu lokalne ekološke hrane.

Bačić: Do kraja desetljeća riješit ćemo sve zaštićene najmoprimce
Potpredsjednik Vlade i ministar Branko Bačić obišao je u srijedu nekoliko lokacija namijenjenih stambenom zbrinjavanju zaštićenih najmoprimaca i istaknuo kako je dosad od 1300 potrebnih nekretnina riješen 391 zahtjev te da se svi zahtjevi planiraju riješiti do kraja desetljeća.
Država za potrebe zaštićenih najmoprimaca mora osigurati 1300 nekretnina, a do danas je riješen 391 zahtjev, rekao je ministar prostornog uređenja, graditeljstva i državne imovine.
Podsjetio je kako su zaštićeni najmoprimci od početka primjene Zakona o načinu izvršenja presuda Europskog suda za ljudska prava u skupini predmeta Statileo protiv Hrvatske i Odluke Ustavnog suda RH mogli birati isplatu umjesto stana, useljenje u državne stanove ili s vlasnicima stana dogovoriti nastavak najma ili otkup stana.
Kako je istaknuo, najveći broj zaštićenih najmoprimaca odlučio se za jednokratnu isplatu.
“Ovisno o broju članova kućanstva imali su značajne popuste i ljudi su preuzeli, odnosno imali su pravo i ministarstvo ih je isplatilo u potpunosti”, rekao je Bačić.
Dio se odlučio za useljenje u stanove u vlasništvu države, a do konačnog rješenja plaćat će vrlo povoljnu najamninu u iznosu od dva eura po metru četvornom. Pružena im je i mogućnost da po vrlo povoljnoj cijeni taj stan otkupe, što je i slučaj sa stanom od 67 kvadrata u Zagrebu.
“Otprilike je cijena tog stana, po tim povoljnim uvjetima 74.000 eura, što je, složit ćete se, u današnje vrijeme i s obzirom na cijene u Zagrebu, više nego povoljno”, istaknuo je ministar.
Dodao je kako je plan da do kraja desetljeća u potpunosti riješe svih 1300 zahtjeva.
“U ovom trenutku državne nekretnine uređuju 355 stanova. Završili su ih 121, od toga 56 u Zagrebu i tim ćemo intenzitetom nastaviti kako bi što je moguće više naših sugrađana koji su zaštićeni najmoprimci uselili u takve stanove”, poručio je Bačić navodeći kako najviše zahtjeva ima u Zagrebu, Splitu i Dubrovniku.
Stanovi se grade u Zagrebu i Splitu
Na lokaciji Blato u Zagrebu trenutno se gradi višestambena zgrada sa 152 stana. Ravnatelj APN-a Dragan Hristov rekao je kako je planirano useljenje za godinu dana.
“Riječ je o zahtjevom objektu neto površine oko 9000 kvadrata. Imat će pet etaža, prizemlje, kat i tri etaže. Vrijednost ovog projekta je oko 20 milijuna eura, uključujući i infrastrukturu i priključke koje treba izvesti, a za to se obvezao Grad Zagreb", istaknuo je Hristov. Nada se da će Zagreb na vrijeme reagirati i svoj dio posla obaviti.
I u Splitu se gradi zgrada od 60-ak stanova koja bi trebala biti dovršena i useljena najkasnije početkom iduće godine.
Na novinarsko pitanje koliko će cijeli proces rješavanja stambenog pitanja za zaštićene najmoprimce stajati, ministar je odgovorio kako to ovisi o lokaciji jer cijena nije ista u Zagrebu, na kontinentu ili na obali.
“S druge strane variraju danas i cijene izgradnje, tako da u ovom trenutku ne mogu dati točan podatak, ali evo ova 152 stana je 20 milijuna eura. Ne možemo to pomnožiti sa osam pa da dođemo na tisuću tristo. To bi bilo negdje oko dvjesto milijuna eura, ali ja mislim da neće biti ni puno manje na kraju od toga svega”, rekao je Bačić ističući kako se sve financira iz državnog proračuna.
Do kraja godine planira se ponuditi i dijelom useliti još oko 107 stanova.
Upitan koliko bi se državnih stanova moglo staviti u funkciju za zaštićene najmoprimce, ministar je odgovorio da je 121 završen, a njih 240 se trenutno obnavljaju ili su u projektiranju
"Bili bi najsretniji kada bi svih ovih 1300 zaštićenih najmoprimaca mogli smjestiti u državne stanove koje obnavljamo. Ali nažalost, toliko stanova nemamo. Radi se o tome što imamo dosta državnih stanova tamo gdje nema zaštićenih najmoprimaca i nije ista jedinica lokalne samouprave, a mi smo prihvatili i zakon je to definirao da morate i trebate po zakonu ponuditi zaštićenim najmoprimcima nekretninu na području jedinice lokalne samouprave na kojoj žive", pojasnio se ministar.
Kakvo je tvoje mišljenje o ovome?

title: How a teacake tycoon helped to save a village's lifeboat station
content:
How a teacake tycoon helped to save a village's lifeboat station
- Published
A decade ago there was a day of celebration in the little Borders coastal village of St Abbs that they will never forget.
The RNLI closed its lifeboat station in 2015 - bringing a 104-year association to an end - saying there was no clear need for it with one nearby in Eyemouth.
The community rallied round to raise the money needed to bring a boat back and found a surprise ally in the shape of the teacake tycoon Sir Boyd Tunnock.
Just a year later, the Thomas Tunnock lifeboat, named in honour of the businessman's late brother and grandfather, was launched to great acclaim.
- Teacakes toasted at lifeboat launch - Published17 September 2016

- Lifeboat link ends after 104 years - Published8 September 2015

The story of the lifeboat station at St Abbs started with tragedy.
In October 1907 the cargo vessel Alfred Erlandsen struck nearby rocks and the villagers who gathered at the clifftop could only listen to their cries for help.
Accounts vary on how many perished; some say 17 including the captain's wife. The only survivor was his great Dane dog Karo which managed to swim ashore.
One of those who witnessed the shipwreck was women's rights campaigner and philanthropist Jane Hay who wrote to the Edinburgh Evening News:" I write to say that personally I shall never rest content till we have a lifeboat and rocket apparatus of our own in St Abbs."
Four years later, in August 1911, the RNLI established one there - the Helen Smitton - with the dog Karo, which had been involved in fundraising, said to have been among the guests who watched the boat arrive.
Over the course of the next century, the St Abbs lifeboat rescued hundreds of people but in 2015 it found itself in need of saving when the charity announced that, following an "extensive review", the service was to be withdrawn.
Cover from nearby Eyemouth was promised instead, but the plans sparked outcry with a petition against the move gathering about 13,000 signatures.
On 8 September 2015, the station closed - swiftly followed by an appeal to raise the £500,000 needed to fund an independent lifeboat.
That was where businessman Tunnock stepped in with a donation which, he said at the time, amounted to a "lot of caramel wafers".
He agreed to put £250,000 towards the boat and, barely a year after the old station closed, the new boat was officially launched.
Current operations manager, Barry Shaw, said that it had allowed them to carry on a service which was highly valued in the village and beyond.
"We've lost some of our old crew from 10 years ago, unfortunately, but we've got new members," he said.
"But the way the lifeboat operates is just in the same way as we were doing 10 years ago.
"We're still answering the calls from the coastguard and we're protecting the people who use the coast around our area."
He said the donation from Tunnock had allowed them to get the lifeboat "a lot quicker than was anticipated".
"Having a lifeboat still here and still operational, I think it's been a massive achievement from all the volunteers, not just the lifeboat crew," he added.
He said the station remained of huge importance to a "very small village".
"It sits right in the heart of the harbour," he said.
"It is still crewed by local people - our helms are local people.
"We've got a dive boat operator, we've got fishermen - they're still helming our boat.
"They know the water like nobody else."
He moved to the village in 2020 and was immediately "invited" to join the crew by neighbour Alistair Crowe - who had led the lifeboat appeal.
"It wasn't like there was an option really," recalled Shaw.
"I popped down, had a word with everybody and thought - I'd like to be part of this."
He started out as boat crew and has occupied a number of roles.
"Volunteering, obviously, you get tremendous satisfaction that you are doing a good job and you are there to help people that are in distress," he said.
He said they covered a wide range of callouts and the importance of the service went beyond its work out on the water.
"It isn't all about just going on the boat - it is about supporting our local community as well," he added.
- Published16 June 2020

title: Two men arrested by corrupt police officer finally have convictions quashed after 50 years
content:
Two men arrested by corrupt police officer finally have convictions quashed after 50 years
Ridgewell framed innocent young black men for his own crimes
- Bookmark
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Join todayAlready a member? Log in
Two men who were wrongfully arrested by a corrupt police officer have had theft convictions quashed after 50 years.
Christopher Poulter and Kevin Biggs were 21 and 18 respectively when they were convicted in 1976 of taking 13 mailbags from a wagon in Clapham goods yard in London.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) referred their case to the Court of Appeal earlier this year after new evidence about disgraced police officer Detective Sergeant Derek Ridgewell.
Ridgewell was jailed for seven years in 1980 after stealing more than £1 million in goods and was found to have framed innocent young black men for his own crimes, the CCRC said.
He was one of three officers said to have seen Mr Poulter and Mr Biggs taking the mailbags and fleeing by car.
The men’s defence was that they had been in a pub in Tooting, south London, all night, before being approached by officers and arrested.
At Inner London Crown Court, Mr Poulter was given a year in prison and Mr Biggs was sentenced to borstal training.
The innocence of Mr Biggs, who died in 2004, emerged through an investigation by the British Transport Police, who were searching for victims of Ridgewell.
He and Mr Poulter are the 14th and 15th people to have their convictions quashed in relation to Ridgewell’s misconduct.
They were convicted alongside a third man, Stephen Simmons, whose conviction was quashed in 2018.
At a hearing on Tuesday, Lord Justice Edis, sitting with Mr Justice Lavender and Mr Justice Linden, said their appeals should have been heard together.
He said: “It had not been possible to add any relatives of Mr Biggs, who had by then died, or find Mr Poulter, so they could be joined on to the appeal by Mr Simmons.”
He added: “The two appeals are allowed and the convictions quashed.”
Speaking after the hearing, Jenny Wiltshire, head of serious and general crime at Hickman and Rose and who has represented many of Ridgewell’s victims, said it was a “disgrace” that British Transport Police had taken so long to track people down.
She said: “It is now half a century since these two men were found guilty of a crime they did not commit.
“The British Transport Police knew for certain that the police officer whose evidence sent them to jail was corrupt just four years after they were convicted, and probably a lot earlier.
“The British Transport Police did nothing at the time; and have only relatively recently started to take this issue seriously.
“As a result of this inaction, Christopher Poulter has lived the majority of his life as a convicted criminal. Kevin Biggs died as one.”
A spokesperson from the British Transport Police previously said: “The corrupt actions of former DS Ridgewell were first brought to our attention in 2020 following the overturning of convictions, and our dedicated team continue to review historic investigations and convictions to establish whether there are any further potential victims of corruption.”
CCRC chairwoman Dame Vera Baird KC said: “It is absolutely right that these men have had their convictions quashed by the court today.
“Anyone else who believes they have been convicted through the actions of Derek Ridgewell should apply to us so we can investigate whether we can also refer your case to the courts.”

title: Vaping rates for schoolchildren appear to drop - is it falling out of favour?
content:
Vaping rates for schoolchildren appear to drop - is it falling out of favour?
- Published
For the first time in several years, the rates of vaping among schoolchildren in Wales appear to be falling.
The most recent data from a survey of more than 130,000 young people in secondary schools showed that across all age groups, habits are changing for both vaping and smoking.
Public health officials say the "significant fall" since 2023 coincides with the ban on disposable vapes being announced, though the impact of the law change is still being evaluated.
The findings are from the student health and well-being survey which has been carried out every two years by a research network made up of Public Health Wales, external, Cardiff University and the Welsh government.
Questions about vaping were added in 2017, and the survey carried out last year shows that 9,100 learners between Year 7 to 11 vape regularly, which is 3,200 fewer than 2023.
Meanwhile, the numbers smoking regularly have halved to 1,600.
The answers rely on self-reporting from young people, meaning the study depends on honesty and accurate recollection from participants, but it paints a snapshot of behaviours over nearly a decade.
Since the last survey in 2023, the proportion of learners in Years 7 to 11 who say they have tried a vape fell from 25.7% to 21%.
In the same period, the number who described themselves as regular vapers or smokers was much lower, and fell from 8% to 5.9%.
Officials said there has also been a faster drop in the numbers who said they smoke regularly, with the rate now just 1.8%.
So why are some young people turning away from vaping, after several years of the numbers going in the opposite direction?
Jay, 17, from Barry Sixth Form, in the Vale of Glamorgan, said he thinks his year group narrowly avoided the hype when vapes first became popular, but they are still far more popular among younger age groups.
"When we were in younger years (in school) it wasn't as common and so that's why I think a lot of people in our year feel like they don't need to do it," he said.
"Whereas I think younger people feel the peer pressure to do it, to fit in with their friend groups."
Amelie, also 17, said her peers in sixth form were more likely to be "more health conscious" which deters them from taking up vaping.
The figures also show higher rates of girls vaping than boys, despite the drop in numbers.
Amelie said colourful packaging was likely to play a part.
"I'd say it's because of the marketing and the product, colourful packages, flavours," she said.
"I'd say vaping is more targeted towards girls than boys."
But she added that lessons in school explaining the risks had been powerful.
She added: "Our school is very supportive, they've taken the correct steps to educate us, including the health education lessons, and they brought in a demonstration of what our lungs could look like - the 'popcorn' lung - so that helped."
Year 10 Whitmore High School student Harrison, 14, said he feels vaping has been normalised among younger people, and there can be pressure to vape.
As a keen footballer in Barry, the risks to his own health and his performance on the pitch have been big drivers for not vaping.
"Social media comes into it, a lot of people on Youtube and TikTok do it, they're smoking or vaping and people think that's cool to do," he said.
It's illegal for under-18s to buy the product, but he said access for some people wasn't difficult.
Anabella, 14, said she had definitely seen interest in vapes decline among her peers.
"I've seen a few people start to quit, people are starting to realise the health risks, and they're seeing the people they're around that do that sort of thing, aren't the people they should be around.
"Everyone was doing it so it was a trend, and now that it's died down, less people are starting in the first place."
Henriette Bertheux is responsible for personal and social education at Whitmore High, and said higher rates of boys being involved in extra-curricular sports was also likely to be a factor in fewer of them vaping, compared to girls.
At one point pupils were requesting frequent toilet trips as they would vape in pairs in the cubicles, which naturally also impacted their learning.
She said a combination of education around the health implications and tighter rules about how many children are allowed toilet breaks at once had helped reduce the problem.
"We had a year group that were targetted quite heavily when they were in year 7 and 8, it was coming on social media and they were susceptible to that," she said, adding that cohort had now left school
"We've definitely seen a drop in the younger years."
Mary-Ann McKibben from Public Health Wales said there had been a concerted effort from schools, public health agencies and government to curb vape use.
She said: "We've had the introduction of some quite strong legislation with the ban on disposable vapes last year and then a lot of publicity surrounding the Tobacco and Vapes Act, external that will be coming into place with restrictions on packaging, marketing and content and flavours of vapes going forward.
"That all influences behaviour change, together with a rising awareness of the harm that vapes can cause.
"Technically young people shouldn't be able to get hold of vapes through legitimate means if they're under 18, so often they are at risk of illicit products that are sold on the black market that may contain all sorts of contents that are even more toxic than the normal vapes.
"So be very, very careful in terms of what you're consuming because it could really damage your health."
She added it's also important that support is offered to young people who have been vaping nicotine products, because of their addictive qualities.

title: Jagtar Singh Johal granted bail nine years after being detained in India
content:
Jagtar Singh Johal granted bail nine years after being detained in India
- Published
A Scottish Sikh activist who has been locked up in India for almost nine years without conviction has been granted bail.
Jagtar Singh Johal, from Dumbarton, was arrested and detained in 2017 in connection with alleged terror offences.
The Indian authorities have accused him of having a role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures.
His family said they were still waiting for the details of what will happen next but are "relieved" by the Indian court's decision.
Court documents show Johal was granted bail at Delhi High Court.
As part of his bail conditions, he has to surrender his passport and is barred from speaking to the media about the case.
He must pay a personal bond of 500,000 rupees (£3,907) and is only allowed to access one phone.
The 39-year-old was acquitted last year in a case in which he was accused of financially supporting terror group the Khalistan Liberation Force (KLF), which has carried out attacks in the Punjab region.
But he still faces federal charges lodged by the Indian authorities.
Johal's imprisonment was recognised by a UN panel as arbitrary detention in 2022 and he has claimed to have been tortured.
Indian authorities have previously denied the torture claim and have repeatedly maintained due process is being followed.
He was arrested in the Punjab region just weeks after his wedding in the country.
His supporters say he was targeted for blogging about alleged human rights abuses against the Sikh community in India and was coerced into signing a false confession to participation in the killings.
His brother Gurpreet Singh Johal has lobbied successive governments calling for his brother's release.
"It is a really important milestone for Jagtar's campaign," Gurpreet told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme.
"It has been a long haul and an expensive rollercoaster but the community and the public have kept me going to campaign to bring Jagtar home.
"This will be a huge relief for him."
He added that while it is a major step and the family are relieved Jagtar can be at liberty, more work will be required to bring his brother back to Dumbarton.
"It is a momentous moment for the family, his wife has been crying since this morning," Gurpreet added.
"Everyone was joyful, my kids went to school saying they cannot wait to see their uncle coming home.
"It is just a first step, but it is a step in the right direction."
Gupreet previously urged the UK government to provide "diplomatic representation" to bring his activist brother home.
He described his last meeting, with then-Foreign secretary Yvette Cooper in December, as "disappointing".
At the time, a spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said concerns about Johal's "prolonged detention" were raised with the Indian government at every appropriate opportunity.
Johal was previously denied bail in 2024.
Johal's family have insisted that no concrete evidence has been presented against him.
They say the case was built on the testimony of unreliable witnesses, some of whom have given statements against him only for them to be later recanted in court.
'Flawed proceedings'
First Minister John Swinney said it was a "significant and positive development".
"I hope to see Mr Johal released from custody as soon as the necessary procedures are completed and continue to underline the importance of a fair, transparent and timely judicial process," he added.
Johal is represented in the UK by the legal charities Redress and Reprieve, which have welcomed the judgement.
Reprieve's deputy executive director Dan Dolan said the news was welcome but Johal still faces the death penalty for "trumped up charges".
He said: "We must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way.
"The conditions attached are likely to be onerous."
Redress senior legal advisor Chris Esdaile said granting bail "can't undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention".
He added: "The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent."

title: From old railways to an oasis of art, food and nature: how an eco-park was born in Greater Manchester
content:
Standing in the open green space of Northern Roots, it is hard to imagine the landscape as it once was.
Two cotton mills, two coalmines and an industrial railway once occupied this 65-hectare (160-acre) site in Oldham, Greater Manchester. Later, about 24 hectares became a tip, with much of the space left to nature.
Over the past five years, Northern Roots, a charity, has been developing this once industrial land, running community programmes including a Natural Health Service.
On 19 September a new facility will open to the public, featuring a cafe, shop, production kitchen, performance space, forestry skills centre, outdoor play areas and an urban farm. The charity’s ambition is to turn what was once a “burden” into the UK’s largest urban farm and eco-park.
The idea began with Oldham council, which wanted to explore green space as an asset. Today the council works in a unique partnership with Northern Roots.
“We wanted to look at what this land could do for Oldham, rather than simply seeing it as land that needed maintaining,” said Anna da Silva, the founder and chief executive of Northern Roots.
The charity’s seven activity programmes, which include farming and food, arts and culture, sports, business and learning, have been designed to appeal widely.
“The hardest part is getting people … physically and psychologically out of their house, down to the site, meeting people where they are on that journey,” said da Silva.
Once they are through the doors, the aim is to encourage continued engagement so they can unlock the environmental, economic and social benefits – a challenge that led to the creation of “participation pathways”.
This philosophy is perhaps best demonstrated by Faiza Awan and Louise Gibbs, who both grew up in the area and became involved with Northern Roots as community champions. Awan said: “It’s really important to have something for everyone.”
Gibbs added: “There’s just so many doors to come in through Northern Roots, and then to continue development.”
Both now have roles as Natural Health Service guardians. Unlike green social prescribing programmes that are centred on exercise or gardening, Northern Roots’ Natural Health Service focuses on intentional connection with nature. In doing so, it embodies the wider aims of creating opportunities for people who might not otherwise come together.
The site sits between two different and historically divided communities, and its outdoor setting helps to make it a space where people feel able to participate. “It’s a very welcoming, inviting environment,” said Gibbs. “With it being outside, people automatically feel comfort.”
Awan said: “There’s something really levelling and very democratic about doing things outside in nature,” adding that it could create a sense of belonging that might be harder to achieve in other settings.
The importance of connection is reflected in the relationship between the community and the site. Gibbs said: “Because [people] are local they feel more connected to the space … it’s giving the ownership to the community.”
The Natural Health Service was commissioned through Northern Roots by NHS England. It launched in 2023 as a six-month pilot with patients from the Hill Top GP surgery in Fitton Hill. It now works with healthcare providers to support people experiencing mental health challenges.
A session may involve foraging, bushcraft, making something from natural materials or simply noticing what is around you. The principle is that being outside, in an environment without the clinical associations of a healthcare setting, can create room to slow down.
Gibbs said: “People might come in and they might be flustered from the morning, the school run or the next 10 things they need to do, but we really encourage people to slow down, to take that breath, to give themselves permission, to spend this time on themselves and to simply just be in this space.”
Independent NHS research published in 2025 found that participants in Northern Roots’ Natural Health Service improved their wellbeing scores by an average of 8.15 points on the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale, a seven-item questionnaire used to measure a person’s recent wellbeing. The project generated an estimated £4,940 in social value per participant.
However, the benefits extend beyond metrics. “You can’t put it in facts and figures, in black and white,” said Gibbs. “Seeing someone’s eyes light up when they’ve said they have not been out for years. They’re excited to come the next week.” The benefits were mutual, she added. “It makes me feel good within myself, seeing that person is happy in that moment.”
Northern Roots is intended to be a model for others. “There are bits of land like this all over the place,” said da Silva. “They’re seen as a problem. We have got an approach to evaluating the place where you are, the site that you have, the needs of the community, the opportunities within the site.”
Northern Roots aims to attract 300,000 visitors a year by 2030, dispense hundreds of Natural Health Service social prescriptions – connecting people to non-medical community-based services – and create employment and training opportunities.
The idea that land can be a resource is part of Northern Roots’ wider proposition: that urban green space should be treated as critical infrastructure in the same way as hospitals and schools. Da Silva said it should be seen as “part of an arsenal of tools that can be used to address issues and support communities”.
The challenge is not simply to demonstrate what the land can provide, but to build the case for investment to make that possible.
“We need commissioners to invest in these spaces in the same way they would built infrastructure,” said da Silva. The aim is to show that relatively modest investment in land can help to reduce pressure on other public services.
For da Silva, however, the value of the project is not only in what it can deliver for public services. It is also in how it changes people’s relationship with the land. The ambition is to change “the way people feel about a place, themselves and their place in that place”.

human_wellbeing_impact.evidence: It now works with healthcare providers to support people experiencing mental health challenges.

social_cohesion_impact.evidence: The site sits between two different and historically divided communities, and its outdoor setting helps to make it a space where people feel able to participate.

evidence_level.evidence: It launched in 2023 as a six-month pilot with patients from the Hill Top GP surgery in Fitton Hill. It now works with healthcare providers to support people experiencing mental health challenges.

benefit_distribution.evidence: The charity’s seven activity programmes, which include farming and food, arts and culture, sports, business and learning, have been designed to appeal widely.

title: Compensation payments to doctors extended to almost all regions of Kyrgyzstan
content:
Starting January 1, 2026, compensation payments for doctors in high-demand specialties are provided in populated areas across Kyrgyzstan, except Bishkek and Osh. This is stipulated in a Cabinet of Ministers resolution regarding payment terms for medical professionals.
The measure applies to pediatricians, neonatologists, general surgeons, and anesthesiologists-resuscitation specialists. Doctors must work in their primary positions at healthcare organizations included in a registry approved by the Ministry of Health and sign the relevant agreement. The compensation payment amounts to 22,222.5 soms for no more than one position.
Until the end of 2025, the payment was designated for specialists working in remote areas, small towns and rural communities. The new resolution expands the geographical scope of the measure.
Clinical residents and interns undergoing postgraduate training at medical organizations outside Bishkek and Osh are eligible for a monthly stipend of 20,000 soms. The stipend is paid under a contract with the authorized healthcare body that requires recipients to subsequently work in the local areas.
For emergency medical doctors in Bishkek and Osh, the resolution provides compensation of 22,222.5 soms for special working conditions. This payment has been in place for this category since July 1, 2024.
The document also sets out payment conditions for the period from July 1, 2024, through December 31, 2025, and repeals Resolution No. 441 of July 31, 2024. The new resolution is subject to official publication; the text specifies that it applies retroactively to arrangements starting July 1, 2024.

title: A long lost cousin who was dying of cancer found me online and saved my life
content:
Cancer has always been present in my life. It pretty much wiped out most of my father’s side of the family – my grandfather in his 50s, my grandmother in her 70s, one aunt when she was in her 30s and a second one before she turned 60.
So, when my dad was diagnosed in 2015 with pancreatic cancer, I knew, from the outset, that the news was not good. He was a larger-than-life, strong-as-an-ox character and, within a few weeks of diagnosis, was a shadow of himself. He died just eight weeks later and it left us all in a state of utter shock.
I hadn’t really joined up the dots before losing my dad, but it now felt clear that cancer was a disease which was prevalent in the family and we might have an inherited risk. I tried to be proactive. I went to see my GP, who referred me for a series of scans. I was relieved to discover that nothing sinister was lurking beneath the surface.
Cases have emerged where officers have encountered vapes containing THC, the primary psychoactive compound in cannabis, and the synthetic drug spice, alongside the use of high doses of common medications such as antihistamines and travel-sickness tablets.
We’re seeing offenders use a wider range of substances than ever before, including everyday medications and substances added to vapes, while increasingly targeting victims in private settings such as homes, parties and student accommodation
Metropolitan police spiking lead Detective Superintendent Dan Thompson
How widespread is the issue?
Over the past year, more than 2,700 spiking-related offences were reported to the Met, but only 131 resulted in a charge, caution or summons.
This marked a 20 per cent increase over the previous year.
More than half the victims were aged 18 to 35.
A YouGov poll from December 2022 found that 10 per cent of women and 5 per cent of men said they had had a drink spiked.

The four key moments from Burnham’s meeting with Trump
Caroline Wheeler
Political Editor
There was no shortage of trip-wires that could have derailed Andy Burnham’s first meeting with Donald Trump, but in the end, it produced remarkably little friction.
Even without the charm offensive, Trump liked Burnham better than Starmer
In July, when Trump met Sir Keir Starmer at the Nato summit in Turkey after he had announced his resignation, the US President said he wanted to “bring him back” and “make him great again”.
Two months on, that affection has evaporated. Asked about a special relationship that has been up and down, Trump said things were “more up than they were under your last prime minister”.
politics
No Trump attack on UK migration policy
Trump has previously said Britain is “on the edge of disaster” because of “insane” immigration policies, but in New York, he called it “a worldwide situation”.
For a Labour Prime Minister under pressure on small boats, being spared a public rebuke on his first outing is significant.
Trump has previously called the UK “essentially bankrupt” for refusing to fully exploit North Sea oil and for relying on green energy. He has also claimed the country is “dying” under alleged mass migration.
This time he said Britain had “tremendous potential” and compared it favourably with other countries whose leaders he meets but in which he sees little promise.
Many expected Washington to condemn Britain’s sanctions on illegal West Bank settlements.
When asked directly, Trump did not engage. He said he did not know about the move and left the question for Burnham to answer.
It was an odd moment, but a useful one for No 10. A US president who wanted to punish Britain had an open invitation to do so and passed it up.

How the licence fee could be scrapped for a new monthly charge
Adam Sherwin
Arts and Media Correspondent
The licence fee could be axed and replaced by an £11-a-month internet levy – and viewers invited to become “BBC members” – under new proposals.
BBC facing funding crisis
The licence fee is becoming increasingly unsustainable, with 3.7 million households claiming to not need one, while half a million households stopped paying last year, forcing the BBC to find £500m in cuts.
A report from the Social Market Foundation warns the BBC would have to axeCelebrity Traitors if the corporation’s public funding is slashed.
‘Home internet levy’ fairest solution
A “home internet levy” method of funding is most likely to command public consent, the report, commissioned by campaign organisation 38 Degrees, found.
A BBC internet levy would cost £11 per month, an average increase of 35 per cent on the current cost of internet bills, but would be £4 a month cheaper than the current licence fee.
The report also proposed radical changes to make the BBC more accountable to the public by becoming a “mutual-style membership” organisation.
Members would be chosen by lottery to take part in a member council, where they would serve terms of up to three years and be paid for their time.
They would “hold the board of the BBC to account, ensuring that the organisation is meeting its duties to the public”.
Under the proposals, the council would have no control over editorial decisions, hiring talent or decisions on programming.
