title: Breaking the Yield Ceiling, Recasting a Continent’s Food Future: Ethiopia’s Agricultural Ascent
content:
Breaking the Yield Ceiling, Recasting a Continent’s Food Future: Ethiopia’s Agricultural Ascent
Addis Ababa, September 21, 2026 (FMC) — For much of the modern era, Ethiopia entered the global food conversation from the wrong end of the equation.
Its name was repeatedly associated with famine, drought, food shortages and appeals for assistance. The country’s agricultural potential was immense, yet the distance between potential and production remained one of the defining constraints on its development.
That equation is now being challenged—not by rhetoric, but by a widening body of production, irrigation, mechanization, diversification and environmental restoration that is changing the scale and direction of Ethiopia’s agricultural story.
The most visible break with the past has come through wheat.
In a transformation that has unfolded with remarkable speed, irrigated wheat cultivation expanded from only 20,000 hectares in 2020 to 3.5 million hectares in 2025.
Wheat production from both rainy- and dry-season cultivation reached 280 million quintals in 2025, according to Ethiopia’s Ministry of Agriculture.
The country says it fully replaced an estimated 2.6 million quintals of wheat previously imported annually, saving about 1 billion US dollars a year in foreign exchange.
What makes the wheat story consequential is not simply the size of the harvest. It is the change in the production system behind it.
Irrigation has pushed cultivation beyond the traditional limits imposed by rainfall. Heat-tolerant varieties have opened new production possibilities in hotter lowland environments.
Mechanization, improved seed, soil management, agricultural research, extension services and organized production have increasingly been brought together around a single objective: turning agricultural potential into dependable productive capacity.
The transformation has already moved beyond import substitution.
In February 2023, Ethiopia made its first international wheat exports. FAO Director-General QU Dongyu subsequently described the country’s wheat self-sufficiency programme as a source of inspiration in Africa and globally, while urging Ethiopia to share its experience with other African countries.
That distinction matters.
A country that once had to look outward to fill part of its wheat requirement has increasingly been able to look inward for supply—and then outward again, this time as a potential supplier.
It is a movement from deficit to capacity.
And wheat is only one field in a much larger agricultural landscape.
According to a 2026 government review, overall agricultural output increased from 41.7 million tons to around 150 million tons over seven years.
Cluster farming has expanded to 9.5 million farmers across 12.8 million hectares, with reported gains of 29 percent in productivity and 18 percent in income. Crop diversification has accelerated, while coffee production has nearly doubled to around one million tons, generating about 2.65 billion US dollars in export earnings in 2024/25.
The transformation is also reaching beyond crops.
Under the Yelemat Tirufat, or Bounty of the Basket, initiative, Ethiopia has been expanding livestock, poultry, fisheries and beekeeping alongside crop production.
The Ministry of Agriculture reports annual milk production rising from 5.8 billion litres in 2022 to 11.7 billion litres in 2026, reflecting a broader effort to turn livestock assets into productive food systems, household income and commercial value chains.
In this emerging architecture, agriculture is no longer being treated simply as the sector that feeds the population.
It is increasingly being positioned as a foundation for industrialization, foreign-exchange generation, rural transformation, employment and economic resilience.
That is where the language of food security begins to meet the language of sovereignty.
Food security concerns whether people can access sufficient food.
Food sovereignty raises a deeper question: how much of that food can a country produce through its own land, knowledge, technology, infrastructure, farmers and institutions, and how resilient is that productive system when international markets are disrupted?
The experience of recent years has made that question impossible to ignore.
Pandemics, wars, disrupted supply chains, fertilizer shocks, food-price volatility and climate extremes have demonstrated that dependence on distant supply chains can quickly become an economic and strategic vulnerability.
For Ethiopia, expanding domestic production therefore carries significance well beyond the farm gate.
Every tonne of wheat produced domestically can reduce import exposure. Every irrigated hectare can extend the productive season.
Every improved seed variety can raise the return on land and water. Every new agro-processing connection can move value closer to the source. Every rural production cluster can create a stronger bridge between the farmer and the wider economy.
This is the logic behind the country’s growing emphasis on agricultural value chains rather than production alone.
It is also why the transformation is increasingly connected to Africa’s own search for food sovereignty.
The African Development Bank has described Ethiopia’s wheat experience as exemplary in the continent’s effort to raise agricultural productivity, while its climate-resilient wheat programme in Ethiopia brings together improved seed, irrigation, soil health, mechanization, post-harvest infrastructure and market access.
The continental wheat workshop now being held in Addis Ababa adds another dimension to that trajectory.
The gathering brings together agricultural policymakers, researchers, seed companies, regulators, farmer organizations and development partners to examine Ethiopia’s experience alongside the broader challenge of accelerating sustainable wheat transformation across Africa.
The emphasis on national seed systems and access to quality seed is especially revealing.
A transformation of this scale cannot depend indefinitely on one breakthrough crop or one production campaign. Its durability rests on science, breeding, seed multiplication, soil health, irrigation, mechanization, extension, finance, storage, markets and the capacity to continuously adapt agricultural systems to changing climates.
In other words, Ethiopia’s agricultural ascent is increasingly becoming a question of agricultural systems engineering.
The yield ceiling is not being challenged by a single intervention.
It is being challenged by changing the system beneath the yield.
And nowhere is that more visible than in landscapes where agriculture itself has changed its geographical boundaries.
In Ethiopia’s lowlands, including areas once regarded primarily through pastoral production systems, irrigation and heat-tolerant wheat varieties have created new possibilities for crop production.
The African Development Bank has documented the rapid expansion of irrigated wheat into Ethiopia’s hot, dry lowlands and linked the transformation to improved varieties, irrigation and technology.
This does not mean that pastoralism has ceased to matter, nor that every arid landscape can simply be converted into cropland.
The significance lies elsewhere: agricultural geography is no longer being treated as fixed.
Water, technology, science and infrastructure can alter the productive possibilities of a landscape.
That principle reaches beyond wheat.
It connects directly with another transformation that has become inseparable from Ethiopia’s development narrative: Green Legacy.
Since its launch in 2019, the initiative has turned environmental restoration into a nationwide undertaking. In 2026 alone, Ethiopia planted 805.3 million seedlings in a single 12-hour campaign with the participation of more than 26.2 million people.
By September, cumulative planting under the initiative had reached 56.8 billion seedlings over eight years, according to Ethiopia’s reported figures.
The significance of Green Legacy for agriculture lies beneath the visible canopy.
Soil, water, forests, watersheds, biodiversity and agricultural productivity are not separate systems. Degraded land erodes productive capacity; degraded watersheds undermine water security; soil loss weakens agricultural resilience.
Conversely, restoration can strengthen the ecological foundations on which farming depends.
Ethiopia’s 2026 National Regenerative Agriculture Strategy reflects this broader understanding, placing soil health, biodiversity and water management at the centre of efforts to build a more sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural system.
This is where the country’s agricultural and environmental narratives converge.
The field and the forest are no longer two unrelated stories.
One produces food.
The other helps protect the ecological conditions that make future production possible.
Together, they form part of a longer national attempt to turn land from a constraint into an asset—and vulnerability into productive resilience.
The international recognition that has accompanied the transformation is therefore significant, but perhaps more revealing as a marker than as an endpoint.
In January 2024, FAO awarded Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed the Agricola Medal, its highest award conferred by the Director-General.
FAO linked the recognition specifically to contributions to rural and economic development, the Wheat for Food Self-Sufficiency programme and Green Legacy. FAO’s Director-General said Ethiopia’s wheat self-sufficiency experience was an inspiration in Africa and globally and described the country’s experience as a model other countries could follow.
Recognition matters because it shows that the transformation is no longer being discussed only within Ethiopia.
But the more consequential measure is what happens when a national agricultural experiment becomes a reference point for continental problem-solving.
Africa has vast agricultural land, a young population and enormous potential, yet remains exposed to food imports and global supply shocks.
The African Union’s development ambitions, including the goals of Agenda 2063, ultimately depend not only on roads, markets and trade agreements, but on the productive capacity to feed African populations and generate value from African resources.
Agricultural surplus therefore carries a meaning larger than the surplus itself.
It can feed cities.
Supply industry.
Reduce import pressure.
Generate exports.
Strengthen rural incomes.
Support regional trade.
And alter the balance between what a country consumes and what it is capable of producing.
That is why Ethiopia’s wheat story has acquired a continental dimension.
The significance is not that one country has solved every food-security challenge. It has not. Ethiopia continues to face climate pressures, regional disparities, production constraints and food-security needs, while the agricultural system itself remains a work in progress.
The significance is that a country with one of Africa’s most powerful agricultural potentials is attempting to convert that potential into scale—and is doing so through a combination of irrigation, science, technology, production reform, environmental restoration and market development.
The old image of Ethiopia was often framed around the question of how much food the country needed from elsewhere.
The emerging question is increasingly different:
How much can Ethiopia produce?
How much more can it produce?
How far can its agricultural frontier extend?
How much value can be created from the harvest?
And how much of that experience can travel across Africa?
Those questions point toward a different national trajectory.
The harvest is becoming more than a harvest.
It is becoming infrastructure for food sovereignty.
The irrigation canal is becoming more than a waterway.
It is becoming an instrument for extending the productive calendar.
The improved seed is becoming more than an agricultural input.
It is becoming a piece of technological sovereignty.
The restored landscape is becoming more than environmental repair.
It is becoming part of the productive foundation of the future.
And the wheat field—once part of an import equation—is increasingly becoming a measure of what happens when science, water, land, policy and productive ambition converge.
Ethiopia’s agricultural ascent is therefore not simply a story of growing more.
It is a story of changing the ceiling.
And as that ceiling rises, so does the horizon of what Ethiopia can contribute to Africa’s search for a food-secure, productive and increasingly self-reliant future.
By Mesafint Brlie

title: ÉDUCATION - Un campus numérique privé pour des bacheliers
content: Des autorités locales de Toliara ont assisté à l’inauguration du campus numérique de l’association ABC Domino.Développer les compétences numériques. Depuis 20 ans, l’association « ABC Domino » œuvre dans le domaine de l’éducation en développant des écoles, collèges et lycées privés à Efoetse, Beheloke et Itampolo, sur le littoral Sud de Toliara. Elle poursuit aujourd’hui son engagement avec l’ouverture d’un nouveau campus numérique à Toliara.L’infrastructure, fraîchement réhabilitée, est sise au boulevard Luautey, au bord de la mer de Toliara. Le campus peut accueillir cent vingt bacheliers et étudiants et offre un cadre moderne pour un établissement d’enseignement. Le campus dispose notamment de salles équipées d’ordinateurs et d’écrans géants, de bureaux, de salles de réunion, d’espaces de détente ainsi que d’une cafétéria.L’inauguration officielle, organisée vendredi dernier, a vu la présence du président international de l’association, Yves Cohen, venu de France pour marquer l’importance qu’il accorde à ce projet. « Ce campus permet à nos élèves d’avoir accès à des compléments de formation à Toliara, une fois qu’ils ont obtenu leur baccalauréat au lycée d’Efoetse. En attendant leur inscription à l’université de Toliara, ils pourront développer leurs compétences numériques, vu l’importance du numérique dans le monde actuellement », a-t-il expliqué dans son discours.OuverturePour l’heure, ce nouvel espace consacré à l’apprentissage et à l’inclusion numérique est réservé aux bacheliers du lycée d’ABC Domino. Chaque année, il accueillera les nouveaux bacheliers. Même après leur entrée à l’université, les étudiants pourront continuer à fréquenter le campus si leurs facultés ne disposent pas d’espaces connectés.Le campus leur permettra également de renforcer leurs compétences linguistiques en français et en anglais. « Il s’agit de leur faire expérimenter les langues d’une manière un peu plus soutenue que ce qu’ils ont appris en brousse et pourront ainsi affronter le monde du travail », explique pour sa part Rachel Rakotoson, présidente de l’association à Madagascar. À elle de souligner que le campus n’est pas encore destiné à servir de logement pour les étudiants. La mise en place de ce campus numérique constitue une nouvelle étape pour l’association qui scolarise près de quatre mille enfants au sein de six écoles primaires, trois collèges et un lycée, dans le district de Toliara II et d’Ampanihy, où l’accès à des infrastructures de qualité reste limité. Dans un futur proche, le campus numérique ouvrira des formations en langues et en compétences numériques aux ONG et entreprises locales qui souhaitent améliorer les compétences linguistiques et informatiques.Mirana Ihariliva

title: Free flu antiviral drug plan extended
content:
As the domestic influenza epidemic enters its peak season and continues to escalate, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) yesterday announced that publicly funded influenza antiviral drugs for seven eligible groups have been extended to Oct. 31, allowing those who develop flu-like symptoms to receive the medication without undergoing a rapid influenza test.
The CDC has extended the expanded use of flu antiviral drugs to seven groups: healthcare and influenza-prevention personnel; residents and staff at nursing homes, long-term care facilities and similar institutions; kindergarten and daycare workers and home-based caregivers; students from kindergarten through high school, vocational high school and the first three years of junior colleges; people who live with or care for those at high risk of severe influenza; livestock and poultry farmers, zoo workers and animal disease-prevention personnel; and personnel in densely populated areas such as military camps where clusters are likely to occur.
The state-funded antiviral medicines are Tamiflu and Eraflu, both oseltamivir drugs, and have been distributed to about 4,000 contracted medical institutions nationwide, the CDC said.
Photo: Taipei Times
People who meet the eligibility requirements and develop flu-like symptoms do not need to take a rapid influenza test beforehand. Doctors can prescribe the drugs based on the patient’s condition and their clinical judgement, the CDC said.
The necessity of administering free antiviral drugs and the timing of treatment are also to be determined by doctors, it said.
The CDC said that influenza can cause serious complications and urged people to seek medical attention as soon as possible if they develop symptoms such as rapid breathing, difficulty breathing, cyanosis, bloody sputum, chest pain, altered consciousness or low blood pressure.
The CDC advised people to wash their hands frequently, practice good cough etiquette and wear a mask when they have respiratory symptoms.
Students with flu-like symptoms should seek medical attention and get plenty of rest, returning to school only after they have recovered to prevent the virus from spreading among classmates.

title: Ethiopia’s Fields Are Becoming a Laboratory for Africa’s Next Agricultural Revolution
content:
Ethiopia’s Fields Are Becoming a Laboratory for Africa’s Next Agricultural Revolution
Addis Ababa, September 21, 2026 (FMC) — Some agricultural transformations are measured in harvests. Others are measured in the number of assumptions they force an entire sector to reconsider.
Across Ethiopia, an increasingly important experiment has been unfolding not inside a single research station or demonstration plot, but across millions of hectares: what happens when improved varieties, irrigation, mechanization, cluster farming, extension systems, climate information and new production practices are taken from the laboratory and pushed toward national scale?
The answer is beginning to reshape the country’s agricultural trajectory—and to attract attention well beyond its borders.
The transformation is particularly visible in wheat. Ethiopia’s rapid expansion of irrigated wheat production brought together several elements that are often treated separately in agricultural development: heat-tolerant varieties, irrigation, improved agronomic practices, organized production, research, extension and market linkages. By 2023, heat-tolerant irrigated wheat production had reached about one million hectares, with average productivity of around four tonnes per hectare, according to research documented through the FAO agricultural knowledge platform. The approach was identified as having potential relevance for wider African food-security efforts.
That is what makes the Ethiopian experience more consequential than a single crop story.
The country has increasingly been using agriculture as a field for systems integration—bringing technologies, institutions and production models together and testing what happens when they operate at scale.
Cluster farming is one such experiment. Rather than leaving millions of smallholders to confront modern agricultural markets and technologies individually, production is increasingly organized around coordinated areas and common production practices. Ethiopia says its cluster-farming system now involves about 9.5 million farmers cultivating 12.8 million hectares, with reported gains in productivity and farmer incomes.
Irrigation represents another major shift.
For generations, much of Ethiopian agriculture has been tied closely to the rhythm of seasonal rainfall. Expanding irrigation changes that equation by allowing farmers to manage water rather than simply wait for it. It can create additional production seasons, diversify crops and reduce exposure to erratic rainfall. The World Bank has identified irrigation as a central pathway for increasing agricultural productivity and strengthening food security in Ethiopia, including through multiple cropping seasons and greater production of diverse and drought-resistant crops.
The significance is not simply that more land is being irrigated.
It is that the production calendar itself can be redesigned.
The same logic extends to seeds. Improved varieties adapted to different agro-ecological conditions—including heat-tolerant wheat—are allowing production systems to move into environments once considered considerably more difficult. Research on Ethiopia’s irrigated wheat expansion has highlighted the role of improved varieties, cluster farming, research institutions, extension services and private-sector actors in bringing these technologies together at scale.
Mechanization adds another layer.
Agricultural modernization cannot be reduced to putting tractors into fields. It involves changing the economics and timing of land preparation, planting, harvesting, threshing, transport and post-harvest handling. Ethiopia’s agricultural development priorities explicitly include expanding mechanization alongside irrigation, horticulture, private-sector participation and institutional capacity.
And increasingly, the experiment is becoming digital.
Weather and climate information, for example, can become a production input in its own right. Research involving Ethiopian farming households found that access to weather and climate services was associated with productivity increases of 27 percent for maize and 17 percent for wheat, underscoring the potential value of information alongside physical inputs such as fertilizer and improved seed.
Taken together, these developments point toward a different understanding of agricultural innovation.
The important question is no longer only whether Ethiopia can produce a better seed, introduce a new machine, expand irrigation or teach a better farming technique. The larger question is whether these components can be assembled into a functioning production system and reproduced at national scale.
That is where Ethiopia’s agricultural experience becomes potentially continental in significance.
Africa does not lack agricultural potential. It has land, water, diverse agro-ecologies, a vast farming population and enormous domestic and regional markets. What has often been missing is the capacity to convert those assets consistently into productivity, reliable supply, commercial value and food-system resilience.
Ethiopia’s ongoing experiment is therefore less about discovering one magical agricultural solution than about testing how several solutions can work together.
Its emerging model is built around a simple but powerful proposition: productivity can be engineered.
Water can be managed. Production seasons can be extended. Varieties can be adapted. Farms can be organized. Information can reach farmers. Machinery can reduce bottlenecks. Research can feed directly into production. Markets can pull output through the value chain.
None of these changes eliminates the country’s agricultural challenges. Ethiopia still faces droughts, floods, pests, conflict-related disruptions, market constraints and serious food-security problems in vulnerable areas. FAO continues to report significant food-security pressures, particularly in pastoral regions affected by climatic and economic shocks.
But precisely because the challenges remain, the scale of the agricultural experiment matters.
Ethiopia is testing whether a predominantly smallholder agricultural economy can progressively move from vulnerability toward greater productivity, diversification and resilience without waiting for every constraint to disappear first.
That makes the Ethiopian countryside something more than the traditional backdrop to a national development story.
It is becoming a living testing ground for African agricultural transformation.
The most consequential harvest may therefore not be measured only in tonnes of wheat, maize, coffee or other crops. It may be measured in knowledge: which technologies work in which environments, which production systems can scale, which institutional arrangements improve farmer productivity, and which combinations can turn Africa’s enormous agricultural potential into dependable food and economic capacity.
If those lessons can travel—from Ethiopia’s irrigated lowlands to other African production zones, from research institutions to farmers, and from individual crops to entire food systems—the experiment taking place in Ethiopian fields could ultimately become part of something much larger.
Not simply an agricultural transformation in one country.
A laboratory for the continent.

title: ÉDUCATION - La Fondation Axian inaugure sa 250e école
content: À Ambahikily, dans le district de Morombe, région Atsimo-Andrefana, l’École primaire publique (EPP) fait peau neuve. Les infrastructures vétustes de l’établissement, dont un vieil bâtiment datant de l’année 1925 et déjà au bord de l’effondrement, ont été réhabilitées. De nouvelles salles ont été également construites. Ainsi, l’établissement dispose de trois nouvelles salles de classe primaires, de trois salles préscolaires, ainsi que de toilettes, d’une station de lavage des mains et d’aires de jeux, et de trois bâtiments existants réhabilités. Ces infrastructures ont vu le jour grâce au soutien de la Fondation Axian et de son partenaire United World School (UWS). Il s’agit de la 250e école construite à Madagascar par la Fondation Axian. Ce cap symbolique marque 15 ans d’engagement pour l’éducation, dans une région où la scolarisation reste difficile. Cette année, près de 1 150 élèves pourront étudier dans de meilleures conditions. L’école accueille aujourd’hui plus de 1 000 élèves, encadrés par 27 enseignants.L’inauguration s’est déroulée en présence de plusieurs autorités, dont le chef de région, le préfet d’Atsimo-Andrefana et des représentants de la Direction régionale de l’Éducation nationale, ainsi que de la directrice exécutive de la Fondation Axian et du directeur général mondial d’UWS. Leur présence montre que ce type de projet ne peut réussir que grâce à la collaboration entre le public et le privé.UWS est le partenaire de longue date de la Fondation dans la région Atsimo-Andrefana. Ensemble, ils ont déjà construit une trentaine d’écoles. En marge de l’inauguration, deux nouvelles initiatives ont vu le jour. UWS a ouvert un centre de formation pour les enseignants de la région, équipé d’ordinateurs fournis par Yas Madagascar. La Fondation Axian et ses partenaires ont aussi posé la première pierre d’un terrain multisport à l’EPP Ambahikily, dans le cadre du programme M’Hetsika MVola.Miangaly Ralitera

title: Two top performing students talk their aspirations
content: It was around 3 p.m. on Friday, September 11, when Henriette Umukundwa received a phone call from her mother in Ruhango District, telling her that she was among the top performers in the Advanced Level national examination results announced that day. Uwukundwa, 19, was washing dishes at her sister’s home in Kigali, where she had gone to visit. “When I heard that I was among the best performers, I was very surprised. I thought it was a scam. I cried a lot, tears of joy. Then I followed the event of the release of the national exams results on YouTube. That's when I confirmed that it was true,” she told The New Times. ALSO READ: Who are the top performers in A-Level national exams? The former student of ACEJ Karama Technical Secondary School (TSS) topped in Accounting with a score of 95.23 percent. Accounting was among the Professional Education combinations. Umukundwa attributed her performance to hard work, following her teachers’ advice to work in teams and conducting extensive research. “My teachers equipped me with skills, encouraged me to do research and also to enjoy teamwork, saying that ‘one pillar doesn’t make a house’. This helped me feel that I need others as they need me, where we shared knowledge and revised together,” she said. Her favourite subjects were auditing, financial mathematics and management. She studied extensively, took notes and made summaries to improve her understanding, and paid attention during lessons. ALSO READ: 94% of A-Level candidates pass national exams She also prepared a revision timetable, identifying subjects and topics she did not clearly understand and giving them more attention. Her parents were also supportive, she said. They supported her and encouraged her to aim high in life. As a child, Umukundwa wanted to become a doctor, but her interests changed as she grew older and she became more drawn to accounting. She now plans to study accounting at university, gain more knowledge and experience, and work towards becoming a qualified accountant. “The advice I can give to others who want to perform well is to focus on their lessons and manage their time well,” Umukundwa said. “They should pay attention in class, listen to their teachers and make enough time for revision and other schoolwork. Staying focused and using their time well can help them keep up with their studies and improve their performance.” Youssouf Bisangabagabo, the headmaster of ACEJ Karama TSS, said Umukundwa was a class monitress and served as an accountant in the Adventist group. She was always among the top three students in her class and was a responsible student who was useful to the community. In her free time, the youngster enjoys reading history books and catching up with friends. Another top performer, Naomie Umunyurwa Karangwa, was with her parents when the national examination results were announced. Karangwa, 17, sat with her parents to watch the announcement, expecting to see good marks. She knew she had qualified for a diploma but did not know she had performed well enough to emerge as the top performer in the Technical Secondary School category. Karangwa scored 94.74 percent. She studied Craft and Recreational Arts at Ecole d’Arts de Nyundo in Rubavu District. As she and her parents watched the results announcement live on YouTube on September 11, Karangwa was waiting for the link to check her individual results and surprise her family. “Then, as they were reading the names of the best performers, I heard my name. I could hardly believe it,” she recalled in an interview with The New Times. “I was really shocked. I replayed that part of the programme more than five times because I could not believe it could be me. I never thought I could perform that well and take the national top position,” Her parents were equally surprised, and the three cried with joy. The results came after a year in which she relied on her usual study habits, including waking up early, revising notes and taking notes in class. But she said discipline and respect were just as important. Karangwa said respect means recognising that no matter how capable one is, there will always be something they can learn from another person. She said having this sense prevents people from seeing themselves as better than others and allows them to learn from those with abilities they may not have. She credits her parents, teachers and friends, as well as the education she received, for supporting her. “My parents always made sure that I did not lack anything I needed for school. They provided my school fees and the equipment I needed, along with parental advice that showed me the right path to success,” she said. Her teachers also supported her through classwork and practical exercises. “They tried their level best to help me, especially when I struggled. Through classwork and practical exercises, they helped me get back on my feet, develop my skills and realise my potential. Their support pushed me to work harder, and my parents continue to encourage me to pursue my ambitions,” she said. Karangwa wants to specialise in industrial design, mainly architecture and 3D art. She is interested in the detailed designs seen in some historic buildings, including relief sculptures and floral patterns. Karangwa said many modern buildings are look very minimalist and have fewer of these artistic details. She wants to bring some of that detail back into modern architectural design by creating complex designs that tell a story. Her interest in architecture has drawn her to the work of the late Iraqi-British architect Zaha Hadid, whom she considers a role model. Hadid faced years of criticism over her curvaceous, and futuristic designs that were considered too radical or difficult to build, with many of her early projects remaining on paper before more of her designs were realised. Karangwa admires Hadid for continuing to pursue architecture despite the criticism she faced. The youngster advises fellow students to work hard, stay disciplined and take advice seriously, saying pressure should be seen as a privilege because it pushes people to work harder. title: Over 600,000 women screened in cervical cancer drive
content: More than 600,000 women have been screened for cervical cancer under Rwanda’s nationwide drive to expand early detection and move closer to its 2027 elimination target, according to the Rwanda Biomedical Centre (RBC). The country aims to screen 70 per cent of women aged 30 to 49 by 2027, with current coverage standing at 37 per cent. Dr Theoneste Maniragaba, Director of the Cancer Programme at RBC, told The New Times that the screening campaign is being expanded across districts, alongside efforts to maintain high human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination coverage, which stands at about 93 per cent. ALSO READ: Inside Rwanda’s push to eliminate cervical cancer ahead of WHO targets The Eastern Province has completed the current screening exercise, with Gatsibo the latest district to finish. In Kigali, Kicukiro and Nyarugenge have also been covered, while Gasabo is yet to be reached. “We are running too fast to make sure that the South and Western provinces can be reached in the short period coming. The focus now is on reaching more women with screening and ensuring those with precancerous lesions receive treatment,” Maniragaba said. Rwanda has set 2027 as its target for eliminating cervical cancer, three years ahead of the World Health Organisation’s 2030 target. The country is targeting about 1.5 million women for screening as it scales up the programme nationwide. Maniragaba said population data is being used to determine the number of eligible women in every district, sector and cell, with community health workers playing a central role in identifying and mobilising them. “Population data is being used to identify the women to be screened in each district, sector and cell, with support from the National Institute of Statistics. Community health workers are helping find women in their communities and homes,” he said. Bringing screening closer to communities One of the approaches being used is community-based self-sampling, where women are taught how to collect their own samples and return them for testing. Community health workers collect the samples and deliver them to health centres, from where they are sent to laboratories. ALSO READ: Women can now self test for cervical cancer Women who test positive for HPV undergo further examinations, including visual inspection with acetic acid, commonly known as VIA. Those found to have precancerous lesions can be treated at health centres, district hospitals and other health facilities. Women suspected of having cancer are referred to specialised centres for biopsy and pathology tests. They can also undergo CT scans and MRI tests at teaching hospitals, which Maniragaba said are covered under the community-based health insurance scheme (CBHI). Patients diagnosed with cancer can access treatment, including surgery and chemotherapy. More cases detected early Maniragaba said the expansion of screening is contributing to more cervical cancer cases being detected at stages one and two, when treatment is more effective. “We are seeing an increase in cases diagnosed at stages one and two as more women are reached through awareness and screening. When the disease is detected early, patients can be treated with surgery and, where necessary, chemotherapy,” he said. Cervical cancer is the second most prevalent cancer among women in Rwanda after breast cancer, but carries the highest cancer burden among women. Rwanda records about 600 cervical cancer cases annually, with about 70 per cent diagnosed at an advanced stage, according to Maniragaba. He said the disease is receiving particular attention because its main cause is known, vaccination can prevent most cases and screening can identify precancerous changes before they develop into cancer. “If we know how many people need to be screened, we know the cause, we have an affordable vaccine and screening is possible, why can’t we do it?” he said. Community health workers at the centre of the drive Kwizera Matabishi, a community health worker in Kicukiro, said community health workers go door to door to raise awareness, encourage women to get screened and explain the importance of early detection. “Those found with HPV or cancer are advised to go to health centres for treatment. We also make sure that people living with cancer can live in the community without stigma,” Matabishi said. Alain Fabrice Mizero, Executive Director of Rwanda Cancer Relief, an organisation that supports improved cancer care, said increased awareness, easier access to screening and the availability of treatment are encouraging more women to participate. “The government, NGOs and other partners are raising awareness about cervical cancer and encouraging women to get screened. Screening services are also being brought closer to communities through primary healthcare, with RBC and the Ministry of Health training community health workers to provide the service,” he said. Mizero said the priority should be to strengthen existing programmes and ensure they reach more women across the country rather than introduce new approaches. “The Ministry of Health has provided the framework under Mission 2027, and we need to make sure it delivers the target. That requires everyone, not only the government, but also NGOs, partners and philanthropists, to put in the resources needed to reach more women and achieve the mission,” he said. Challenges slowing expansion Despite the progress, Maniragaba said limited access to testing and laboratory services, implementation gaps and coordination challenges continue to slow the programme. Other constraints include high screening costs, procurement delays, a shortage of trained health workers and limited equipment. He said more health workers need to be trained at health centres, district hospitals and other facilities to expand screening capacity. The programme also plans to have testing machines in every district, reducing the need to transport samples from one district to another. Rwanda has largely relied on schools to reach girls aged 13 to 15 with the HPV vaccine, with vaccination coverage standing at about 93 per cent. Maniragaba said efforts are now being made to reach girls who are out of school so they can also receive the vaccine. How HPV spreads Maniragaba said cervical cancer itself cannot be transmitted from one person to another, but HPV, the virus responsible for most cervical cancer cases, can spread through intimate skin-to-skin contact around the genital area. He said HPV transmission differs from HIV because sexual intercourse is not required for transmission. The virus can be present on the skin around the vagina or penis and can be passed from one person to another through close skin contact.

title: After more than two years waiting for childcare aid, one Colorado family gets help
content:
Sign up for Chalkbeat Colorado’s free daily newsletter to get the latest reporting from us, plus curated news from other Colorado outlets, delivered to your inbox.
Stormi Kujawa was at a prenatal doctor’s appointment to check on her high-risk pregnancy when she got good news. It wasn’t about her baby. It was about a program that could help pay for childcare for her toddler daughter, Presley.
A local program was available for Larimer County families like hers, a social worker told her. Kujawa was so excited that she applied on her cellphone before even leaving the doctor’s office. A week later, she and her husband, Riley, were approved.
“I was shocked,” said Kujawa, who’d been on the waitlist for the state childcare subsidy program for more than two years. “I could not believe it.”
Languishing on a long waitlist for the Colorado Child Care Assistance Program, or CCCAP, is a familiar experience for thousands of low-income parents who need help paying for childcare so they can work or go to school. But the Kujawas’ story shows how one community is working to address that problem with a locally funded assistance program.
The program, which is currently funded by United Way, is small, serving several dozen families. But it’s about to get much bigger. In January, the Kids Thrive Fund will launch using proceeds from a new county sales tax increase approved by voters last November. The tax — 25 cents on every $100 purchase — is estimated to raise around $28 million a year for a variety of early childhood initiatives. All families will be eligible for some aid, but lower-income families will get the most.
Larimer County is one of several Colorado counties, cities, or regions where voters have approved new taxes to support childcare efforts in recent years.
The Kujawas, who live in Fort Collins, and other families in the United Way program will transition to the Kids Thrive Fund in 2027. The goal is to help 800 to 1,000 families through sliding-scale awards based on income, said Christina Taylor, CEO of the local early childhood council, Kids Thrive Northern Colorado.
It won’t be enough to satisfy local demand for childcare aid, but it represents “a huge step forward,” she said.
“The amount of revenue that we can dedicate to tuition is amazing,” Taylor said. “Like 800 to 1,000 families is nothing to sneeze at.”
State childcare assistance programs are underfunded
In 2025-26, CCCAP, Colorado’s $159 million childcare subsidy program, served more than 21,000 children, a spokesperson for the Colorado Department of Early Childhood told Chalkbeat. More than 14,000 Colorado children are still waiting.
Nationwide, hundreds of thousands of children were on waitlists for their states’ childcare subsidy programs last spring, according to an analysis by The Associated Press.
Childcare assistance, funded by the federal government with help from states, is supposed to aid working parents who have low incomes, are homeless, or care for foster children. But waitlists have ballooned since 2023, when eight states had them, according to the AP analysis. Reporters collected waitlist and enrollment data from 47 states and the District of Columbia.
Many of the waitlists emerged after $28 billion in pandemic aid expired in fall 2024. The Republican-led Congress declined to extend the extra money. Some states have increased funding to try to fill the gap, but families’ need for childcare assistance has only grown as they’ve faced mounting costs for food and gas.
While eligible families sit on waitlists, untold numbers of adults are sidelined from education or the workforce because they can’t afford childcare. Parents who remain in school or keep working make difficult tradeoffs. In interviews with the AP, parents described forgoing necessities, falling behind on bills, or relying on acquaintances to watch their children. Unable to find viable childcare, some have resorted to bringing their children with them to work or class.
Stormi Kujawa, who also has two school-age daughters, used to bring Presley to her job as a peer support specialist for mothers recovering from addiction. It worked when Presley was an infant and slept contentedly in her car seat, but not when she became a wiggly toddler. That’s when Kujawa stopped working.
Kujawa often called or emailed the county to see if she was close to moving off the CCCAP waitlist, but it never happened. Things got more challenging when her doctor placed her on bed rest because of preeclampsia, a serious pregnancy-related blood pressure condition. Riley Kujawa paused his job with a moving company a couple of months ago to stay home with Presley.
Looking toward the future
Presley, who will be 2 in November, proudly wore a lanyard with her father’s keys around her neck as the two played on the family’s apartment balcony on a recent sunny afternoon.
Stormi Kujawa sat at her kitchen table, contemplating the future. In the middle of the table, a blood pressure cuff served as a reminder of the constant medical monitoring her pregnancy requires.
When the Kujawas found out earlier this month they’d been approved for childcare assistance, they rushed to tour nearby childcare centers with Presley. They chose the one Presley didn’t want to leave. It had a modern security system and strict rules governing who could enter.
Presley will start there Oct. 1, about a week before the new baby is due. Tuition is $1,900 a month, but the Kujawas will only pay about $142 through the county program.
Riley will return to work shortly after the new baby arrives, and the family will be able to start catching up financially.
“I’m so stoked,” Stormi Kujawa said. “I’m nervous, but I’m really grateful I got the opportunity for this to happen.”
Ann Schimke is a senior reporter at Chalkbeat. Contact Ann at aschimke@chalkbeat.org.

title: Building a Black Honors Community
content:
California State University, Sacramento
When Naomi Thrower was applying to college, she knew she wanted the historically Black college or university experience but hesitated to leave the community she had built in California, which does not have a traditional HBCU.
So she applied to HBCUs across the country, as well as to California State University, Sacramento, the state’s first Black-serving institution.
“Sacramento State is the only California school I applied to. The rest were all East Coast HBCUs,” Thrower said. “I do have family on the East Coast, but none I felt strongly connected with. So I would be leaving my family, my friends, the life I’ve built here, and that was a little nerve-racking.”
Now a fourth-year deaf studies major, Thrower has found a community in the university’s Black Honors College, a first-of-its-kind program that provides a culturally responsive curriculum and inclusive academic community for students focused on the Black experience.
“It really provided me with a strong social foundation,” said Thrower, who was part of the college's inaugural cohort in 2024. “I knew everybody in my cohort, so when I was in my classes, when we started for the first day, I was nervous, but I already saw familiar faces, and so the [Black Honors College] provided me with that community feel.”
A growing community: Originally announced in 2023, Sacramento State’s Black Honors College offers smaller, specialized general education classes and is open to students of all races and majors. It also provides dedicated mentorship, paid internships, residential living-learning options and scholarships. The model offers a window into what can happen when an honors college centers Black history, culture and experiences in its curriculum while emphasizing community and belonging.
The Black Honors College admits incoming first-year students each fall, while transfer students and continuing Sacramento State sophomores and juniors can apply each spring. Students must have a 3.5 GPA at the time of application and maintain a 3.0 GPA or higher to remain enrolled.
Boatamo Ati Mosupyoe, dean of students and chief academic officer at Sacramento State, said the college initially planned to admit only 50 students in fall 2024, but growing interest led it to admit 80. The fall 2025 class grew to 262 students; this year's class is 414 students, bringing the total enrollment to 914.
Mosupyoe attributes that growth in part to the environment the college has sought to create, one that emphasizes students’ strengths rather than approaching them from what she described as a deficit perspective.
“We are creating a welcoming environment to the students,” Mosupyoe said. “This program doesn’t look at the students as deficient, and we don’t subscribe to a deficit model. We look at the potential of what these students are going to do.”
Matthew Ward, vice president of strategic enrollment management and chief enrollment officer, said the Black Honors College has become part of a broader effort at the university to intentionally support Black students and celebrate Black culture.
“We have lots of students who think about HBCUs but have to consider traveling across the country to go to an institution where they’re going to find that Black joy, Black excellence, Black dignity,” Ward said. “From what I’ve seen, in terms of the broader growth … word travels fast. There is definitely among students and families and school districts and educational leaders a real focus on Sacramento because it’s doing something that’s against the grain.”
That sense of community appealed to Manuel Tellez, a transfer student who grew up in Sacramento’s Oak Park neighborhood. Entering Sacramento State as a first-generation student, Tellez said he knew he needed the guidance of a strong Black community to feel comfortable and push himself academically, which he found in the Black Honors College.
“The Black Honors College pushed me to the next level [and] held me to a higher standard,” Tellez said. “Ever since then, my GPA has climbed, and I’ve been comfortable with going to school.”
Leland O’Neal, assistant program coordinator for the Black Honors College, said another strength of the college is the range of students and experiences represented within its cohorts.
“The pace of expansion has surprised me a little bit, but in a grand way,” O’Neal said. “We have students in that cohort, like Manuel, who are transfer students, but we also have students coming in who are as old as 69 or students who are as young as 19. So I think you really get a diverse array of perspectives and experiences.”
Building a network: As the Black Honors College has grown, so have its student supports. The college now offers financial literacy workshops, access to an in-house licensed therapist and events that celebrate Black culture. Mosupyoe said the number of professors affiliated with the college has also grown from 20 when the college began to 30 today.
“We have a community of administrators, staff and professors who are helping us really make sure that we provide what we have promised to students,” Mosupyoe said.
For Thrower, that support has extended beyond the classroom. She now works as a student assistant for the college and in that capacity has helped organize programming with the nonprofit Black Deaf Project to connect and socialize with students. The experience ultimately led her to an internship with the organization.
“The first piece of advice I got before college was that your net worth is your network,” Thrower said. “The Black Honors College has been that foundational network hub. I know people all over campus, and if I don’t know where to find some information, I know that I can go to the Black Honors College and they can direct me towards somebody who can help.”
(Updated 9/23, 12:20 p.m. to reflect the total number of students in the college.)

title: The fish skin that becomes one with your body
content: Guðmundur Fertram Sigurjónsson, an inventor and CEO originally from a small Icelandic fishing village, was looking at fish scales for wound healing, and realised fish skin is structurally similar to human skin. And this makes it an interesting alternative for dressing wounds. Unlike conventional wound dressings – which need to be replaced, potentially damaging fragile new tissue – North Atlantic cod skin stays on the wound. The body's cells grow into it, and as new human tissue develops, the cod skin is gradually absorbed and replaced by the patient's own living tissue. Humans have used animal skin to cover wounds since as far back as the 16th century. Pigs became the dominant donor in modern medicine, largely for their affordability as well as their similarity to human skin. But while mammal skin needs to undergo harsh treatment to eliminate the risk of disease transmission, cod skin may carry little risk of spreading disease to humans, since certain pathogens adapted to cold-water fish struggle to survive in the warmer human body, Sigurjónsson explained to us. What the science says Using fish skin instead of mammal skin may reduce the risk of disease transmission because fish are biologically more distant from humans. However this doesn't necessarily mean fish skin is safer or more effective, Dimitri Beeckman, professor of nursing science at Örebro University and Ghent University, told us. So far, more than 100 scientific studies have looked at fish skin. The largest randomised trial to date, partly funded by Kerecis (a company founded by Sigurjónsson), included 255 patients with deep diabetic foot ulcers. After 16 weeks, 44% of wounds treated with fish skin had healed, compared with 26% with standard care. After 24 weeks, those figures rose to 55% and 38% respectively. Yet more clinical research is needed to establish whether fish skin can really be used as an alternative to products made from pig or human tissue. “There have been some direct comparisons, including with porcine material, but these were mainly small studies using experimental wounds in healthy volunteers,” said Beeckman. From Iceland to the frontlines That doesn't stop Sigurjónsson from applying the method in practice. He founded his company Kerecis in 2013, and has since worked with humanitarian organisations, hospitals, and surgeons. Today, Kerecis has an expanding presence in Europe and across the world. According to Sigurjónsson, Kerecis has treated hundreds of thousands of patients worldwide using fish skin. They've donated their fish skin product to Ukrainian patients who have suffered injuries and are being treated in Ukraine and in neighbouring countries. Because fish skin is lightweight, has a long shelf life, and can be stored at room temperature, it is particularly useful for treating wounds in war zones. The price of healing faster So why is fish skin as wound treatment not more widespread? Cost is one important factor, as it is generally more expensive than standard care, although this depends on the healthcare system. “Costs and reimbursement differ between countries, and more independent health-economic research would be useful,” Beeckman told us. Fish-skin grafts are a promising addition to standard care for selected patients, according to Beeckman. But more independent trials, real-world evidence, and research into cost and benefits are needed.

title: Students at the Indiana School for the Blind and Visually Impaired make coding more accessible
content:
Sign up for Chalkbeat Indiana’s free daily newsletter to keep up with Indianapolis Public Schools, Marion County’s township districts, and statewide education news.
Arabella Zink softly touches the keys of her laptop, leaning forward to listen to the voice coming from the computer speakers.
The seventh grader is building code, dragging and dropping elements on a screen to turn the educational technology known as micro:bit into a die. The small piece of educational technology, which connects to the computer in the shape of a chip, encourages students to learn to block code — a highly visual activity.
Arabella, however, does it without vision.
She’s one of seven students at the Indiana School for the Blind and Visually Impaired who helped develop a new accessibility feature for the micro:bit, expanding coding to blind and visually impaired students.
The accessibility initiative began last year, after the Micro:bit Educational Foundation reached out to the school’s media specialist, Shawn Humphrey. The foundation was seeking blind students who could read Braille to give input on screen reader compatibility and the accuracy of Braille instructions for visually impaired students, Humphrey said.
Arabella and her peers got to work, editing Braille materials and testing whether the screen reader could read what the computer was showing in a way they could understand within the Microsoft MakeCode program.
The project — developed with the foundation and the educational open source coding tools Microsoft MakeCode and Blockly — makes the micro:bit compatible with computer screen readers that tell students what is on their screen.
The micro:bit tool is used in 85 countries to bring coding to the classroom, with lessons that include how to program the tool to play games like rock, paper, scissors, or clap to turn on its lights. And now, with input from ISBVI students, coding is accessible not only to visually impaired students who use the Microsoft MakeCode platform, but all other coding programs built on Blockly’s software.
On a recent September afternoon, Arabella was learning how to make the micro:bit tool into a die that would light up with a number ranging from one to six when shaken. Students could identify which number it landed on by the number of beeps the micro:bit emitted after a shake.
Humphrey recalls seeing Arabella light up when she was told that she was one of the first students in the world to try a particular coding lesson using the accessible version of micro:bit.
“It’s one of the coolest things I’ve ever heard in education, having our students have that opportunity,” he said. “It has opened up coding for visually impaired students.”
Maddilyn Peters, a seventh grader with a penchant for horror stories who also helped develop the accessibility feature, has an interest in coding in order to make robots. Specifically, she said, she’d like to make animatronics like the ones in the horror film “Five Nights at Freddy’s” come to life.
“But not hostile,” she clarified. “I’m just going to make them not attack people.”
Amelia Pak-Harvey covers schools for Chalkbeat Indiana. Contact Amelia at apak-harvey@chalkbeat.org.

title: California Tribes receive beach and ancestral village site back from transportation authority
content:
- The U.S. state of California has returned 55 hectares (136 acres) of Northern California coastline, including Blues Beach and the village site of K’etim, to three Coastal Yuki tribes.
- It is the first land Caltrans, the state transportation department, has ever returned to Indigenous ownership.
- Tribes first asked for the site in 2005, after learning looters were digging into archaeological sites and uncovering ancestral remains.
- The tribe hopes to use the land for education and gatherings, but the beach will remain open to the public.
On the Northern California coast, where the tall trees meet the sea, ancestors of the Coast Yuki people lie buried in an old village site above the bluffs in the U.S. state. Yet despite its cultural significance, the land has been owned by the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) until very recently.
A deed recorded July 6 transferred 55 hectares (136 acres) of that coastline to Kai Poma, a nonprofit founded by representatives of the Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians, the Round Valley Indian Tribes and the Sherwood Valley Band of Pomo Indians, the Ancestral Descendants of Coastal Yuki and Yuki.
It is the first time land held by Caltrans has been returned to Indigenous ownership, according to Kai Poma.
“We always felt this was ours,” Eddie Knight, chairman of Kai Poma and historic preservation officer for Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians, who is of Coastal Yuki descent, told Mongabay. “It may have been owned privately by somebody, but we still knew it was ours.”
The property sits just south of the small community of Westport, California, about 187 miles (300 kilometers) north of San Francisco. Visitors know the beach here as Blues Beach, but a major village site there is called K’etim by the Coast Yuki and Pomo lineages.
K’etim, according to the tribe’s traditional stories, is “where Seaweed Woman who lived at Mussel Rock met and fell in love with Coyote,” Kai Poma explained in a press release. This origin story “explains the creation of the coastline and its people. These teachings remain alive through the descendants who continue to revere, gather, camp, commune with, and steward their ancestral places.”
In 2005, word reached Knight and others that looters were digging at K’etim and uncovering human and archeological remains. “K’etim has endured substantial damage from off-road vehicle activity and widespread looting of archaeological sites,” Kai Poma stated.
In response, members of Sherwood Valley and Coyote Valley wrote to Caltrans that year asking for stewardship of the site and were granted a meeting. When the land was not handed over, Knight said, “we just kept on being persistent and said ‘give it to us.’”
It took many years of relentless efforts and a new law to make the transfer a reality. In 2021, Senator Mike McGuire wrote Senate Bill 231, specifically authorizing Caltrans to transfer Blues Beach “at no cost to a qualified nonprofit corporation.”
The three tribes formed the non-profit organization Kai Poma to receive the land.
The law requires Kai Poma to keep the land open to the public free of charge, bars commercial development, and returns the land to Caltrans if the nonprofit fails to maintain it or dissolves.
“This is beyond huge,” J. Carlos Rivera, tribal chairman of the Sherwood Valley Band of Pomo Indians, told the Los Angeles Times. “It’s enormous from our tribal perspective that we are basically obtaining the land that our people once lived on before colonization.”
The land is made up of about a half mile (800 meters) of beach, a terrace above the beach of roughly 40 hectares (100 acres), “which has our archaeological sites under it,” Knight said, as well as 16 hectares (40 acres) of old grazing land sloping from Highway 1 down to the ocean.
The sloping ground is the part Kai Poma can build on. Future management plans still need to be agreed upon by the three tribes, but Knight raised the possibility of building a traditional roundhouse, holding ceremonies and hosting an educational program.
The beach will remain open to the public. Cars have been prohibited from the beach by Caltrans but that rule was not strictly enforced. Kai Poma is still deciding how they will manage these issues.
“We want to protect the natural habitat,” Knight said. And to educate youth on “how to harvest our native foods, our sea foods, our seaweeds, our kelps and how to fish. Allowing our youth to get an idea of how they can use it in the future and use it now. It’s going to take a little time, but we do have a plan.”
The nonprofit has held a grant since 2023 for an archaeological survey to identify every site on the property, but could not begin the work, Knight said, until they had secured the deed. Now they plan to move forward and are planning a celebration and ceremony for all eight bands in Mendocino County.
This deed transfer is part of a larger Land Back movement: The push to return land to tribes, Traditional Owners and ancestral descendants of the land.
California has returned tens of thousands of acres to tribes in the past two years. The Yurok Tribe reclaimed more than 19,000 hectares (47,000 acres) along the lower Klamath River, the largest land return in state history. The Tule River Indian Tribe regained 6,890 hectares (17,030 acres) in Tulare County, and the Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California reacquired 4,158 hectares (10,274 acres) of former Sierra Nevada ranchland.
“136 acres of coastal lands have now been officially transferred into tribal stewardship, forever protecting one of the most spectacular stretches of the Mendocino Coast,” McGuire said in a statement. “This agreement, the first of its kind in California, gives the Sherwood Valley Band of Pomo Indians, Round Valley Indian Tribes and Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians the rightful opportunity to reclaim sacred lands and cultural traditions on this special piece of earth. And it’s about damn time.”
Banner image of Blues Beach, California with vehicles parked. Image courtesy of Kai Pomo.
First ever U.S. Indigenous Marine Stewardship Area declared in California

title: Kouluvaari | Ismo Ylisellä on aikaa, joten hän haluaa käyttää sen hyvään
content:
Aarnivalkean koulun neljäsluokkalaisilla on ollut mieluisa kotitehtävä viikonlopulle: syö Pringles-purkki tyhjäksi ja tuo se kouluun.
Nyt he tekevät sipsipurkeista majakoita. Työhön tarvitaan talttaa, sahaa ja hiomapaperia, joita oppilaat lähtevät hakemaan työkalukaapista.
Kymmenestä oppilaasta monella on vielä suunnitelmat kesken. Millaisen sillan tekisin? Käyttäisinkö majakkasaaren talon materiaalina vaneria vai lautaa?
”Ismoo, voiksä tulla auttaa!”
Kevättalvella 2014 Ismo Ylinen osallistui tyttärentyttärensä luokan avoimien ovien päivään.
Hän oli kuullut, että entinen työkaveri oli vapaaehtoisena kouluvaarina.
Ylinen päätti kysyi Aarnivalkean koulun silloiselta rehtorilta Marjatta Larsiolta, olisiko joutilaalle vaarille jotain hommaa.
Rehtori toivotti tervetulleeksi.
Pitkään Ylinen kävi Espoon Tapiolassa sijaitsevassa koulussa kahtena, kolmena päivänä viikossa.
Viimeiset vuodet hän on ollut paikalla kaikkina koulupäivinä, tällä hetkellä jopa kuusitoista tuntia viikossa.
”Jos minulla on omia tekemisiä, niin menen sitten omille reissuille. Mutta pääsääntöisesti olen täällä”, Ylinen kertoo.
Hän on diplomi-insinööri, joka teki työuransa Nokialla. Viimeiset vuodet kuluivat projektipäällikkönä Nokia Siemens Networksilla.
”Enää siitä ei ole mitään hyötyä, mitä on joskus oppinut, koska kaikki tekniikka ajaa ohi. Se, mitä mulla on jäljellä, on aika.”
Sen hän haluaa antaa mahdollisimman hyvään käyttöön.
Iiris Tapio, 10, sahaa. Isla Jalasto, 9, talttaa.
Kumpikin pitää Ismosta. He ovat oppineet häneltä paljon.
”Että pitää olla tässä tunnilla varovaisesti. Ja vaikka että millaisia sahoja kannattaa käyttää ja millaisia työvaiheita on”, Jalasto kertaa saamiaan oppeja.
Kouluvaaripestinsä Ylinen aloitti kuitenkin lukuvaarina. Silloin hän teki lukuharjoituksia yhden lapsen kanssa kerrallaan.
Ylinen kuunteli, miten ääneen lukeminen sujui, ja selitti lapselle epäselvien sanojen merkityksiä.
Toiset lukivat jo toisella luokalla Harry Pottereita ja toisilla taas oli enemmän haasteita, Ylinen kertoo.
”Mutta jos joku on oikein sellainen sujuva lukija, olen yleensä kysynyt, että onko sinulle luettu lapsena paljon. Poikkeuksetta on.”
Reilun kymmenen vuoden aikana lukuvaarina Ylinen ei havainnut, että lasten lukemisessa olisi tapahtunut suuria muutoksia, vaikka juuri sinä aikana älypuhelimien käyttö yleistyi suomalaislapsilla.
Kolmensadan oppilaan alakoulussa työskentelee 25 ihmistä. Kouluvaari Ylisen lisäksi koulussa on seitsemän koulumummoa.
Aarnivalkeassa kouluisovanhemmat ovat pitkä perinne. Erillisiä sopimuksia heillä ei ole. Vapaaehtoistyöstä on sovittu suullisesti rehtori Erja Oilan kanssa.
Yhteydenottoja tulee sen verran paljon, että nykyään Oila kehottaa halukkaita olemaan yhteydessä muihin kouluihin. Ei siksi, että ”vapaaehtoiskiintiö” olisi täynnä, vaan siksi että muissa kouluissa tarve voisi olla suurempi, Oila ajattelee.
”Eikä kaikilla lapsilla ole isovanhemmat lähellä. On tärkeää, että he saavat kohtaamisia koulumummojen ja -vaarin kanssa.”
Vapaaehtoiseksi haluavat käyvät Mannerheimin lastensuojeluliiton päivän koulutuksen. Liiton työntekijät esittelevät esimerkiksi vaitiolokäytäntöjä ja tarkistuttavat kurssilaisten taustat.
”Ettei kenellekään tule mieleen, että kukas vaari tänne tulee lasten kanssa huseeraamaan”, Ylinen sanoo.
Ylinen hoitelee koululla oppituntien lisäksi sivuaskareita, kuten kiristelee löystyneitä ruuveja tuoleista ja korjaa huonekaluja.
”Kaikenlaista lapsen kynsien leikkauksesta opettajien niskahierontaan.”
Toisinaan hän on mukana myös luokkaretkillä. Ylisellä on kouluun oma avain ja kulkulupa. Koululounaan hän saisi maksutta.
Ylisestä tuntuu, että hän ja koulumummot ovat kuin vakituista henkilökuntaa. Pikkujouluihinkin tulee kutsu.
Kerran eräällä oppilaalla ”meni överiksi”. Hän raapusti luokan oveen hakaristejä. Opettaja pyysi, voisiko Ylinen auttaa oppilasta sotkun siivoamisessa.
”Minä sitten neuvoin, ja hän ihan kiltisti hioi ja lakkasi sen pinnan. Ei me siitä asiasta keskusteltu, olin vaan läsnä. Katsoin, että saadaan hoidetuksi.”
Jälkeenpäin oppilaan äiti tuli kiittämään, kuinka tärkeää oli, että joku aikuinen auttoi eikä ainoastaan tuominnut.
77-vuotiaan Ylisen silmäkulmat vettyvät, kun hän muistelee hetkeä.
Hänestä parasta vapaaehtoistyössä on, kun lapsi oppii uutta, ja on pystynyt itse auttamaan siinä.
Ylisen kokemuksen mukaan lapset myös ottavat lähes aina mielellään apua vastaan.
Kurinpitoon hän ei puutu.
”Mutta jos huomaan, että joku tekee jotain sellaista, mikä saattaa olla vaarallista, niin sellaiseen katson kansalaisvelvollisuudekseni puuttua.”
Luokanopettaja Olli Mattila tekee oppilaiden puupaloille Aih!”-testejä. Hän kuljettaa oikean käden etusormeaan pitkin työstettyä pintaa. Jos pinnassa on karheutta, hän huudahtaa dramaattisesti ”aih!”
Moni palanen palaa hiottavaksi.
”Ismo on suurena apuna, ihan valtavana apuna”, Mattila huikkaa.
”Harvassa kouluissa on puutyötunnilla toinen aikuinen koko ajan auttamassa. Etenkään semmoinen, joka on rakentanut itse useamman talon.”
Mattilan mukaan Ylinen on kärsivällinen toisten ihmisten kohtaamisessa.
”Ismosta huokuu sellainen ystävällisyys, lämpö, läsnäolo ja vilpitön halu auttaa kaikkia.”
Elokuussa Espoon kaupungin mitalitoimikunta myönsi Yliselle Espoo-mitalin, jonka saa tunnustuksena kaupungin hyväksi tehdystä työstä. Tänä vuonna mitalin saajia oli Ylisen lisäksi kymmenen.
Hakemuksen tekivät Aarnivalkean koulun kuudesluokkalaiset. Sen allekirjoitti jokainen koulun oppilas.
Kaksoistunti on lopuillaan.
Oppilaat siivoavat harjoilla sahanpurut lattialta ja asettelevat työkalut sekä majakkasaaret takaisin kaappeihin.
Ylinen vahtii, että luokka tulee siistiksi.
Sitten oppilaat hakevat tietokoneensa, joihin he kirjaavat loppuraportit siitä, mitä tänään tunnilla tehtiin ja miten se sujui.
Sekä neljäsluokkalaisten että Ylisen koulupäivä on ohi. Ylisellä oli tänään kaksi puutyön kaksoistuntia. Välissä hän kävi kotonaan Iivisniemessä lounaalla, kuten tapoihinsa kuuluu.
Kuinka kauan aiot jatkaa kouluvaarina?
Ylinen virnistää.
”Tällä hetkellä ajattelen, että niin kauan kunnes kielletään.”

social_cohesion_impact.evidence: Kolmensadan oppilaan alakoulussa työskentelee 25 ihmistä. Kouluvaari Ylisen lisäksi koulussa on seitsemän koulumummoa.

evidence_level.evidence: Viimeiset vuodet hän on ollut paikalla kaikkina koulupäivinä, tällä hetkellä jopa kuusitoista tuntia viikossa.

benefit_distribution.evidence: ”Eikä kaikilla lapsilla ole isovanhemmat lähellä. On tärkeää, että he saavat kohtaamisia koulumummojen ja -vaarin kanssa.”

title: Syria's first women graduate from new police academy
content:
Around 150 women have graduated from Syria's new police academy in Al-Tal, north of Damascus, after six months of training.
The ceremony shows them marching and performing exercises.
The course covered military and physical skills, as well as police procedures, law and field work.
The academy is part of efforts by Syria's new authorities to rebuild the security forces and increase the role of women in policing.
One graduate, 22-year-old May Aklajneh, says becoming a policewoman was a childhood dream and that she joined as soon as recruitment opened.
The first cohort is expected to join Interior Ministry units across the country.
