title: De nouveaux logements locatifs abordables à Esch
content:
Cette nouvelle résidence a été inaugurée dans le quartier de Nonnewisen. Elle compte 30 logements locatifs abordables.
Le parc immobilier de la ville se dote de nouveaux logements sociaux. Une nouvelle résidence vient d’être inaugurée à Esch-sur-Alzette, dans le quartier de Nonnewisen. Au total, 30 logements locatifs abordables sont sortis de terre. Ces biens ont été acquis en VEFA (vente en l’état futur d’achèvement) pour une surface habitable totale de 2 600 m². «Il s’agit de la première résidence dont la Ville est propriétaire à disposer d’un tel espace collectif», souligne la commune dans un communiqué.
Les 30 appartements ont été mis en location par le biais du Réseau national du logement abordable (RENLA), la Ville d’Esch demeurant le bailleur social. La commune a bénéficié d’une convention d’aides à la pierre, signée le 24 février 2025, lui accordant des subventions étatiques à hauteur de 75 %.
Cet immeuble s’inscrit dans un ensemble de projets menés en collaboration avec la Société nationale des habitations à bon marché (SNHBM). Deux autres résidences ont déjà été achevées et ont accueilli leurs premiers occupants, tandis qu’une dernière doit être finalisée d’ici la fin de l’année.

title: 코로나19 이후 추락한 美 학생들 문해력 회복세
content:
코로나 이후 정체된 美 학생 읽기 성적 회복세
팬데믹 학업 격차 3분의 1 만회 성과
'읽기의 과학' 파닉스 교육 확산이 배경
전체 내용을 이해하기 위해서는 기사 본문과 함께 읽어야 합니다.
송고 2026년09월20일 21시00분
코로나 이후 정체된 美 학생 읽기 성적 회복세
팬데믹 학업 격차 3분의 1 만회 성과
'읽기의 과학' 파닉스 교육 확산이 배경
구글 검색에서 연합뉴스 기사를 우선적으로 보여줍니다.
(서울=연합뉴스) 신재우 기자 = 코로나19 팬데믹 이후 장기간 정체됐던 미국 학생들의 읽기 성취도가 최근 회복세를 보인 것으로 나타났다.
20일(현지시간) 미국 정치전문매체 더힐에 따르면 교육연구기관 NWEA가 유치원생부터 한국의 중학교 2학년에 해당하는 8학년 학생들의 읽기 성적을 분석한 결과, 지난해부터 올해 사이 성적이 개선되면서 팬데믹 이후 벌어진 학업 격차의 약 3분의 1을 회복한 것으로 나타났다.
NWEA의 메건 쿠펠드 성장모형·분석 담당 국장은 팬데믹 이후 4년간 읽기 성적이 사실상 정체돼 있었던 만큼 이번 개선은 의미가 크다고 평가했다.
전문가들은 최근 성적 개선의 배경으로 각 주가 도입한 읽기 교육 접근법인 '읽기의 과학'(science of reading)을 꼽고 있다.
팬데믹 이후 미국의 약 절반에 해당하는 주(州)가 학교 읽기 교육을 '읽기의 과학'에 맞추도록 법률을 제정하거나 관련 교육 기준을 도입했다.
'읽기의 과학'은 학생들이 글자와 소리의 관계를 체계적으로 익히도록 하는 파닉스 교육에 중점을 두는 교육 방식이다.
개별 글자가 어떤 소리를 내는지, 여러 글자가 결합했을 때 발음이 어떻게 달라지는지를 가르쳐 처음 보는 단어도 스스로 소리 내 읽을 수 있도록 하는 접근이다. 이 방법은 어휘력과 문장의 의미를 파악하는 독해 교육도 중시한다.
이는 미국 학교들에서 그동안 널리 활용돼온 '균형적 문해교육'(balanced literacy)과는 다소 차이가 있다.
균형적 문해교육은 학생들이 모르는 단어를 만났을 때 글자의 개별 소리를 하나씩 익히기보다는 문맥이나 그림 등 여러 '단서'(cue)를 활용해 단어의 의미를 추론하도록 하는 방식이다.
다만 미국 학생들의 읽기 성취도 회복세가 계속될지는 불확실하다.
미국 학생들의 읽기 성적은 1990년대부터 2013년까지 꾸준히 개선됐지만 이후 상승세가 꺾였다. 한 교육 보고서는 이런 학습 정체가 소셜미디어가 확산한 시기와 맞물려 나타났다고 지적했다.

부산 동백전 캐시백 이달 30일까지 최대 15%
추석 맞아 QR결제 쿠폰 지급 등 소비 이벤트
소상공인 정책지원금·카드수수료 지원 병행
구글 검색에서 연합뉴스 기사를 우선적으로 보여줍니다.
(부산=연합뉴스) 손형주 기자 = 부산시는 시민의 생활비 부담을 덜고 소상공인의 경영 비용을 완화하기 위해 이달 30일까지 동백전 캐시백을 최대 15%로 한시 상향한다고 20일 밝혔다.
연 매출 10억원 이하 가맹점의 기본 캐시백률은 기존 10%에서 15%로, 10억원 초과 30억원 이하 가맹점은 8%에서 13%로 각각 5%포인트 오른다.
추석을 맞아 소비 활성화 이벤트도 진행된다. 21일부터 오는 28일까지 동백전으로 누적 10만원 이상 결제한 회원을 대상으로 자동 응모 추첨을 통해 2만2천명에게 5천원 상당의 QR결제 전용 쿠폰을 지급한다.
이어 10월부터 11월까지는 3천원 상당의 QR결제 전용 쿠폰을 매월 1만5천명에게 선착순 발급한다.
소상공인을 위한 지원책도 병행된다. 행사 기간에 QR 가맹점으로 신규 가입하고 12월 20일까지 결제 실적이 있는 가맹점 중 6천500명을 추첨해 동백전 정책지원금 3만원을 지급한다.
또한 연 매출 10억원 이하 가맹점을 대상으로 10∼11월 카드 결제 실적 기준 6개월분의 카드수수료(0.15% 상당)를 지원한다.
전재수 부산시장은 "시민이 체감하는 혜택은 높이고 소상공인의 부담은 낮춰 지역 경제에 선순환 구조를 만들겠다"고 밝혔다.

title: "라이더 대기 시간도 돈 줘야"…배달앱 1800억 '폭탄' 터졌다 [곽용희의 일자리노트]
content:
AI 추천 뉴스




"라이더 대기 시간도 돈 줘야"…배달앱 1800억 '폭탄' 터졌다 [곽용희의 일자리노트]
도어대시, 뉴욕시에 1793억원 지급 합의
배달노동자 26만명 임금 체불 및 지연 지급
주문 기다리는 ‘대기시간’ 최저보수도 쟁점
뉴욕시, 플랫폼 데이터 1.5억건 직접 분석
플랫폼 데이터 제출 의무화...단속에 활용
배달노동자 26만명 임금 체불 및 지연 지급
주문 기다리는 ‘대기시간’ 최저보수도 쟁점
뉴욕시, 플랫폼 데이터 1.5억건 직접 분석
플랫폼 데이터 제출 의무화...단속에 활용


미국 음식배달 플랫폼 도어대시(DoorDash)가 배달노동자 임금 체불과 관련해 뉴욕시에 1억3150만달러(약 1793억원)를 지급하기로 합의했다. 뉴욕시 역사상 최대 규모의 노동 관련 합의이자 미국 음식배달 노동자를 대상으로 한 최대 규모의 합의금이다. 특히 뉴욕시가 도어대시의 1억5200만건의 결제 내역과 1억1000만시간의 노동 데이터를 직접 분석해 26만4000여명의 피해 노동자를 찾아냈다는 점에서 주목된다.
23일 월스트리트저널(WSJ), AP통신 등에 따르면 뉴욕시 소비자·노동자보호국(DCWP)은 도어대시와 배달노동자 임금 문제에 대해 1억3150만달러 규모의 합의를 체결했다. 이 가운데 1억1500만달러 이상(약 1569억원)은 노동자들에게 직접 지급되고, 1670만달러(약 228억원)는 벌금과 행정비용으로 뉴욕시에 귀속된다. 이번 조치는 양측이 합의한 것이다.
이번 합의는 배달노동자들이 임금을 제대로 받지 못했거나 지급이 늦어졌다는 민원을 제기하면서 시작됐다. 이에 따라 뉴욕시는 방대한 결제 및 노동 관련 데이터를 확보했고 이를 분석해 노동자별 지급액과 실제 노동시간을 대조했다. 그 결과 뉴욕시는 26만4000명 이상의 배달노동자가 임금이 체불되거나 법정 기한보다 늦게 지급된 것으로 조사됐다.
특히 뉴욕시의 배달노동자 최저보수 제도 위반 사례가 확인되면서 문제가 커졌다. 특히 '대기시간'이 핵심 쟁점이 됐다. 뉴욕시는 배달노동자가 앱에 접속해 다음 주문을 기다리는 시간까지 최저보수 산정에 반영해야 한다는 입장이다. 도어대시는 대기 시간을 뉴욕시와 다르게 계산했지만, 분쟁을 이어가기 보다는 합의를 선택한 것이다.
이에 따라 이번 합의에서 8300만달러 이상(약 1132억원)이 최저보수 산정 방식과 관련된 보상에 투입된다. 별도로 1230만달러(약 168억원)는 실제 미지급 또는 지연 임금과 관련된 노동자 보상에 사용된다. 추가 보상도 합의금에 포함됐다. 예를들어 1000달러(약 136만원)를 지급받지 못한 노동자는 3000달러(약 409만원)를 받게 되며, 1000달러를 법정 기한보다 늦게 받은 노동자는 2000달러(약 273만원)를 받는다.
도어대시는 고의적인 임금 착취가 아니라 기술적 오류와 복잡한 배달 과정에서 발생한 문제라고 주장했다. 뉴욕시 경계를 넘는 배달이나 복수의 픽업·배달, 주문 취소 과정에서 오류가 발생했으며 일부 지급 지연은 노동자가 잘못된 은행 정보를 입력하면서 발생했다는 설명이다. 회사는 문제가 된 기술적 사항을 수정했다고 밝혔다.
노동자가 별도로 피해 사실을 입증하거나 소송을 제기할 필요도 없이 뉴욕시가 플랫폼 데이터를 바탕으로 대상자를 특정하고 개인별 지급액을 산정한다. 정부가 플랫폼 데이터를 이용해 수십만명의 피해자를 일괄적으로 찾아냈다.
뉴욕시가 플랫폼 데이터를 직접 들여다볼 수 있었던 것은 배달노동자 최저보수 제도를 도입하면서 플랫폼에 데이터 제출 의무를 부과했기 때문이다. 뉴욕시는 2023년 미국에서 처음으로 앱 기반 음식배달 노동자를 대상으로 별도의 최저보수 제도를 도입했다. 법정 공방 끝에 같은 해 12월 4일부터 제도가 시행됐으며 당시 최저보수는 시간당 17.96달러(약 2만4500원)였다. 이후 차츰 인상돼 현재는 시간당 22.13달러(약 3만200원) 수준이다.
이번 사건은 이 데이터가 어떻게 노동 감독의 수단으로 활용될 수 있는지를 보여준다. 전통적인 근로감독은 감독관이 사업장을 방문해 임금대장과 근로계약서를 확인하는 방식이었다. 하지만 배달플랫폼은 배달기사가 언제 앱에 접속했는지, 얼마 동안 대기했는지, 어떤 주문을 수행했는지, 얼마를 지급받았는지가 모두 플랫폼 데이터로 남는다. 플랫폼 노동에 대한 노동감독이 ‘사업장에 가는 감독’에서 ‘데이터를 분석하는 감독’으로 바뀔 가능성을 보여주는 대목이다.
곽용희 기자 kyh@hankyung.com
23일 월스트리트저널(WSJ), AP통신 등에 따르면 뉴욕시 소비자·노동자보호국(DCWP)은 도어대시와 배달노동자 임금 문제에 대해 1억3150만달러 규모의 합의를 체결했다. 이 가운데 1억1500만달러 이상(약 1569억원)은 노동자들에게 직접 지급되고, 1670만달러(약 228억원)는 벌금과 행정비용으로 뉴욕시에 귀속된다. 이번 조치는 양측이 합의한 것이다.
이번 합의는 배달노동자들이 임금을 제대로 받지 못했거나 지급이 늦어졌다는 민원을 제기하면서 시작됐다. 이에 따라 뉴욕시는 방대한 결제 및 노동 관련 데이터를 확보했고 이를 분석해 노동자별 지급액과 실제 노동시간을 대조했다. 그 결과 뉴욕시는 26만4000명 이상의 배달노동자가 임금이 체불되거나 법정 기한보다 늦게 지급된 것으로 조사됐다.
특히 뉴욕시의 배달노동자 최저보수 제도 위반 사례가 확인되면서 문제가 커졌다. 특히 '대기시간'이 핵심 쟁점이 됐다. 뉴욕시는 배달노동자가 앱에 접속해 다음 주문을 기다리는 시간까지 최저보수 산정에 반영해야 한다는 입장이다. 도어대시는 대기 시간을 뉴욕시와 다르게 계산했지만, 분쟁을 이어가기 보다는 합의를 선택한 것이다.
이에 따라 이번 합의에서 8300만달러 이상(약 1132억원)이 최저보수 산정 방식과 관련된 보상에 투입된다. 별도로 1230만달러(약 168억원)는 실제 미지급 또는 지연 임금과 관련된 노동자 보상에 사용된다. 추가 보상도 합의금에 포함됐다. 예를들어 1000달러(약 136만원)를 지급받지 못한 노동자는 3000달러(약 409만원)를 받게 되며, 1000달러를 법정 기한보다 늦게 받은 노동자는 2000달러(약 273만원)를 받는다.
도어대시는 고의적인 임금 착취가 아니라 기술적 오류와 복잡한 배달 과정에서 발생한 문제라고 주장했다. 뉴욕시 경계를 넘는 배달이나 복수의 픽업·배달, 주문 취소 과정에서 오류가 발생했으며 일부 지급 지연은 노동자가 잘못된 은행 정보를 입력하면서 발생했다는 설명이다. 회사는 문제가 된 기술적 사항을 수정했다고 밝혔다.
노동자가 별도로 피해 사실을 입증하거나 소송을 제기할 필요도 없이 뉴욕시가 플랫폼 데이터를 바탕으로 대상자를 특정하고 개인별 지급액을 산정한다. 정부가 플랫폼 데이터를 이용해 수십만명의 피해자를 일괄적으로 찾아냈다.

title: Rinden homenaje a víctimas y rescatistas de los sismos de 1985 y 2017 en la Ciudad de México
content:
Rinden homenaje a víctimas y rescatistas de los sismos de 1985 y 2017 en la Ciudad de México
Autoridades capitalinas encabezaron un homenaje en memoria de víctimas y rescatistas de los sismos de 1985 y 2017; Clara Brugada destacó la solidaridad ciudadana y el avance en la reconstrucción.
En un emotivo acto de memoria y reconocimiento, realizado en el Jardín Tlallipan, autoridades del Gobierno de la Ciudad de México rindiendo un homenaje a las víctimas, brigadistas, rescatistas y colectivos de damnificados al cumplirse un aniversario más de los sismos del 19 de septiembre de 1985 y 2017.
Durante la ceremonia, la jefa de Gobierno, Clara Brugada, reconoció la respuesta solidaria de la ciudadanía que emergió de las calles para salvar vidas ante la emergencia.
Adenas, destacó la valentía de los equipos de emergencia y la organización popular histórica que nació tras las tragedias, mencionó de manera especial la lucha del Sindicato de Costureras 19 de Septiembre y de movimientos sociales que sentaron las bases de la transformación comunitaria en la capital.
Recordamos con emoción y dolor a quienes perdieron la vida. Recordamos las calles cubiertas de polvo y de silencio, pero esta ciudad tiene siete siglos de memoria y no olvida. Cuando todo parecía derrumbarse, el pueblo permaneció de pie”, expresó.
Asimismo, evocando las palabras del poeta José Emilio Pacheco, se expresó: “Para los que ayudaron, gratitud eterna o homenaje. Si el mundo no se vino abajo sobre México fue porque lo asumieron en sus espaldas”.
En el mensaje lamentó la actuación gubernamental del pasado, contrastó la negligencia y la corrupción de administraciones anteriores con la dignidad de la población organizada. Además, garantizó que la atención a los afectados se mantendrá como una responsabilidad pública estricta hasta concluir el último compromiso pendiente.
Se informó que el programa registra un avance general superior al 97 por ciento. Hasta la fecha se han entregado 20 mil 556 viviendas y las obras restantes mantienen un progreso superior al 60 por ciento.
Para consolidar estas acciones, la inversión pública total destinadas a la recuperación de los inmuebles rebasará los 15 mil 500 millones de pesos.
Durante el homenaje estuvieron presentes representantes de organizaciones civiles creadas a raíz de estos dos sismos.

title: El ecoturismo y la ‘economía emocional’ han logrado la conservación de la Sierra Gorda de Querétaro
content:
Para quienes gustan de manejar en carretera y pueblear, hay una ruta peculiar que incluye diversos atractivos. Comienza en el Pueblo Mágico de Peña de Bernal, en Querétaro, y luego se enfila hacia la Sierra Gorda, donde se encuentran las Misiones que fundó Fray Junípero Serra en el siglo XVIII: de Santiago de Jalpan, de Nuestra Señora de la Luz de Tancoyol, de Santa María del Agua de Landa, de San Francisco de Asís del Valle de Tilaco y la de San Miguel Concá, todas con inverosímiles fachadas por las que en 2003 fueron declaradas Patrimonio Mundial por la UNESCO. De ahí, al punto final cruzando hacia el estado de San Luis Potosí, Xilitla, que también es Pueblo Mágico y alberga la casa surrealista que construyó Sir Edward James, conocida como Las Pozas.
Todos esos puntos de la ruta son espectaculares, pero lo mejor de todo es que buena parte del trayecto se realiza cruzando la Sierra Gorda de Querétaro, que ofrece su propio espectáculo, el de la naturaleza, donde habitan más de cien mil personas distribuidas en 638 comunidades dispersas en 383 mil 567 hectáreas de Área Natural Protegida, declarada como tal por el presidente Ernesto Zedillo en 1997.
Actualmente, en este lugar funciona una red de alrededor de 65 microempresas comunitarias de Ecoturismo, en las cuales trabajan trescientas familias y grupos comunitarios que ofrecen diversos servicios a los visitantes, desde caminatas guiadas y experiencias culturales, hasta alojamiento en cabañas de barro, comida –cuentan con 26 fondas-- y espacios para acampar, además de talleres artesanales como elaboración de quesos, bordados y herbolaria, entre otros, con lo que ponen en valor lo que la naturaleza les dio: una gran biodiversidad y la belleza escénica del paisaje, recursos que llegan directamente a los negocios locales, haciendo de la conservación del sitio una actividad lucrativa.
Pero esto no surgió de manera espontánea, tiene su historia, ya larga, cuando Pati Ruiz Orozco, maestra de música en una secundaria de la ciudad de Querétaro, se mudó con su familia a una comunidad en las montañas de la Sierra Gorda, para en 1987 fundar junto con habitantes locales el Grupo Ecológico de la Sierra Gorda (GESG), con el objetivo de crear conciencia sobre la biodiversidad, sus amenazas y un movimiento de base para construir un futuro regenerativo en la región. Diez años después, lograrían que se les decretara como Área Natural Protegida y Zedillo la nombró directora federal de la Reserva de Biosfera Sierra Gorda, cargo que desempeñó hasta 2009. Entonces regresó a dirigir el GESG.
Pati –como gusta que le digan-- desarrolló lo que denomina “economía emocional” y que define como un “conjunto de valores, emociones, conocimientos, capacidades y sentimientos que permiten que una comunidad se involucre en la conservación y mantenga en el tiempo las soluciones que hacen posible regenerar la naturaleza”.
Pero los retos han sido muchos, por ejemplo, la basura. Pati Explica que en una zona montañosa, con pequeñas comunidades distantes unas de otras, recolectar y transportar basura representa un enorme reto logístico. Para enfrentar este problema que durante décadas contaminó los cuerpos de agua y degradó el suelo, han construido, apoyado y equipado más de 170 centros de acopio comunitarios, en los que cada año recolectan nueve mil toneladas de materiales reciclables como vidrio, plástico, cartón, Tetra Pack y hasta chatarra de carros, que cada uno vende en Querétaro y en cuya comercialización no interviene el GESG.
Catalogada como una Institución de Asistencia Privada, el GESG es una Organización no Gubernamental que se sustenta en donaciones de particulares, fundaciones, organismos internacionales y fondos públicos como los de Sello Querétaro, un programa del gobierno estatal que implica un impuesto de carbono para las empresas más contaminantes. Las comunidades pusieron 50 mil hectáreas en modo de regeneración natural y a cambio reciben recursos de este programa.
Pati se emociona, y con razón, al hablar de todo lo que hecho durante ya casi cuatro décadas, labor que le ha merecido cincuenta premios internacionales y el reconocimiento de las comunidades.

title: How New Zealand’s Asian communities celebrate a mid-autumn festival in spring
content:
Asian communities nationwide are marking mid-autumn celebrations in their own ways.
The celebrations fall on the 15th day of the eighth month of the lunar calendar, a time traditionally associated with harvests and a full moon in the Northern Hemisphere.
In Auckland, a three-day Moon Festival is poised to begin on Friday.
The event marks the arrival of the Mid-Autumn Festival, known as Zhongqiu Jie (中秋节) in Chinese, one of the most important celebrations in the Chinese calendar.
However, the festival is only one expression of much broader traditions.
South Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese communities across the country are also observing the season through customs shaped by their own history, food and family rituals.
In Vietnam, the celebration is called Tết Trung Thu and is often described as a festival for children.
This year, Tết Trung Thu falls on Friday.
In Lower Hutt, the Vietnamese community plans to mark the occasion a day later with the Moonlit Memories Festival at Te Mako Naenae Community Centre.
Vinh Nguyen, director of event organiser Viet Hub NZ, said the festival would give the wider community a chance to experience the atmosphere of celebrations he remembered from childhood.
Activities are set to include lion dancing, bánh Trung Thu (mooncakes), star lanterns, Vietnamese crafts and masks, children's games, storytelling, food and cultural performances.
Nguyen said the festival had long held a special place in Vietnamese culture.
She said the celebration allowed Vietnamese children growing up in New Zealand to maintain a connection to tradition.
"I think that says a lot about the migrant experience. Home may look different now, but our stories, traditions and memories travel with us," she said.
"And I hope our children grow up knowing that they don't have to choose between being Kiwi and being Vietnamese. They can be both and be proud of both."
New Zealand's South Korean community celebrates Chuseok, also known as Hangawi, at the same time of year.
It's one of South Korea's most important traditional holidays.
Falling on Friday this year, Chuseok will be marked at several schools and universities across New Zealand, giving Korean students and families a chance to celebrate the holiday away from home.
Long Bay College in Auckland will mark the occasion on Friday with traditional Korean food and games, while the University of Canterbury Korean Society is planning a Chuseok Festival on Saturday that will include cultural performances and activities.
Soo Jung, vice-president of the University of Canterbury Korean Society, said the festival had been held annually on campus since 2023.
This year's programme will feature samul nori (a modern form of traditional Korean percussion performed with four instruments), buchaechum (a traditional Korean fan dance), a gumdo sword arts demonstration and K-pop dance performances.
Visitors will also have the chance to sample traditional festival food, including songpyeon - half-moon-shaped rice cakes with a variety of fillings, traditionally steamed over pine needles and said to symbolise growth and progress.
Jung said the event would give people from across Christchurch an opportunity to experience South Korean culture and traditions together.
"It is definitely a great opportunity for Kiwis, and people from any background, to experience Korean culture in a fun and welcoming environment," Jung said.
New Zealand's Japanese community traditionally observes Tsukimi at this time of year.
Literally meaning "moon viewing", Tsukimi is a centuries-old tradition of gathering to admire the large celestial body in the autumn night sky.
Tsukimi falls on Friday, with celebrations including such things as poetry, traditional music and dance.
Food also plays an important role.
Among the best-known offerings is tsukimi dango - small round rice dumplings whose shape evokes the full moon.
In Auckland, libraries and community groups are hosting a series of Tsukimi-themed events this year, bringing Japanese moon-viewing traditions to local families.
At Point Chevalier Library, a Tsukimi celebration will be held on 1 October.
The Japan Kauri Education Trust will also host a Japanese Moon Festival at Ōwairaka Connecting Communities Hub on 28 September, inviting visitors to create their own rabbit-inspired kaleidoscopes and learn about the stories and traditions behind Tsukimi.
This year, some community events are also bringing different cultural traditions together in a single celebration.
At Epsom Community Centre, a Moon Festival on 3 October will combine Chinese and Korean traditions.
Visitors will be able to make Chinese mooncakes and paper lanterns, prepare South Korean songpyeon rice cakes, try on traditional hanbok and take part in a hanbok runway.
Sanjay Pereira, manager of the community centre, said Epsom was home to a large and diverse Asian population, and that festivals tied to the lunar calendar held particular significance for many families in the area.
He said he hoped the event would give Asian families a chance to reconnect with their cultures and customs, while also giving the wider community an opportunity to experience diversity.
Yoona Song, a senior library and council services assistant who helped organise a Moon Festival cultural event at Botany Library on Sunday, said the celebration also brought together people from a wide range of cultural and ethnic backgrounds through traditional games and craft activities from several Asian cultures.
"Our goal was not only to celebrate the Moon Festival," Song said. "We hoped this would encourage greater cultural understanding, curiosity and appreciation within our diverse community."
Although Asian communities mark the season in different ways, Song said events such as the Moon Festival could make those traditions more accessible to people from all backgrounds.
"We hope the event encourages Aucklanders to explore and appreciate the diverse cultures that make up our community, while also fostering a sense of belonging and inclusion," Song said.

title: From wanting to be seen as white to finding his way back to te reo Māori
content:
Ake, Ake, Ake - A forever language
Nathan Grey (Ngāti Porou, Ngāti Tūwharetoa, Ngāti Raukawa) grew up knowing he was Māori but not knowing much about what that meant.
His grandparents belonged to a generation where te reo Māori had been suppressed, and he was taught that success meant moving away from his Māoritanga, his identity.
"I didn't grow up with te reo. I didn't know anything and I didn't actually want to know anything," he said.
"I was always told that to be successful you had to be white.
"So I made that my mission to surround myself with Pākehā... in high school I was white.
"I was called the Dalmatian and I was proud of that. I was like, yo, that means it's working. Like I am brown, but actually people see me as white."
His older brother would eventually give him a different way of seeing himself.
After his brother completed a full-immersion te reo Māori course at Te Wānanga Takiura, Grey felt a pull to reclaim his ancestral language.
Grey enrolled at the same wānanga and began a journey that would eventually lead him to teaching te reo Māori himself.
Looking back, he said he had always known he would return to a part of himself that had been missing.
"You sort of know somewhere that you end up returning to the place of which has been missing from you for a while," he said.
"And because of suppressing the person who I was in high school, that was bound to come up eventually after that. So I like to think it naturally happened."
But reconnecting with that part of himself was not easy. Grey said learning te reo brought up feelings of mamae he had spent years pushing away.
"Honestly, it was like one of the hardest things.
"Because for 20 years I just put these feelings away and then having to get into a space where you have to face that... You're like, whoa, what is happening?"
He described the experience as scary but said Takiura taught him to lean on the people around him.
"They're all doing the same thing. They're all going through that same feeling as well," he said.
"And you just talk about it and you just come to understand like, oh my God, like yeah, this isn't the fault of ours.
"We shouldn't have to feel ashamed or embarrassed about the feelings, about us not knowing what we should know."
Now a kaiako of te reo Māori at Selwyn Community Education, Grey said learning te reo Māori has only opened more doors.
"It sort of got me into spaces like this [teaching], got me into spaces working with people, like social work and things like that.
"So very grateful that I've been able to actually learn about who I am. Because it's not like just the language, it's about you and then whatever follows that as well."
His ākonga all come from many different backgrounds, including fifth generation Pākehā and tauiwi learners from countries such as Argentina.
Many tell him they want to learn because they want to respect and better understand the country they live in.
Grey said he loves seeing people from different backgrounds come together through te reo Māori.
"I think it's super important for the reo to be shared in a way that is mindful of what you're sharing, but also not trying to make it a scary experience for those who are wanting to embark on it, but are a little bit whakamā," he said.
"They don't know how to approach it, but they want to approach it in a respectful way."
He said the more people who learn te reo Māori, the more understanding there can be of Māori culture and people.
"I just think the more people who speak te reo, the better," he said.
"The better the country, the more understanding we have to the culture and the people.
"Things that are good for Māori are good for everyone."
Grey hopes his students leave knowing they are capable of learning the language, even if they feel whakamā at first.
"I hope that they take away that they can actually do it, that they have the ability to do so, and then there's people around them to tautoko them for that," he said.
"And you can see the keenness that they have for it. So I just hope they hold on to that keenness and carry on, really, with their mahi."

title: 'Get on board':Te reo Māori offers a deeper understanding of Aotearoa
content:
The evolving education of te reo Māori in Aotearoa
Te reo Māori is being learnt by more people across Aotearoa, as the language continues to be revitalised across generations.
This year's Te Wiki o Te Reo Māori theme, Ake, Ake, Ake - A Forever Language, reflects that intergenerational journey and the role each generation plays in keeping the reo alive and passing it on.
Māori Language Commissioner Professor Rawinia Higgins describes it as a three-generation kaupapa, where every step towards learning and using te reo contributes to the next generation.
At Selwyn Community Education in Tāmaki Makaurau, those journeys are coming together in one classroom.
For fifth-generation Pākehā Rebecca Jerram, learning te reo Māori is about understanding the relationship between Māori and Pākehā and what that means for future generations.
"I think we actually owe it to our future New Zealanders, to be honest," she said.
"If you've been here a long time, then maybe the onus is on us even more to make sure that, hey, we've been hanging out here for quite a while, and we really need to understand te ao Māori and te taiao, and all the concepts that come with being a partner with Māori."
Jerram has been learning te reo Māori for around five or six years. She teaches landscape architecture at Unitec and said she wants future generations of Pākehā and tauiwi to better understand the partnership between Māori and Pākehā.
"We are in a partnership, and some might say it's a forced marriage, or it's an arranged marriage. But it's a marriage nonetheless.
"We're married, and I guess you've got to get to know your partner. So in my mind, it's about really getting to know that partnership and understanding what we bring to it together. And we shouldn't be flying blind."
Jerram said Māori have also created space for Pākehā to learn and engage with te ao Māori.
"Māori have been very patient with Pākehā in that they've actually opened their world to us. It's up to us to reciprocate," she said.
"It's never been, or not in my lifetime, has it been thrown at us. It's not been taunted for not speaking the tongue of the whenua.
"We've been coached and manaaki-ed through with a lot of awhi, and how lucky are we that Māori are prepared to take a long walk.
"It's a long, long walk, it's generational, and I still encourage Pākehā to join that walk."
Jerram said she sees learning te reo as part of that long-term commitment to the relationship between Māori and Pākehā.
"I just think it's on our generation, as much as it has been to our tūpuna that have gone, to actually ensure that the people coming through do understand this partnership as well."
Argentinian ākonga Facu Cuello said learning te reo Māori was one of the first things he did after moving to Aotearoa three years ago.
"I moved to a new country, I need to learn the language of the country. I already spoke English, but from my perspective, Māori is the native language of the country, so for me moving from overseas into the country, the least I can do is to make an effort to learn the language."
He hoped that more people shared that whakaaro.
"I wish more people had the same perspective, that you're moving to a country that speaks Māori, and you should make an effort at least to pick up the basics, or do as much as you can, and it's within your reach in your day-to-day, to honour the language, honour the people, and contribute to the revitalisation of a language that needs it."
Cuello said learning te reo has changed the way he experiences the country around him.
"When you start learning about all those stories and those perspectives and ways of thinking, it really gives it a different meaning."
For Māori ākonga Aidan Te Whata, learning te reo is about reconnecting with a language that was not passed down through his whānau.
Te Whata, who has whakapapa to Ngāti Porou, Te Whānau-ā-Apanui, Rongowhakaata and Ngāpuhi, grew up in te ao Pākehā, speaking English.
He said the attitudes he encountered towards te reo when he was younger became internalised.
"You hear, 'oh, what's that language? Oh, it's a dead language.' It's like, you kind of just bury it within you and you believe it yourself. It starts to manifest as a belief."
Now in his 30s, Te Whata said his relationship with the language has changed.
"I no longer believe that. And I'm finding ways to reconnect with my whakapapa, my language."
His reo journey has also brought him closer to his whānau and tūrangawaewae.
"Your whakapapa and your ancestors are looking down and going, you know, look at you go. You're carrying that with you. You carry your whānau with you."
He said being part of a generation helping revitalise te reo is something to be proud of.
"I was going to say it's been lost. It's not been lost. It's been revitalised.
"And we're the ones that are to bring it back. And it's exciting. And something to be proud of."
Te Whata said having Pākehā and tauiwi alongside him in the classroom also shows the language is being embraced by people from across the world.
"I think it's beautiful...it shows us, the love will always overcome hate."
Te Whata wants to continue learning until speaking te reo Māori becomes second nature.
"I want to do this more, and I ain't going to stop until I begin thinking in Māori. That's when I'm like, 'ooh, I've made it'.
For many, learning te reo is a way to deeper understand the place they call home.
Jerram said the country has felt increasingly divided in the last few years and believes te ao Māori can offer a way towards greater understanding.
"I think the sea has been choppy in the last two to three years particularly. There's been storms coming through, and they are still coming.
"I think we need to look to a place where Tangaroa is calm.
"We need the seas to just settle. We need people to understand why it's so important to have that settling, because we're a country that's at peace in a really mixed-up world."
Jerram believes it's on the generation that she belongs to, to see themselves as part of continuing the change.
"I was going to say proponents of change, but Māori themselves have driven that."
"The least we can do is get on board."

title: More than 374k Auckland households to get $377 from Entrust
content:
Why do I pay tax on my KiwiSaver?
Auckland households are in for a windfall when they receive their annual payment from their lines company.
This is something that happens around the country at different times of the year, but Auckland's payment from Entrust, which owns 75 percent of Vector, is one of the largest.
The payments occur because community and consumer trusts often own shares in their local lines company. Wellington Electricity and Powerco are notable exceptions.
Each year, the lines company may pay a dividend to shareholders, or the trust may have its own accumulated funds, and this money is paid out to the trust's beneficiaries - consumers of power.
Entrust said more than 374,000 households and businesses in central, east and south Auckland would receive a payment of $377 each.
"There's a real sense of excitement when the dividend arrives. For some people it helps with everyday costs, for others it's an opportunity to treat themselves or put a little extra aside," chair Denise Lee said.
"We know this dividend makes a real difference in people's lives because they tell us."
Since 1994, Entrust has paid more than $2.5 billion in dividends to eligible Aucklanders.
The dividend is paid either as a direct credit to bank accounts or as a credit on the recipient's next power bill, depending on the payment method selected. Those whose payment could not be completed will be sent a notification from Entrust.
The Entrust District covers central, east, and south Auckland. It is the areas of Auckland, Manukau, northern Papakura, and eastern Franklin that were formerly part of the old Auckland Electric Power Board.
To receive the 2026 dividend, people must have been the named power account holder on the Vector electricity network in the Entrust district at midnight on August 12.
Financial coach Shula Newland said it would be welcome for households where money was tight.
But she said many people would probably prefer to have cheaper power through the year.

title: Thousands of children under 5 receive flu vaccine as sickness overwhelms health system
content:
Thousands of children under five have had a flu shot since it was made free for all of them.
On 1 September, Pharmac made vaccinations free for under fives after hospitals and clinics became overwhelmed with this season's very infectious strain of influenza A.
In figures provided on Tuesday, Health NZ said 3,843 under-fives had had their flu shots between then and 20 September.
Of these, 1723 were in the Northern region, with more than 800 each in the lower North Island and the South Island regions, and 435 in the Midland region which comprises Taranaki, Waikato and Bay of Plenty.
The number vaccinated in those 19 days was three and a half times the amount of the two weeks before the vaccination was free.
Auckland GP Mamaeroa David said a vaccination clinic at a Kōhanga Reo shortly after the change was one of the highlights of her career.
As well as under fives, the team immunised kuia and parents, including the whānau of a three-day-old baby. They also did catch-up vaccinations for a two-year-old who had never been vaccinated, she said.
"The whānau were really ready to engage because they had suffered a hard flu season this year - in fact there was still a third of that kōhanga reo roll not at kohanga on the day," she said.
"It was just amazing to be able to not have those whānau pay for those little kōhanga reo pēpē to have their flu vaccine."
It was heartening to know they were helping protect whole families, said David, who is also the senior Māori medical advisor for the Immunisation Advisory Centre.
In figures released last week, hospitalisations for children with flu-like illness had finally dropped, after spending weeks climbing.
But David warned there were still a lot of "snotty illnesses" circulating and there was often a sting in the tail of the winter season.
Health NZ was also encouraging parents to get their children immunised.
The flu vaccine was free for children from six months until their fifth birthday. Previously, it was only free for those at higher risk of serious disease.
The immunisation director of Health NZ's National Public Health Service, Nikki Canter-Burgoyne, said it was not too late for anyone to protect themselves.
"Vaccination remains important, even for people who have already had influenza this season, as it helps protect against influenza viruses they may not have previously encountered," she said.
This season's vaccination would be available into the new year, she said.
It was free for many others, including those over 65 or people who had health conditions that put them at greater risk.

title: Timaru woman finds rare moa bones during daily beach walk
content:
Timaru woman finds rare moa bones during daily beach walk
Family stumbles upon Moa bones on daily beach walk
A family is buzzing after a woman stumbled upon moa bones during her daily beach walk south of Timaru.
Pippa Yates found what she suspected to be the bones of the now-extinct New Zealand bird at St Andrews Beach, which the South Canterbury Museum confirmed after closer inspection.
Yates told Checkpoint the discovery was all the family could talk about.
"Anytime we get a spare moment, we clean the bones that we've got. We've got probably a good half a bucket full of moa bones now, so they're seemingly coming up a lot better than we expected they would," she said.
"The museum said they'd crumble apart, so far we've got some really big pieces that have actually made it through being cleaned very carefully."
Yates said the family were just using plain water to clean the bones to try and emulate natural washing on the beach.
She said she's had to sacrifice her daughter's plastic basin previously used for cleaning baby bottles.
"We put a bit of cold water over the bones, which are sort of still within clay in big chunks, and swish the water over them from side to side, let them sit for an hour or more, and then drain the water out and start again, being careful not to lose any of the tiny bits of bone as well, so it's a slow process," Yates said.
Yates said the family had been scaling the beach for about four years after hearing about a man finding a moa footprint and bones.
"I walk looking at my feet basically the entire time where we walk, specifically in all the clay banks, we always look in those areas thinking we might see a footprint, and that's something I can bring my daughter back to see," she said.
"We as a family have quite a collection of bones and oddities in our little bone cabinet at home, so we're quite familiar with the look of bone.
"The porosity of the bone, I could tell looking down on it that it looks sort of like a cross section of a bone as opposed to a piece of driftwood or something else stuck in the mud."
Yates' four-year-old daughter, Lucy, is part of an explorer club at the museum.
She said she's been going ever since she could walk.
"She's obsessed with the museum, and she knows where everything is and likes to show anybody that comes to visit us where everything is in the museum," Yates said.
"So yes, she's got a keen interest on all those kinds of things. Her dad has got her quite interested in it as well, if we find skeletal remains of any kind, dead bird, on the beach, we bag it up and bring it home for dad to make it into a display for our bone cabinet.
"We have quite a lot of seagulls and all sorts of things in the bone cabinet."
Yates said the family planned on keeping a few of the larger bones to possibly piece them together.
She hoped to put it on display in their home for visitors.
"But any of the really obviously bone-looking bones, we're going to try and give back the museum, which will be nice to have on display," she said.
"Molly's my daughter who was on my front while we were walking on the beach. So, when she has children one day, she can go and say, 'this is the bones that mum and I found when I was just a baby on her front' and her children and her great grandchildren and those kinds of things.
"It's a legacy to have it on display, and any of the tiny little bits of we're going to put in specimen jars and bring them to the (kindergarten) and the school to have a look at as well."

title: South African circus gives young performers a new route forward
content:
Circus
Clutching an aerial hoop on a Johannesburg circus stage, a young performer pauses for a split second before launching into the air and gliding, drawing cheers from the crowd below.
For 29-year-old Brian Ngobese, who grew up in South Africa’s impoverished Alexandra township, moments like this mean more than applause. The circus has given him a stage, a livelihood and a way to turn his talent into work.
“We just want to show people that we can make it out of the township,” said Ngobese. “What you want to accomplish, you can actually make it.”
Behind the colorful spectacle is a social program that helps performers from under-resourced communities turn talent into opportunity and paid work.
Alexandra is one of Johannesburg’s most densely populated townships, marked by high poverty and unemployment despite being just a few kilometers from Sandton, a major financial district dubbed the “richest square mile in Africa.”
For many young South Africans, missing out on training opportunities often means spending years on the fringes of the labor market.
Many tend to stay unemployed rather than move into informal work, according to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development.
Unemployment among 18 to 34-year-old South Africans was about 45% in 2025, according to Statistics South Africa.
Performers train for years to build the strength, flexibility and discipline needed to work professionally. Some become instructors, while others take paid work with production companies or The Cirk, a professional Johannesburg circus company.
The program is designed to sustain itself through training, performances and other circus work rather than relying entirely on outside funding.
Ngobese’s older brother first introduced him to South African street and social dancing. He later moved into contemporary, hip-hop and other styles, building on a love of performing that began in childhood.
He found circus almost by accident after auditioning as a dancer for a Joburg Theatre production in 2019. What began as a short job became a career when The Cirk invited him to stay and train.
Ngobese received support for training and transportation through Jozi Circus School’s youth development program. The school partners with The Cirk, where he now works.
“Cirk was like an adventure,” he recalled. “When I saw people flying, I was like, ‘Is this what they’re doing here?’ Okay, this is life. I’m like, ‘Let’s go for it.’”
Years later, Ngobese would quickly mend a tear in his costume, his eyes streaked with red and yellow makeup, as he prepared to go on stage.
The animal-free circus show blends choreography with gravity-defying acrobatics on silks and hoops. Ngobese plays a “little star” journeying through oceans, fantastical lands, and fiery fortresses in search of what will make him shine.
The role reflects Ngobese’s own journey into a world he had never imagined for himself.
Circus also brought Ngobese together with Zenzele Letsoela, a fellow dancer from Alexandra.
“I’m grateful to Cirk for bringing me another brother I didn’t know I actually needed in my life,” said Ngobese.
Together, they combined dance with circus skills and began attracting attention beyond the school. “People were like, ’Where are those guys? We want those guys. We want to see more,” he said.
Letsoela, 38, trained in ballet and pantsula, a fast-paced South African township dance style. Moving into aerial acrobatics brought an unexpected challenge: he is terrified of heights.
“I wouldn’t say I’ve learned to overcome my fear of heights, but I’ve learned to work around it,” he said.
Hoisted about two meters above the stage as a magical tree, Letsoela stays in character despite the nerves.
“People don’t see that I’m actually nervous going into the air. I look very comfortable,” he said. “And I’m like, if only you guys knew, I am dying inside.”
By the end of the show, Ngobese, glittering in gold as the little star who has finally found where he belongs, was back in the air — hanging from an aerial silk by one arm as gasps gave way to more cheers.

title: Cameroon Trains 34 Instructors to Expand Local Sports Equipment Manufacturing
content: Cameroon has trained 34 new trainers under a program designed to expand local production of sports equipment and support youth-led businesses in a market partly supplied by imports. The participants received their certificates in Yaoundé on September 17 under the Project for the Socio-economic Integration of Young People through the Creation of Micro-enterprises for the Manufacture of Sports Equipment, PIFMAS. The program is run by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Civic Education, MINJEC, in collaboration with the Conference of Ministers of Youth and Sports of La Francophonie, CONFEJES. The beneficiaries completed 10 days of technical and business training. Of the 34 participants, 15 were trained in ball manufacturing, 13 in net production and six in entrepreneurship support. They are expected to transfer their skills to young people across the country’s 10 regions. The initiative is also intended to create a local value chain around the production and commercialization of sports equipment. The revamped PIFMAS program, launched in 2024, is designed to support the development of production and incubation capacity across Cameroon. MINJEC says more than 500 young people have already been trained in the production of sports equipment ...

title: Mali : l'hôpital de Sikasso et dix artisans dotés d'installations solaires pour sécuriser leur approvisionnement
content:
Mali : l'hôpital de Sikasso et dix artisans dotés d'installations solaires pour sécuriser leur approvisionnement
Dans le cadre des œuvres sociales de la présidence, l'hôpital régional de Sikasso et dix artisans ont reçu des équipements solaires pour garantir leur approvisionnement électrique.
Dans le cadre des œuvres sociales du Président de la Transition, le Général d’Armée Assimi Goïta, l'hôpital régional de Sikasso et dix maîtres artisans ont été dotés, samedi 19 septembre 2026, d'équipements photovoltaïques destinés à sécuriser durablement leur alimentation électrique.
Le Conseiller spécial du Chef de l'État, Aguibou Dembélé, a procédé à l'inauguration de l'installation photovoltaïque de l'hôpital régional de Sikasso ainsi qu'à la remise officielle d'équipements solaires à dix maîtres artisans de la troisième région administrative du Mali. La cérémonie s'est déroulée en présence de la Gouverneure de la région, Marie Claire Dembélé, des autorités et légitimités traditionnelles, ainsi que de la délégation des œuvres sociales venue de Bamako.
D'une capacité de 1 075 kWh, l'installation de l'hôpital, composée de panneaux photovoltaïques, de batteries de stockage et d'onduleurs intelligents, vise à garantir la continuité des soins. « Nous ne voulons plus d'arrêt des soins à cause du manque d'électricité », a déclaré Aguibou Dembélé, précisant que le Président de la Transition avait instruit l'installation de panneaux solaires dans plusieurs centres de santé à travers le pays.
La Gouverneure de Sikasso a souligné le caractère essentiel d'une électricité disponible en permanence pour l'éclairage des salles de soins, la conservation des médicaments et le fonctionnement des équipements médicaux, avant de solliciter l'octroi d'ambulances supplémentaires pour l'établissement. La Directrice générale de l'hôpital, le docteur Assetou Cissouma, a estimé que cette installation permettrait de renforcer l'alimentation électrique de la structure et d'améliorer la prise en charge des patients.
Les dix bénéficiaires, comprenant huit menuisiers métalliques, un menuisier bois et un tailleur, ont également reçu leurs équipements à l'issue de la cérémonie, marquée par la coupure du ruban symbolique et la visite des installations. L'un d'eux, Sory Diaby, a indiqué que les difficultés d'accès à l'électricité avaient jusqu'ici limité sa production. Les bénéficiaires ont par ailleurs formulé des vœux pour la stabilité, la paix et la croissance économique du Mali.

title: Ooredoo Tunisie et Kafel El Yatim accompagnent 400 enfants à l’occasion de la rentrée scolaire
content:
À l’occasion de la rentrée scolaire, Ooredoo Tunisie poursuit son engagement en faveur des enfants et des familles à travers une nouvelle action Back to School, menée en partenariat avec l’Association Kafel El Yatim, dans le cadre de son programme de responsabilité sociétale Tounes T3ich.
Cette année, Ooredoo a offert à 400 enfants des cartables entièrement équipés de fournitures scolaires, afin de leur permettre d’aborder la nouvelle année scolaire dans les meilleures conditions. L’initiative a bénéficié à des enfants issus de presque tous les 24 gouvernorats de Tunisie, permettant ainsi à cette action solidaire de toucher des communautés à travers tout le pays.
Au-delà de la distribution des fournitures scolaires, Ooredoo a également accueilli un groupe d’enfants dans ses locaux à l’occasion d’une célébration spéciale de la rentrée. Un moment convivial et joyeux leur permettant de partager ensemble l’enthousiasme d’un nouveau départ avant de retrouver les bancs de l’école.
À cette occasion, Eyas Assaf, CEO de Ooredoo Tunisie, a déclaré :
« La rentrée scolaire doit être pour chaque enfant un moment d’enthousiasme, d’espoir et d’opportunités. À travers Tounes T3ich et notre partenariat avec Kafel El Yatim, nous sommes fiers d’être aux côtés de 400 enfants à travers la Tunisie et de contribuer, à notre manière, à leur offrir les meilleures conditions pour commencer cette nouvelle année scolaire. Soutenir les enfants et l’éducation demeure une dimension essentielle de notre engagement envers les communautés que nous servons. »
Cette initiative Back to School s’inscrit pleinement dans les priorités de Tounes T3ich, le programme de responsabilité sociétale de Ooredoo Tunisie, qui place notamment l’éducation, l’inclusion sociale et le bien-être des communautés au cœur de ses actions.
À travers la continuité de sa collaboration avec l’Association Kafel El Yatim et ses différents partenaires de la société civile, Ooredoo Tunisie réaffirme sa volonté de développer des initiatives répondant à des besoins concrets et générant un impact positif dans les différentes régions du pays.
Parce que chaque rentrée marque le début de nouveaux espoirs, Ooredoo Tunisie souhaite à tous les enfants tunisiens une année scolaire pleine d’apprentissage, de réussite et de nouvelles opportunités.

title: Ebola en RDC: MSF lance un projet pour tester l'efficacité d'un vaccin contre le virus Bundibugyo
content:
Ebola en RDC: MSF lance un projet pour tester l'efficacité d'un vaccin contre le virus Bundibugyo
L’ONG Médecins sans frontières a lancé, samedi 19 septembre, le projet Bravo, afin de récolter les données sur les effets d’un vaccin Evrebo inoculé à 20 000 personnels de santé dans et autour de Bunia. Si l’objectif est la protection des personnes en première ligne dans la lutte contre Ebola, l’étude doit aussi permettre de tester l’efficacité du vaccin contre le virus Bundibugyo.
Publié le :
« On veut apporter le maximum de protection aux personnels de première ligne », déclare d’emblée Mathilde Lagarde, coordinatrice du projet « Bundibugyo, répondre avec la vaccination – on est ensemble » (Bravo) impulsé par Médecins sans frontières.
Alors que la pire épidémie d'Ebola qu’ai connu la RDC sévit toujours dans l'est du pays, l’objectif de cette étude tend à montrer si le vaccin disponible – efficace contre le virus Ebola Zaïre – « permet de réduire les formes graves de la maladie et s’il permet d’en réduire la mortalité », précise l’humanitaire.
À lire aussiEn quoi consiste la stratégie de protection contre Ebola RDC ?
Grâce à la vaccination des personnels de santé, en première ligne et souvent premières victimes de la maladie, docteurs et épidémiologistes pourront recueillir des données permettant d’apporter des « informations sur la réalité de ce vaccin qui seront utiles pour cette épidémie et toutes les suivantes », continue Mathilde Lagarde, alors que des vaccins sont pour l’heure en phase de test.
Selon un communiqué de l’ONG, le vaccin Evrebo disponible pourrait donc représenter une solution temporaire, dans l’attente des résultats des recherches.
On veut apporter le maximum de protection aux personnels de première ligne. Dans toute épidémie, on cherche toujours à utiliser le meilleur vaccin disponible. Et aujourd'hui, le vaccin Ervebo est le seul vaccin validé et disponible à grande échelle. Aujourd'hui, dans l'étude de ce qu'on va regarder, c'est si Ervebo permet de réduire le risque d'infection, s'il permet de réduire les formes graves de la maladie et s'il permet aussi de réduire la mortalité. Évidemment, l'objectif est dans un premier temps de vacciner les personnels de première ligne et de générer des données solides qui pourront en effet apporter des informations sur la réalité de ce vaccin qui seront utiles pour cette épidémie et pour toutes les suivantes. Mais il y a aussi, en parallèle des essais cliniques qui sont en cours. Donc à un moment donné, si les vaccins spécifiques sont disponibles, et comme dans toute épidémie, on utilise le meilleur vaccin disponible, ce seront les vaccins spécifiques qui seront utilisés. Ça permettra quand même de démontrer quel est le degré d'efficacité de Ervebo contre la maladie à virus Bundibugyo.
Mathilde Lagarde, coordinatrice MSF du projet Bravo

title: Slik vart prestekrisa løyst: – Vi hadde ingen søkarar
content:
Over heile landet står prestestillingar tomme. Den norske kyrkja hadde ved inngangen til året 101,4 tomme stillingar, men no ser fleire prosti lys i tunnelen.
– Vi tullar med å seie at du blir sikra jobb når du er ferdig.
Nytilsett prest i Jølster, Selma Dahle Kraft, kunne fått jobb kor ho ville. Men ho valde å takke ja til jobb i Sunnfjord.
Under heile studieløpet har ho vore klar over at mangelen på prestar er prekær over heile landet.
– Det har vore tema heile vegen. Eg er eigentleg frå Oslo, men eg hadde lyst til å kome meg ut av byen, oppleve naturen.
Lange periodar utan søkarar har tvinga fram mellombelse løysingar og bruk av pensjonistar.
– For eit år sidan gjekk eg ut og sa at vi treng fem nye prestar, og vi hadde ingen søkjarar. Men no har vi fått tilsett i alle dei fem stillingane. Det er vi ganske stolte av, seier prost i Sunnfjord, Knut Magne Nesse.
I dei seks åra han har sete i stillinga, har den uavklarte mannskapssituasjon vore eit gjennomgåande problem.
– Når det blir mellombelse løysingar, blir det ikkje noko langsiktigheit eller målretting i arbeidet. Det går ofte utover arbeidet med konfirmantar, barn og unge. Det er veldig flott at vi har pensjonistar som kan hjelpe oss, men dette var ein situasjon vi måtte ut av.
Satsar på lønn under studiane
Bak den positive snuoperasjonen ligg ein bevisst strategi frå bispedømmet. I Bjørgvin har dei teke i bruk nye og utradisjonelle rekrutteringsmetodar for å trekke til seg folk.
Eitt av dei mest effektive grepa er å tilby studentar som enno ikkje er ferdige med teologistudiet full lønn mot at dei studerer delar av tida.
– Vi har gjort grep i Bjørgvin bispedømme som har gjort at vi har fått mange nye til å søke på prestestillingane, seier biskop Ragnhild Jepsen.
I tillegg har utradisjonelle utdanningsvegar, som erfaringsbasert master, opna dørene for kandidatar med ein annan fagbakgrunn. Jepsen fortel at dei fleste ho har vigsla til prest det siste året, har gått denne vegen.
– Dei får 100 prosent lønn, men dei jobbar 60 prosent og får lov til å studere i 40. Då får ein både praksis samstundes som ein har moglegheit til å følgje studiane. Det ser vi har ein klar effekt, forklarar biskopen.
15 nye prestar det siste året
Resultata av nytenkinga viser seg no over heile bispedømmet. Det siste året er det tilsett 15 nye prestar.
– Ingen kyrkjelag er per i dag heilt utan prest. Vi skaffar prestar til alle gudstenester og kyrkjelege handlingar, seier Jepsen.
Sjølv om bispedømmet framleis er avhengig av pensjonistar i periodar, har tiltaka ført til ei etterlengta fornying i presteskapet.
Heidi Voltersvik Styve har vore kateket i Sunnfjord i 22 år. Tilbodet om løn medan ho studerer var avgjerande for at ho tok steget vidare som prest.
– No kan eg ta det på deltid og jobbe samstundes, og eg har stor glede av det.
I Nidaros bispedøme har mange gjort som Styve i Sunnfjord. Heile 10 prosent av prestestaben har blitt rekrutterte via den nye ordninga.
– Prest under utdanning er ein styrke for kyrkja. Vi hentar folk med ulike erfaringar og bakgrunn, og mange av dei har lokalt tilknyting, seier HR-sjef Håkon Olaussen i Nidaros.
Han strekar under at dei framleis har stillingar som står tomme, men at dei no har 10 nye prestar under utdanning. 6–7 prestar har alt fullført løpet.
Leiar i Kyrkjerådet, Harald Hegstad, meiner erfaringane frå mellom anna Sunnfjord og Nidaros viser at fleire av tiltaka kyrkja har satsa på dei siste åra, verkar.
– Det er eg veldig glad for. Det viser at systematisk og langsiktig arbeid med rekruttering ber frukter. Vi ser det i Sunnfjord, men også andre stader i landet, seier Hegstad.
Han peikar særleg på ordninga med prestar under utdanning og den erfaringsbaserte masterutdanninga, som gjer det mogleg å rekruttere folk som allereie bur i lokalsamfunn som treng prestar.
– På den måten får ein også sterkare lokal forankring, og prestar i lokalsamfunn der det kan vere vanskelegare å få nokon til å flytte til, seier han.
Samstundes meiner Hegstad at tiltaka har hindra at prestemangelen har utvikla seg til ein større krise når store prestekull no går av med pensjon.
Gler seg over unge nyutdanna
Blant dei fem nyutnemnde prestane i Sunnfjord er det også unge, nyutdanna prestar. Det er ikkje kvardagskost i distrikta, der slike kandidatar ofte kan velje og vrake mellom stillingar i heile landet.
– Dei nyutdanna er veldig attraktive. No har vi fått kandidatar som har lyst til å komme til oss. Det er veldig motiverande og gjev ein fantastisk fornying i presteskapet, seier prost Nesse.

title: Liberia: Fishermen Turn to God for Protection At Sea
content:
Sam Weah has just returned from his all-night fishing trip after three days of fasting and prayer. Customers who had been waiting on Popo Beach, New Kru Town, rushed to the canoe to make wholesale purchases to sell at retail in the Duala market, one of the most popular commercial hubs in Liberia.
As usual, Weah and his co-fishermen came back safe and unharmed--a routine that has been ongoing for more than two decades. Weah attributed this good luck to an annual fast and prayer organized by the Borough of Fishermen in Popo Beach that started in 2015.
"This fast is very good. We pray for God's protection, and he's [God] always hearing us," said Weah, who backs his fishing job with daily motorbike riding in Point Four, Bushrod Island.
As a fisherman, Weah cannot escape their annual fasting and prayer. Many fishermen here believe in dedicating their canoes and fishing activities to the Almighty God by Christians.
Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn
Deacon Hilton S. Smith, head of the fishermen known as the "Sea Chief," said that, growing up, they saw their fathers engaging in diabolical activities in their quest to protect themselves at sea, including drowning and canoe capsizing. As a generation, they decided that these practices were from the devil and sought a different path.
"Suddenly, fishermen will leave in the water, so as we watched these things years past in the 70s and 80s, since we came up, we have decided the things that our old people did that were hunting them have to go," Smith said.
Commercial fishing ranks among the most hazardous professions globally. Data from the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) indicate that the sector results in approximately 24,000 deaths each year, yielding a mortality rate that can be 50 to 100 times greater than the average across all other worldwide industries.
These findings highlight that despite technological progress, the hazards of commercial fishing remain deeply rooted. Furthermore, many fishers still head out to sea without life jackets, which are critical for survival if a canoe capsizes.
According to Smith, since they started their annual fasting and prayers, "the issue of human casualties has been minimized. Where, sometime during the year, three to five persons will go missing at sea, but since the intervention of God, turning everything over to God, God's protection has been with us."
Solomon N. Daryoue, director for maritime fisheries at the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority (NaFAA), said NaFAA supports prayers and fasting carried out by fishermen. However, he urged them to balance prayers and fasting with protective gear, including life jackets, whenever they go to sea.
According to him, Liberia is not the only nation where fishermen pray and fast. He says, fasting and prayers have existed in the fishing sector long before he was born. "And I have even traveled to some other countries like Ghana. I see that it is even more in those countries than in Liberia."
"People do sacrifices," he says. "They have shrines and these things according to them, have worked, and even in Liberia I have also experienced that they have a particular period that they conduct their prayers, so we respect those views."
Bishop Nicholas Kofa Ansah, Sr., head of the All Believers Church International (ABCI), preaching on the theme "Walking In Your Season of New Beginnings"admonished the fishermen to prepare for both difficult and good times.
"Life is full of seasons. Though, every season of life is not permanent," he says.
"There are seasons of planting and seasons of harvest. There are seasons of waiting and seasons of manifestation. There are seasons when God closes one chapter and opens another. You may have experienced a difficult yesterday, but your yesterday does not have the authority to determine your tomorrow."
A Serious Business
During these three days of fasting and prayers, all fishermen, fishmongers, and fish dryers are not allowed to eat and drink until after 12 pm. They are not allowed to go fishing or sell fish. The sea is closed to all fishing activities at 12 am on the first day of the fast and reopened at 12 am on the last day of the fast. They are also not allowed to drink alcohol and must abstain from sex, even for wedded couples.
Businesses in and around the sea are halted. This year's gathering brought more than a hundred fishermen, fishmongers, and leaders to the Christ Center of Praise Full Gospel Ministry (CCOP) under the theme "Walking In Your Season of New Beginnings" with a supporting scripture text: Isaiah 43:18-19, which says, "Forget the former things; do not dwell on the past. See, I am doing a new thing! Now it springs up; do you not perceive it? I am making a way in the wilderness. And streams in the wasteland."
It began in the early morning hours on Wednesday, September 2. One by one, fishermen walked in to take their seats at the CCOP church before the start of the service. Fishing folks, fish processors, fish dryers, and women dressed in white suits and head ties gathered. Some are mothers of the fishermen, while others are wives gathered to offer prayers for the protection of their loved ones at sea. It marks the 12th edition of the event.
The service started with praise and worship. The singers raised their voices: "Open the floor gates of heaven and cause your rain to fall on me. You are Yahweh, Alpha and Omega."
"Everything God blesses the lives of fishermen, we come to say thank you. Thanking God for the fishing season and committing the next fishing season into the hands of God."
Opening of this year's fasting and prayers which ran from Wednesday, September 2 to Friday, September 4.
Fishermen's Protection is Big on NaFAA's Agenda
In the past year, fishermen have received life jackets to reduce risks at sea and improve sales. Life jackets were distributed by former President George Weah under the Free Marine Life Jackets Initiative.
However, the bulk of these donated vests are not seen on fishermen. It is alleged that some stole theirs, and many do not carry these jackets when going fishing. Liberia has nine coastal counties out of its fifteen.
What mechanisms are in place to ensure protection for fishermen at sea?
According to Daryoue, one of the ways NaFAA is addressing fishermen's safety at sea is the establishment of Collaborative Management Associations (CMAs) in coastal fishing communities as the primary institutional link between fishing communities and NaFAA.
He says each CMA operates under governance safeguards, including mandatory annual elections and a minimum of 40% women's representation in decision-making. CMAs support communication of safety information, coordinate with traditional authorities including sea chiefs, and serve as the first point of contact for reporting incidents and resolving disputes within and between fishing communities.
"NaFAA has distributed life jackets to fishing communities to help address the shortage of basic safety equipment and has also distributed Yamaha outboard engines to fishers, replacing older or unreliable engines that are a common cause of vessels being stranded or disabled at sea," he says.
According to him, both distributions have been carried out in phases through CMAs, and NaFAA recognizes that continued expansion is needed to reach full coverage across all coastal counties.
No Record on Casualties at Sea
NaFAA does not currently maintain a comprehensive, centralized system for recording at-sea deaths or accidents across all landing sites nationally. Incidents are sometimes reported informally through CMAs, county offices, or the Liberia Coast Guard, but this does not yet amount to a systematic national record.
"We recognize this as a data gap, and improving safety-incident reporting alongside our broader catch-and-effort data systems is something NaFAA considers a priority for strengthening. We would rather state this plainly than offer a figure we cannot stand behind," Daryoue noted.
Daryoue, director for maritime fisheries at the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority (NaFAA), noted that NaFAA's principal equipment programs to date are the distribution of life jackets and Yamaha outboard engines to fishing communities through the CMA structure.
NaFAA does not consider the shortage of adequate life jackets resolved; coverage remains incomplete relative to the size of the artisanal fleet, and this is a concern NaFAA takes seriously rather than downplays. Expanding both programs, alongside safety-at-sea training, is a stated priority for NaFAA going forward, including through proposals to link fisheries and aquaculture development with technical and vocational training in basic navigation, safety at sea, and emergency response.
NaFAA's seasonal closure of the artisanal fishery each July and August is also relevant here: it is timed in part around the rainy season, when rough seas pose the greatest risk to small open canoes, and it also supports stock recovery. NaFAA is committed to working with the Liberia Coast Guard, county authorities, and development partners to expand equipment access and training over time and would welcome the opportunity to discuss specific timelines with you as they develop.
The three days climaxed with a parade. Members were dressed in green T-shirts. The crew marched from Popo Beach to the central police station and back to the CCOP church to end with a prayer service, followed by shared food. 1,200 Liberian dollars were collected from each member to support the T-shirts, parade, and food.
On the third day, they marched from Popo Beach wearing white and green T-shirts.
Reflecting on the event, Leona Red said, "It is not the first time we are fasting; sometimes even if you don't eat, it is good, sometimes you reference God. Our community is peaceful, especially this church, always praying for us. The pastors from this church pray for us. That's the time we reference God in the month. The fast lasts from the morning to 12 pm. Once you break, a few times... But as for me, I believe in God; God is the best God. That's why we call for this gathering. You believe in anything, it can carry you far. I live here, and this is my church."
She sings in the choir and serves as an usher, noting, "I can carry the fish around to people."

title: Portrait : Doumta Jacob, un non-voyant battant
content:
A Sarh, au quartier Baguirmi, dans le 1er arrondissement municipal, Doumta Jacob, un non-voyant, a choisi de faire de son handicap une raison de se battre plutôt qu’un obstacle.
Né à Sarh, chef-lieu de la province du Moyen-Chari, en 1972, Doumta Jacob perd progressivement la vue alors qu’il était encore sur les bancs de l’école. C’est en classe de CM2, à l’âge de 14 ans que ses problèmes de vue ont commencé.
La maladie s’aggrave ensuite et l’oblige à abandonner les études. « Je voyais difficilement le tableau lorsque j’étais à l’ecole et c’était difficile pour moi de lire et d’écrire », raconte-t-il.
Lire aussi : Tchad : une nouvelle association pour l’autonomisation des femmes déficientes visuelles
Contraint de rester à la maison, Doumta Jacob était découragé. Pour l’occuper, sa grand-mère lui remet une somme de 2 000 francs CFA . Avec cet argent, il commence par vendre des cigarettes. Les petits bénéfices réalisés lui permettent ensuite de développer d’autres activités, notamment la vente de bouteilles et la recharge de téléphones portables.
Au fil des années, ces petits commerces lui permettent de construire une chambre et de participer aux dépenses de sa famille. Malgré sa déficience visuelle, il apprend à identifier les différentes pièces et coupures de monnaie, une manière pour lui de s’adapter à son quotidien et à la vente de ses articles.

A 53 ans, Doumta Jacob encourage les jeunes à ne pas attendre uniquement un emploi a la Fonction publique. Selon lui, une petite activité peut progressivement devenir une véritable source de revenus.
Son parcours prend une autre dimension lorsqu’il découvre l’écriture braille grâce à un ancien formateur aujourd’hui décédé. « Cette formation m’a permis de lire, d’écrire et de continuer à apprendre malgré mon handicap. Grâce à cette nouvelle forme d’écriture, je compose des chansons. »
La musique devient également une partie importante de sa vie. Dans le monde musical, il se fait appeler Général Litakoï. Comme source d’inspiration, les réalités sociales. Cependant, aucune de ses compositions n’est enregistré au studio, faute de moyens.
« A travers mes chansons, je sensibilise les jeunes sur la consommation excessive de l’alcool, le temps consacré à certaines habitudes qui, selon lui, ne leur apportent pas de bénéfices et la protection de l’environnement. J’ai plusieurs chansons qui sont dans les tiroirs, mais je n’ai pas les moyens de les enregistrer. Je voudrais m’en servir pour sensibiliser les jeunes », explique-t-il.
Doumta Jacob lance également un message aux personnes vivant avec un handicap. Il les invite à identifier leurs capacités et à chercher une activité adaptée à leur situation, plutôt que de rester dans l’attente d’une assistance.
Il plaide enfin pour davantage de possibilités de formation et d’accompagnement en faveur des déficients visuels. Pour lui, un meilleur accès à l’education et aux activités professionnelles pourraient permettre à plusieurs personnes handicapées de devenir davantage autonomes.

title: Sénégal : le président gracie 984 détenus
content:
Par décrets signés ce 21 septembre 2026, le président de la République du Sénégal, Bassirou Diomaye Faye a accordé une grâce « exceptionnelle » à 984 condamnés. C’est ce qu’annonce le ministère de la Justice dans un communiqué de presse publié ce mardi 22 septembre 2026 à Dakar.
921 condamnés hors catégories bénéficient d’une remise totale de peine ; 21 détenus grands malades, sur avis du médecin-chef de l’Administration pénitentiaire, bénéficient d’une remise totale de peine ; 19 détenus mineurs et 1 détenu âgé de plus de 65 ans bénéficient d’une remise totale de peine ; 18 condamnés bénéficient d’une remise partielle de peine; 4 condamnés à la réclusion criminelle à perpétuité voient leur peine commuée.
Lire aussi : Sénégal : le gouvernement prévoit 5 milliards pour dédommager les victimes de la période pré-électorale
Selon le ministère de la Justice, cette mesure s’inscrit dans le cadre de la politique pénitentiaire conduite par le chef de l’État, visant à l’amélioration des conditions de détention, à la réduction de la population carcérale et à la réinsertion sociale des personnes graciées.

title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship
content:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally.
Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide.
Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax
— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026
“I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.”
Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”.
“I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.”
Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”.
Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania.
During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter.
In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family.
American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today”
He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026
There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it.
The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed.
Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland.
Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik.
Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US.
The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026
The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live.
The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship.
One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics.
Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago.
Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026
Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342.
However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty.
Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland.
Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage.
Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski has announced he wants to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors.
His best 100m time of 9.89 seconds is the 9th fastest in the world this year and over a tenth of a second faster than Poland's national record https://t.co/S2tZsiSAhh
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026
