title: Living with Alzheimer’s: How 87-year-old learnt to spell her name again
content:
Living with Alzheimer’s: How 87-year-old learnt to spell her name again
Simple tasks, repetition, cognitive training, early assessment and everyday activities can support functionality even as Alzheimer’s progresses in a patient. A World Alzheimer's Day special
At 87, Tara Pal was losing herself. As Alzheimer’s disease steadily chipped away at the memories that had held together a lifetime of names, places, routines and her identity, words began to slip away and even the simplest tasks became difficult. The woman who had once carried a lifetime of knowledge in her head could no longer always find her way back to it.
Then, almost playfully, she began again. Sitting with her grandchild’s alphabet blocks, Tara started forming words with her. At first, the letters made no sense. Then, one afternoon, they came together to spell her own name: TARA. She smiled as she struggled to put the letters in a row, her frail fingers losing grip every time. Then she went on to spell her daughter’s name, pronounce her husband’s name, call out to him and, eventually, memorise her own address. Tara had not suddenly “recovered” from advanced Alzheimer’s disease. What had changed was her ability to engage with a familiar task, learn through repetition and respond to cues. “With supportive care mechanisms, you can improve the quality of life for an Alzheimer’s patient,” says Dr Prasun Chatterjee, geriatrician and researcher, whose work has explored cognition, ageing and Alzheimer’s disease.
Her story points to a less obvious truth about dementia: the loss of memory is not necessarily the loss of every capacity to learn. “Alzheimer’s does not destroy all types of memory and learning at the same rate,” explains Dr Chatterjee. “Different memory systems rely on different brain networks. Alzheimer’s particularly affects the hippocampus and related medial temporal-lobe networks, which are important for forming new memories. Late-stage Alzheimer’s can leave some forms of learning relatively intact, particularly learning based on repetition, habit and emotional familiarity, even when conscious memory and the ability to learn new facts are severely impaired.”
Currently toggling roles as the WHO TAG Member for Healthy Ageing, president of the Indian Academy of Geriatrics, and Group Clinical Lead, Geriatric Medicine and Longevity Science, Apollo Hospital Delhi, he has examined Alzheimer’s and cognitive decline from several directions. From interventions that may support cognition before dementia develops, to behavioural changes that may precede Alzheimer’s, and to biological markers that could eventually help identify the disease earlier.
“Alzheimer’s disease is a neurodegenerative disorder in which abnormal protein clumps called amyloid (plaques) and tau (twisted tangles) build up in the brain and destroy the patient’s memory, thinking skills and the ability to carry out simple daily tasks,” he says. It is the most common cause of dementia, but the two terms are not interchangeable.
Dementia is a clinical syndrome; Alzheimer’s is a disease. Dementia refers to a decline in memory, thinking, behaviour or other cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with everyday life. Alzheimer’s disease is one specific neurodegenerative disease —and the most common cause of dementia. The distinction matters because the underlying cause can influence investigation, treatment and care. “India is looking at an old age pandemic as its ageing population increases,” he adds.
How to look for early signs
One of Dr Chatterjee’s patients is 78-year-old Kamla Mehra* from Noida. Her warning sign was deceptively ordinary: she began asking her son the same question —“Did you go to the market?”— again and again, sometimes five times within an hour. Soon she struggled to name everyday objects and would repeat questions just minutes after receiving an answer. “The family could have dismissed it as normal ageing. Instead, they sought help. A comprehensive assessment identified mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a stage in which cognitive abilities have begun to decline but substantial independence may still be preserved. Unlike Tara, Kamla came to us at a much earlier point in her cognitive journey and opened a very different window for intervention,” says Dr Chatterjee.
For generations, memory loss in an older person has often been treated as an inevitable consequence of getting old. But Alzheimer’s is not a normal or inevitable consequence of ageing. “India’s ageing population means that this casual dismissal is becoming increasingly consequential,” he adds. The nationally representative research from the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India estimated that about 7.4 per cent of Indians aged 60 and above — roughly 8.8 million people — were living with dementia based on data collected during 2017–2020.
The more detailed LASI-DAD research has highlighted an even larger population living with milder forms of cognitive impairment. Researchers estimated the prevalence of major neurocognitive disorder at 7.2 per cent and mild neurocognitive disorder at 17.6 per cent. Among people aged 80 and above, the estimated prevalence of major neurocognitive disorder was 15.2 per cent.
And as India’s population over 80 grows, Alzheimer’s will increasingly intersect with another major problem: who will provide the care? “That’s why diagnosing mild cognitive impairment is important. Some people remain stable; others improve when reversible or contributing factors are identified and treated. The signs are many — losing your train of thought, struggling to follow a book or movie plot, or getting easily distracted. Taking longer to find the right word during a conversation. Finding it harder to make decisions, finish multi-step tasks, or pay bills on time. Some could feel disoriented even in familiar places. Irritability, anxiety, depression, acting out of character are all signs of a person losing control over their familiar self,” explains Dr Chatterjee.
What happens when we look beyond memory?
Kamla’s assessment went beyond asking whether she could remember a list of words. “The six core areas used in medicine to evaluate cognitive impairment are learning and memory, executive function, language, complex attention, perceptual-motor function, and social cognition. The brain has multiple domains, and rehabilitation has to think in multiple domains too. All of these have to be activated to keep the brain functional,” says Dr Chatterjee. At his geriatric clinic, Kamla underwent a comprehensive clinical evaluation and neuropsychological assessment. Using the validated Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination-III (ACE-III), her initial score was 67/100. Further investigations included scans and blood biomarkers.
The science of neuroplasticity
Dr Chatterjee often tells patients and families that the brain is not a static organ and that one can make it work all the time. “The brain is vastly more complex than a muscle. It responds to experience, practice and stimulation throughout life. It keeps emotions intact. This capacity for adaptation is broadly described as neuroplasticity. So, if you work the brain, it can keep going till the very end. I see 100-year-olds with no dementia or Alzheimer’s. Cognitive decline should be addressed as a whole-body and whole-person problem, not simply as a memory disorder.” he says.
Kamla’s “brain gym” was an intensive non-pharmacological programme. Her son was particularly clear that he did not want to continue medications that made his mother excessively sleepy and confused. She had computer-based cognitive training for approximately 40–45 minutes per session, with repeated sessions over three months. She thought she was learning a new skill. Exercises targeted attention, memory, executive function, language and processing speed.
But the more important intervention happened outside the clinic. “At home, the family transformed ordinary life into a cognitive training environment. That’s why caregiving is so important. She maintained a diary. She practised recall. She did backward counting, played word and number games. She started learning music, which she always loved. She was made to participate in financial calculations and household activities. All of these may seem simple but engage the brain’s cognitive and functional domains repeatedly and meaningfully,” says Dr Chatterjee.
Perhaps the most powerful component of the intervention was not the computer. It was Kamla’s son. During their commute from Noida to Delhi, he would point to vehicle number plates and ask his mother to remember and recite the numbers backwards. At home, he created a large diary where she would write her address, a mantra and details of what she had done. “A simple activity recruited several abilities at once: attention, language, writing, sequencing, recall and fine-motor coordination. This is particularly relevant in India, where families continue to provide a large proportion of dementia care. Depending on specialist appointments will never be sufficient for a country of India’s size,” says Dr Chatterjee.
How the simplest interventions help
After three months, Kamla’s ACE-III score rose from 67/100 to 87/100. She became more conversational, participated more confidently in social gatherings and helped a local NGO. “You can have reasonable functional skills while living with a neurodegenerative disease. And when you intervene earlier, there may be substantially more capacity to preserve independence and build compensatory strategies,” says the doctor.
Dr Chatterjee always has counselling sessions with family members and asks them to repeatedly tell the patient how much they are loved and wanted throughout the day or that they are safe. “The emotional brain can remain deeply responsive even when factual memory has deteriorated. So, an Alzheimer’s patient senses rejection, alienation and disappointment and spirals down if you say, ‘Do you remember me?’ Instead say, ‘I’m here with you.’ That’s why the language of dementia care matters,” he adds.
How to prevent Alzheimer’s
The prevention conversation needs to move much earlier, in midlife. “We only talk about the heart, liver, diabetes. I would say include brain health in that discussion. Current evidence supports attention to several modifiable risk factors, including hypertension, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, lack of sleep, smoking, harmful alcohol use, hearing loss, depression, social isolation and other cardiovascular and lifestyle factors. And get a cognitive assessment at 65 instead of 75,” he says.
Of course, research shows that walking and diet changes help in managing every kind of dementia, leading to targeted interventions. “For example, the brain’s energy metabolism changes in Alzheimer’s disease, and a keto diet works because it provides an alternative fuel source to a brain that can no longer efficiently process glucose for energy. But restrictive diets should always be considered alongside other body conditions and guided,” says Dr Chatterjee.
Where the new drugs fit
The emergence of anti-amyloid therapies has added an entirely new dimension to Alzheimer’s treatment. Their cost and infrastructure requirements raise major questions about equitable access in India. For example, donanemab costs ₹91,688 per 350 mg vial in India. Introduced by Eli Lilly and Company under the brand name Lormalzi, this is the first once-monthly amyloid plaque-targeting therapy commercially available in the country. So, Dr Chatterjee overrules the pill dependence. “Instead, India needs to build a dementia-care system that begins before the patient reaches the neurologist. Our questions should be about how early can we identify it, how much function can we preserve, and how can we help the person and family live well with it. The answer will always be yes, something can still be done.”
(Names changed to protect privacy)
Rinku Ghosh is the Health Section Lead at Read More

title: Ahead of Leh killings anniversary, Ladakh withdraws 20 cases
content:
3 min readSrinagarUpdated: Sep 24, 2026 04:28 AM IST

A year after four civilians were killed in police firing after protests turned violent in Leh, Ladakh Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena on Wednesday announced the withdrawal of criminal cases against 20 of the 87 people booked in the aftermath of that incident. This includes Jigmat Dorjay, Rinchen Dadul, Stanzin Namgail and Tsewang Thirchin, who have died in the past year, as per officials.
Withdrawal of criminal cases has remained one of the key demands of Ladakh’s representatives during ongoing talks with the Ministry of Home Affairs.
This comes a month after the administration stated that it would be filing closure reports for 25 of the 87 people booked in the aftermath of the violence on September 24 last year. Of the 87 identified accused in the rioting cases, 81 were arrested, and criminal proceedings have begun against them.




Ladakh chief secretary Ashish Kundra had earlier said that nine people had been chargesheeted, suggesting that “there is evidence of their involvement” in the incident. He had also stated that LG’s office had directed the Ladakh DGP to “review the cases of the rest of the people who are still part of the investigation”.
On Wednesday, the administration announced the withdrawal of more cases, with LG Saxena stating that the move is “in the larger interest of peace, public tranquillity, and social harmony in Ladakh”.
“Following a comprehensive review, the Ladakh police recommended a closure report for 20 individuals, in FIR no. 144/2005, registered at PS – Leh, under section 360 of the BNSS,” Saxena said in a communique from Lok Niwas.
This decision, he added, ensures that these 20 individuals move forward positively with their lives and careers. “By prioritising justice and healing over protracted litigation, the decision aims at fostering a more peaceful, united, and harmonious society in Ladakh. I extend my sincere gratitude to Hon’ble Union Home Minister, Shri @AmitShah ji for his constant guidance and sympathetic approach, in matters pertaining to the victims and their families.”
Story continues below this ad
This also comes days after the Centre proposed a constitutional provision of ‘Article 371(K)’ in a bid to extend additional protections to Ladakh during a meeting of the sub-committee with the MHA earlier this month. Quashing of the cases has been a key demand of the representatives who have been part of a dialogue with the Centre seeking greater democratic representation and constitutional protections for the region.
The development coincides with a symbolic 20-km march that Ladakh climate activist Sonam Wangchuk will lead to mark the anniversary of the civilian killings in Ladakh.
Four protesters were killed and 44 injured as police fired after a protest for statehood and the Sixth Schedule for Ladakh turned violent in Leh on September 24 last year. After the protests, Wangchuk, who was on a hunger strike at the time of the incident, was booked under the National Security Act (NSA) and lodged in Jodhpur jail for six months.
On September 13, the administration had sanctioned compensation of Rs 15 lakh to the next of kin of each of the four deceased in the September 24 violence. An ex-gratia payment of Rs 3 lakh for those with major injuries and Rs 1 lakh for minor injuries had also been approved.

title: Bhat-Bhateni rebuilds 10 stores damaged during Gen Z uprising
content:
Money
Bhat-Bhateni rebuilds 10 stores damaged during Gen Z uprising
Despite the destruction and damage to its stores on September 9, 2025, the supermarket chain continued paying over 10,000 employees and began clearing debris within a week.Yagya Banjade
A year ago, Bhat-Bhateni Supermarket, Nepal’s largest retail chain, faced one of the biggest crises in its four-decades-long history.
On the second day of the Gen Z uprising on September 9, 2025, twelve of its outlets and its Baluwatar warehouse were completely destroyed or gutted while several others outlets were vandalised and looted.
The company has since rebuilt and reopened 10 of the 12 severely damaged outlets, with its Damak and Hetauda stores expected to resume operations by December and January, respectively.
“There was pain in our hearts and tears in our eyes as we watched our stores burn,” said Chairman and Managing Director Min Bahadur Gurung on Monday while reopening Bhat-Bhateni’s outlet in Tangal. “But we didn’t forget our responsibility towards the state and our employees. We started work within a week, clearing hot ash, steel rods and bricks, and have managed to reopen 10 stores in a year.”
The recovery stands out against the scale of the damage. The company reported losses of more than Rs11 billion after the protests. Bhat-Bhateni filed a claim exceeding Rs11 billion across 20 stores, including 12 that were completely destroyed. More than Rs500 million worth of goods were reportedly looted.
The Post reported that 21 of Bhat-Bhateni’s 28 outlets were damaged during the unrest. The attacks came on September 9, a day after dozens of protesters were shot dead during anti-corruption demonstrations that were triggered by social media ban. Bhat-Bhateni was among the private businesses targeted by protesters amid anger towards political parties and figures associated with the then ruling CPN-UML. Gurung had drawn controversy in 2024 after donating land for the UML’s central office.
For Bhat-Bhateni, the destruction also threatened thousands of jobs. Around 5,000 of its roughly 10,000 employees worked at the affected outlets and warehouse.
“Although our business infrastructure was destroyed, the company decided not to remove employees from their jobs,” said chief operation officer Panu Paudel. “We retained more than 10,000 employees and also paid the festival [Dashain] bonus that was due after the Gen Z movement.
Rebuilding began within days and continued around the clock. Teams had to reconstruct buildings, electrical and technical systems, equipment, sales areas, storage arrangements and customer service facilities.
“This was not an ordinary reconstruction,” said Paudel. “We had to rebuild the entire system needed to operate a store. We worked 24 hours a day. Once one store was ready, teams moved to the next.”
The Baluwatar warehouse, crucial to the company’s supply chain, was brought back into operation within 70 days. The Koteshwar outlet followed within four months. Maharajgunj, Chitwan, Pokhara, Baudha, Biratnagar, Birtamod, and Dharan have since reopened, with Tangal, the chain’s first-ever outlet, becoming the latest to resume operations.
The company estimates that rebuilding the 12 severely damaged outlets will cost about Rs15 billion. Paudel said work on the remaining two is progressing, with Damak targeted for reopening in December and Hetauda in January.
The recovery comes as businesses across the country continue to deal with the wider economic fallout of the September unrest.
Before the unrest, the affected outlets were among Bhat-Bhateni’s major revenue-generating stores. The company reported average daily transactions of about Rs105 million across its network. Reopening them therefore meant restoring not just buildings, but the supply chain and customer-service systems supporting thousands of jobs.
For Gurung, rebuilding quickly was also about keeping the company functioning and its employees at work. “We considered our work a duty to the country and its citizens,” he said. “We moved forward despite everything that had happened.”

title: Horse race returns to Palestinian village after wartime halt
content:
The annual race in the Israeli-occupied West Bank had been suspended for the past two years in the wake of the Gaza war, but the tradition returned this week, despite ongoing tension.
“Our ambitions are constrained by a lack of financial and logistical resources needed to support the riders, so we simply try to provide whatever we can,” said event coordinator Ismael Abu Awad.
After the starting gun was fired, the riders set off along the winding dirt track cutting through the rocky landscape, while spectators cheered the course and on rooftops.
The competition culminated in jubilant celebrations, with supporters surrounding the winning jockey and lifting trophies above the crowd.
Arabian horses occupy a special place in Palestinian culture, and horse races and equestrian beauty championships are held across the West Bank, drawing competitors from different towns and villages.
Open land has become becomes increasingly scarce amid expanding Israeli settlement construction in the West Bank, occupied since 1967.
But horse culture still draws Palestinians together, from urban neighbourhoods to rural villages.
For the local community, Friday’s race was more than just about sports. It was aimed at “preserving a form of Arab heritage that our ancestors cherished and that we continue to uphold today,” Abu Awad told AFP.
The event also provided an opportunity for local jockeys who cannot easily participate in international races to showcase their skills, the organiser said.
“Some horses and riders face difficulties travelling to Jordan or abroad,” he said.
Despite the challenges, participants spoke of dreams that stretch beyond the local track.
“My ambition is to travel to Italy to ride horses,” said racer Mohammed Al-Ajlouni. “We ride here now, but for the future, that is what I hope for.”

title: ADEM program drives equal education access across Indonesia: Ministry
content:
Puslapdik delegate Setyo Utomo said in a written statement received here on Monday that the secondary education affirmation program gives underprivileged children in remote, frontier, and outermost regions the opportunity to obtain a good education.
"Through this secondary education affirmation program, 57 children from the Highland Papua region have completed senior high school in East Java, Central Java, and Bali since 2023-2026. The program continues this year with 100 students studying in West Java, Banten, East Java, and Central Java," he said.
According to him, the 57 students from Highland Papua who received the scholarship were spread across three regions: 26 in East Java, 13 in Central Java, and 18 in Bali.
"We certainly hope that after completing their studies in Java and Bali, their character, discipline, and mindset will improve, so they can become a generation that brings change to the Highland Papua region," he said.
He explained that these 57 children represent extraordinary potential for the Highland Papua region, especially for its eight districts: Jayawijaya, Yahukimo, Nduga, Tolikara, Pegunungan Bintang, Lanny Jaya, Yalimo, and Mamberamo Tengah.
"We really hope these 57 children can serve as an example for other children in Highland Papua, so that they can follow the same path and become the future generation of Highland Papua," he said.
He expressed hope that children given the opportunity to study outside Papua would receive support, especially from their families.
"We hope parents will also give full support to their children who have the opportunity to study outside Papua. They study outside Papua so that their character, personality, spirit, and mindset can change to help develop their full potential," he said.

title: Minister support recycled plastic waste as prosthetic leg initiative
content:
Indonesia's Environment Minister Jumhur Hidayat voiced support for waste recycling initiatives, praising prosthetic legs made from plastic waste, by Yayasan Kaki Kita Se-Nusantara (YKKS), a foundation dedicated to assisting people with limb disabilities.
Hidayat emphasised the importance of waste segregation at the source and called for innovative approaches to maximise the value of inorganic waste, including plastics.
Hidayat made the remarks during a meeting with senior YKKS representatives, according to a statement received in Denpasar, Bali, on Monday.
The foundation showcased two prosthetic legs during the discussion, one made from high-density polyethylene (HDPE) and another from a blend of multilayer plastics and HDPE.
Related news: Gov't prioritizes emergency waste areas for WTE plants: Minister
Chairperson of the YKKS Board of Trustees, Putu Ivan Yunatana, said the foundation's innovations demonstrate how plastic waste, often viewed solely as an environmental pollutant, can be transformed into products that deliver both social and economic benefits.
"These two prosthetic legs show plastic waste can offer benefits and be economically valuable if supported by a well-managed ecosystem," he said, noting that YKKS focuses the initiative on underprivileged individuals with disabilities.
In collaboration with several corporations and supported by public donations, he added, the foundation has provided prosthetic limbs to beneficiaries across Bali and other regions, including Lombok Island in West Nusa Tenggara and Palu City in Central Sulawesi.
Yunatana said YKKS is also involved in educational initiatives and a waste-to-fuel programme.
Meanwhile, YKKS Chairman, Made Adhitiasthana, explained the foundation can convert around five kilograms of plastic waste into a single prosthetic leg, each featuring distinctive color patterns derived from the plastic materials used.
"The colors are derived directly from the plastics. For example, a white leg with black speckles is made from waste colored white and black," he explained, adding the color combinations can be customised to suit beneficiaries' preferences.

title: Anti-bullying tribunal receives 55 complaints, 5 settled
content:
Five of the cases were decided through various awards, including bullies being made to apologise to their victims, undergo counselling or, in one case, pay RM2,000 in damages, she said.
“These measures show that the tribunal is punishment-oriented but also focusses on rehabilitation of victims and the perpetrators’ behaviour,” she said in a statement.
Azalina said the Anti-Bullying Act 2026 and the tribunal provided a specific mechanism for dealing with bullying through a restorative approach that was faster and more cost-effective, while placing greater emphasis on protecting and rehabilitating victims.
However, she said, laws alone would not be enough to tackle bullying.
“The victims must come forward to seek help, while those who witness bullying must have the courage to speak up because bullying is not a joke and must not be normalised under any circumstances,” she said.

title: 11,297 acres returned to Maine’s Penobscot Nation after more than a century
content:
A vast stretch of Maine forest has changed hands in a return more than a century in the making. On September 16, 2026, 11,297 acres surrounding the East Branch of the Penobscot River were returned to the Penobscot Nation, marking the first phase of a larger effort to restore more than 30,000 acres of ancestral homeland. The Trust for Public Land, which is partnering with the Penobscot Nation on the project, said the wider effort began in 2023 with a $32.5 million fundraising goal. So far, $20.7 million has been raised, with additional funding still needed to complete the remaining phases.
A first step toward returning more than 30,000 acres
The 11,297-acre transfer is part of the Wáhsehtəkʷ land-return effort, named for the East Branch of the Penobscot River. The property lies near the base of Katahdin and just south of Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument. The first phase covers an area roughly comparable in size to the city of Portland, Maine. It includes about 15 miles of cold-water streams, 865 acres of ponds and wetlands, and habitat used by species including Atlantic salmon, brook trout and moose.
The project is being carried out through a partnership between the Penobscot Nation and the Trust for Public Land. The conservation organisation purchased the broader property from timber harvesters after it came onto the market more than three years ago, while working with the Nation to raise the money needed to return the land.
The partnership's broader goal is to return more than 30,000 acres to the Penobscot Nation. Completing that effort will require another $12 million, according to the Trust for Public Land and Maine Public.
Land with cultural and environmental importance
The returned property is significant not only because of its size but also because of its connection to Penobscot culture and the East Branch of the Penobscot River. The Nation plans to take an active role in caring for the landscape, including restoring habitats around waterways and monitoring wildlife and ecological conditions. Planned work includes tracking ticks and monitoring bat populations, alongside broader efforts to protect habitats and waterways.
The land also creates opportunities for Penobscot citizens to access natural resources. Those plans include hunting, harvesting and potential economic development, according to Chuck Loring, the Penobscot Nation's natural resources director, as reported by Maine Public. For the Nation, the difference between advising on conservation and actually owning the land is significant. Ownership gives the Penobscot Nation greater authority over how the property is managed and conserved.
The 11,297-acre transfer is part of the Wáhsehtəkʷ land-return effort, named for the East Branch of the Penobscot River (Image Credit: Chris Bennett/ Trust for Public Land)
A potential new route to Katahdin Woods and Waters
The land return could also affect access to the nearby Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument. One long-term possibility is the creation of a southern access route through the returned land near Millinocket. Currently, there is no southern access route into the monument, and the proposed connection could eventually make the area easier to reach.
However, the access-road proposal is still in development. Details regarding its route, construction and timing have not yet been finalised. According to the Trust for Public Land, improved access could also benefit communities around the Katahdin region by making it easier for visitors to reach the monument and potentially increasing activity for local businesses, including restaurants, lodging providers and outdoor recreation operators.
Part of a larger Wabanaki land-return effort
The Penobscot project is also connected to a broader effort involving Maine's Wabanaki Nations. The Wáhsehtəkʷ project forms part of Tributary Land Returns, a collaboration involving the four federally recognised Wabanaki tribes in Maine and seven conservation organisations. The wider initiative seeks to return more than 50,000 acres through 11 projects.
The Penobscot Nation currently stewards approximately 140,000 acres, according to the Trust for Public Land. The organisation said the four Wabanaki Nations collectively hold only about 1% of their ancestral lands in Maine, placing the current project within a much larger history of land ownership and restoration. The partnership also reflects a shift in how conservation organisations approach Indigenous communities. Rather than treating tribes only as advisers or stakeholders in conservation projects, land-return initiatives place ownership and stewardship directly in tribal hands.
What happens next
The September 2026 transfer completes only the first phase of the Wáhsehtəkʷ project. The partners are continuing to raise money for the remaining land, with the overall campaign targeting $32.5 million and $20.7 million already secured. Once the full project is completed, more than 30,000 acres around the East Branch of the Penobscot River could be under Penobscot ownership and stewardship.
For the Nation, the returned 11,297 acres represent more than a large tract of Maine forest. The property reconnects Penobscot people with land, waterways and natural resources tied to their culture, while creating opportunities for conservation, recreation and future economic activity. The first transfer therefore marks both the completion of one phase and the beginning of the next: a continuing effort to return the remaining acreage and restore Penobscot ownership across a much larger part of the ancestral landscape.

title: Timely emergency care saves Chinese passenger from critical condition
content:
QUẢNG NINH — A Chinese passenger who had fainted and lost consciousness has been provided first aid by the Móng Cái International Border Guard Station, helping him through a critical episode.
At around 2pm on Friday, while processing passengers at the immigration counter at the Móng Cái International Border Gate, the officers noticed Liang Ruizhuang, 67, Chinese nationality, suddenly faint, lose consciousness and become unable to stand unaided.
Immediately upon noticing the incident, Lieutenant Colonel Dương Đại Thắng and Lieutenant Colonel Hoàng Trung Thanh quickly approached, administered first aid and carried out an initial check on the male passenger.
Observing that Liang Ruizhuang was weak and foaming at the mouth, the officers urgently contacted and coordinated with the international health quarantine force to examine and check his health, and to continue monitoring his condition.
Thanks to the prompt detection, assistance and intervention, after about 30 minutes Liang Ruizhuang recovered and regained consciousness.
Afterwards, the male passenger was taken to the Móng Cái Regional General Hospital for further treatment. — VNS

title: Legarda welcomes historic Bangsamoro polls, condemns violence
content:
Legarda welcomes historic Bangsamoro polls, condemns violence
MANILA, Philippines — The Bangsamoro parliamentary elections on Sept. 14 were a “historic first step” to self-governance in the region, Sen. Loren Legarda said in a statement.
“After generations who endured conflict and uncertainty, the people held in their hands the most powerful instrument of democracy—the ballot. Every vote cast carried with it the hopes of a people who have fought long and hard for peace, dignity, and the right to shape their own future,” Legarda said.
She is a co-author and co-sponsor of the measure that became Republic Act No. 12317, which set the first regular parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). She also served as co-chairperson of the Philippine Congress–Bangsamoro Parliament Forum (PCBPF) and chairperson of its Senate panel, the institutional mechanism for cooperation and coordination between the Philippine Congress and the Bangsamoro Parliament.
READ: Parties led by ex-rebels dominate BARMM polls
The exercise paved the way for the transition from the Bangsamoro Transition Authority to the region’s first elected Parliament.
“For many years, the Bangsamoro peace process was carried forward through negotiations, agreements, legislation, and the difficult work of building institutions. The September 14 elections gave the Bansamoro people the opportunity to choose their leaders under the parliamentary system envisioned for the region. That achievement deserves recognition and protection,” she stressed.
‘No room for violence’
Legarda condemned, however, the violence surrounding the vote, with two shooting incidents in Cotabato City that left four people dead and 18 others wounded, according to Chairman George Garcia of the Commission on Elections.
“At the very moment when the Bangsamoro people were exercising their right to choose their leaders, lives were lost, and families were left grieving. I condemn these acts in the strongest terms,” Legarda said.
“There’s no room for violence and threats in elections borne out of a long peace process and the recognition of the Bangsamoro’s right to govern its own region. No political ambition, rivalry, or disagreement can justify violence. The will of the people must be determined by their votes, never by fear, intimidation, or force,” she added
Legarda called on election authorities and law enforcement agencies to investigate the incidents of violence, protect affected communities, and ensure that accountability follows wherever the evidence leads.
She also urged candidates, political leaders, and their supporters to respect the results and refrain from actions that could further endanger communities or undermine public confidence in the electoral process.
“The measure of this historic election will not end when the last ballot is counted. It will be measured by whether communities become safer, whether children have greater opportunities to learn, whether families can build dignified livelihoods, and whether the people of Bangsamoro, regardless of faith, ethnicity, or political affiliation, can see themselves represented in their government,” Legarda said.
READ: Unfinished peace process: What’s next after BARMM polls?
Partners in government
She urged Congress to remain a committed partner of the elected Bangsamoro Parliament.
“We reached this historic moment because generations of Filipinos, especially the Bangsamoro people, chose, again and again, to believe that peace was possible. Some of them did not live to see this election. We honor their sacrifices by protecting what has been built and by ensuring that democracy takes deeper root in the Bangsamoro,” she said.
Legarda also congratulated the newly elected members of the Bangsamoro Parliament.
“I congratulate the newly elected members of the Bangsamoro Parliament on the trust and confidence placed in them by the Bangsamoro people. As the first elected leaders of the Parliament, you have the unique opportunity to help shape this new chapter in the region’s history. I trust that they will honor that mandate through principled, inclusive, and responsive leadership,” Legarda said.
“For my part, I will continue to work with the Bangsamoro Parliament and our partners in government to strengthen the institutions of self-governance, advance peace and development, and help build a safer and more prosperous future for the people of the Bangsamoro. The work does not end with this historic election. We must continue it together,” she added. /atm

title: Girls organise science research programme to grow interest in STEM among S’pore female students
content:
Girls organise science research programme to grow interest in STEM among S’pore female students
The TL;DR: Teens organised a two-month-long research programme with academics and industry experts as mentors to encourage female students to pursue their interest in STEM.
- Teen girls in Singapore organised a two-month science research programme to encourage female students' interest in STEM, with mentorship from academics and industry experts.
- The programme involved 66 girls from 13 schools working on diverse projects, including nuclear fusion and local wildlife, fostering teamwork and research skills.
- INTEGIRLS Singapore aims to increase female STEM participation, addressing underrepresentation and inspiring girls through accessible, peer-led initiatives that offer real-world STEM experiences.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – From finding out about the effects of food-waste antioxidants on repeatedly heated hawker-centre cooking oil, to observing the routine of otters in Singapore, 66 girls put their research skills to the test in a two-month-long science research programme.
They did so in a programme their own peers, a group of schoolgirls aged 16 and 17, put together from scratch and which lasted from early July to early September.
The girls-for-girls programme, the INTEGIRLS Singapore Science Research Program, was spearheaded by five teens who are part of INTEGIRLS Singapore, which was set up here in 2022 as a chapter of an existing US-based group.
The five are: Singapore American School students Amber Anbei Chi, 16, and Jenny Jeong, 17; United World College Dover Campus students Lauren Pak and Nayoon Kim, both 16; and Raffles Institution student Stephanie Jeslyn Goutama, 17.
INTEGIRLS Singapore aims to encourage interest in STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) among girls.
In Singapore, the number of women working in STEM jobs was 35 per cent in 2024, up from 29 per cent in 2014, and above worldwide figures.
Globally, women are underrepresented in the STEM workforce. The World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report 2024 found that women represented 28.2 per cent of the STEM workforce compared with 47.3 per cent in non-STEM sectors. This could also contribute to a gender wage gap due to the higher salaries in the STEM sector.
This was the first time INTEGIRLS Singapore had organised a longer-term programme, though it had one-off events in the past.
Amber, the INTEGIRLS co-chapter head, said she had joined many maths, robotics and science competitions and programmes. She noticed “in many of those spaces, I often found myself as one of only a handful of girls in the room”.
She added: “Through INTEGIRLS, we hope to make some of these opportunities more visible and accessible, allowing girls to meet researchers and mentors, experience STEM beyond the classroom, and discover for themselves where their interests and strengths may lie.”
Lauren, the group’s other co-chapter head, said of organising the research programme, a first for the group: “During the planning period, we worked on the programme structure, contacted mentors and participants, looked for sponsors and partners, prepared for the opening ceremony, organised the research teams, and planned for the in-person showcase logistics. Altogether, we sent more than 420 e-mails to mentors, participants and sponsors.”
The girls recruited the participants from 13 different international and MOE schools, including Nan Hua High School, National Junior College, Nanyang Junior College and Temasek Junior College. They also recruited mentors, including faculty members from local universities, to guide participants in their projects.
One of the participants, Raisa Saluja, 15, from UWCSEA Dover, said she joined the research programme as she was interested in exploring research projects outside of school and wanted the chance to work under a mentor.
Saying that she was excited about the “more independent and collaborative environment”, she added: “The programme has made me more interested in considering a STEM-related major or career, since I enjoyed exploring and putting our research into action to investigate complex problems.”
Her team’s research project focused on nuclear fusion and investigated how magnetic field strength affects the electrical power output of a simulated tokamak (a doughnut-shaped magnetic chamber), work that could potentially add to the development of fusion power plants.
Lee Seok Woo, the programme director of the Master of Science in Nanotechnology and Nanoscience, and an associate professor at the School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering at Nanyang Technological University, mentored her team.
Said Lee: “In the STEM field, there is always a strong need to discover and encourage more female scientists. So, when I was first approached by INTEGIRLS, I was both surprised and absolutely delighted to learn that middle and high school students had taken the initiative to organise such a meaningful event themselves.”
Another participant, Zoe Alaia Djojonegoro, 14, researched smooth-coated otters, which contributed to observations of local wildlife. Said the Singapore American School student: “The most interesting finding was that the morning routines of otters are quite flexible and they don’t have a fixed schedule.”
Said Michelle Tan, an NUS Department of Biological Sciences alumnus and member of the Otter Working Group, one of the mentors for wildlife biology projects: “Overall, INTEGIRLS is a valuable opportunity for female students to not only gain exposure and interest in STEM subjects, but also learn soft skills such as teamwork, resilience, communication and responsibility.”
INTEGIRLS’ Amber said of the feedback received from the programme: “Some also commented that student-organised programmes like this can, in certain ways, work better than traditional university-organised outreach activities because young people often understand what interests and engages other young people.”
For more information: https://singapore.integirls.org/

title: Thái Nguyên pilots new approach to cardiometabolic disease management and care
content:
Thu Trang
THÁI NGUYÊN — Instead of waiting for people to come to hospital when their illness has reached serious levels, a new model in Thái Nguyên is bringing prevention, screening and management of cardiometabolic diseases closer to communities.
Digital technology, community health workers and primary health care facilities are being connected to identify risks early, link people to appropriate care and support long-term follow-up appointments.
Physician Hoàng Tuấn Du, from the Hợp Thành Commune Health Station, feels his work is now much more effective than in previous years.
“Back then, we usually managed patient records on paper, with a very large volume of documentation,” he said.
Now, health workers like Du are using the Sức Sống Mới (New Vitality) app – a practical, user-friendly digital system that allows health staff to enter health indicators, screen residents’ risk levels, refer high-risk individuals to higher-level facilities and link data with other health data platforms.
This ensured health workers have full, accurate information on each patient’s condition in their area, Du said.
Dương Thị Hiến, a village-based health worker in Na Tủn Village, Hợp Thành Commune, said that in previous years, they had to visit every household without knowing who was ill and who was not.
“After the Sức Sống Mới app was introduced, we could identify who needed treatment first and who needed to be referred to higher-level facilities," Hiến said.
"Reports are submitted via mobile phone, and residents can also check their own health status.”
After training sessions, village health workers went door-to-door to measure blood pressure, provide lifestyle counselling and guide residents on installing the Sức Sống Mới app on their phones.
The app is not only for health workers.
Community members can complete a short risk-screening questionnaire, enter their blood pressure readings, and immediately receive information on their risks of cardiometabolic diseases. If they are at risk, they are directly connected to a health facility, and can also read disease-prevention guidance on their phones to adjust their daily habits.
Phạm Ngọc Tân, 71, a hypertension patient from Phú Nam Village, Vô Tranh Commune, said the app is very useful for people like him, because today is the information age and almost everyone has a mobile phone.
“Just by turning on our phones, we can see everything we need to do, how to prevent illness, and how to live in a healthier way,” he said.
Noncommunicable diseases
Thái Nguyên – a province known for its vast tea hills and expanding industrial zones – was facing a growing threat.
Lê Ái Kim Anh, deputy director of the Thái Nguyên Provincial Centre for Disease Control (CDC), said that non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and metabolic disorders, are now the leading causes of death in Việt Nam, accounting for about 81 per cent of all deaths each year.
Worryingly, access to local screening programmes in provinces such as Thái Nguyên remains limited, and many cases are only detected at late stages.
The biggest challenge is the gap between residents and the health system as people live far from facilities, health workers are overburdened and there are no systematic tools to connect them.
The key question for the province is how to shorten that distance.
Bringing primary health care closer to communities via an interoperable digital platform and community engagement.
Du, Hiến and Tân are among those benefiting from the project 'Strengthening the primary healthcare system in preventing cardiovascular and metabolic disorders (CMDs) through community engagement' – a solution to Thái Nguyên’s challenge.
Since 2024, the project has been implemented in 32 health facilities across two districts in Thái Nguyên Province, covering around 300 villages.
So far, 32 primary healthcare facilities strengthened in managing and caring for patients with cardiovascular and metabolic disorders.
As many as 168,000 adults (aged 40 and above) have been provided with information and health education on risks of cardiovascular and metabolic disorders.
About 39,000 residents have been monitored for blood pressure control, blood glucose control and weight management.
A total of 450 community health workers trained on the app.
Nearly 87 doctors and health staff trained clinically on diagnosis, treatment, integrated management and psychosocial support for people with cardiovascular and metabolic disorders.
Nguyễn Hải Thượng, deputy director of the Primary Health Care Programme at PATH, said that PATH, together with the provincial CDC and the provincial Department of Health, initially designed a community- and health-system-based model for cardiometabolic diseases management and care.
The model is built on three strategic pillars, including comprehensive integration of services and the grassroots health system, strengthened community engagement through a network of community health collaborators, and digital health innovation via two mobile applications – one for health workers and one for community residents.
Messages on NCDs prevention are broadcast regularly over the loud speaker system, helping village health workers reach residents more easily and invite them to participate in follow-up community activities.
Trần Thị Quỳnh Trang, from the Disease Prevention and Food Safety Unit at Phổ Yên Ward Health Station, said health screening sessions had shown clear, significant effectiveness. Participation rates are very high.
“Screening has been highly effective thanks to project support in terms of supplies, equipment, communication materials, and the app, which helps residents track and manage their health. Residents receive structured, comprehensive counselling and support,” she said.
Phạm Thị Lệ Thu, head of the NCDs Prevention Division at Thái Nguyên CDC, said the NCDs management had seen very practical changes, particularly through community participation. Residents can now proactively assess their risk, monitor their health, and access information on cardiometabolic diseases prevention and control.
Looking ahead
Lê Ái Kim Anh, deputy director of Thái Nguyên CDC, said: “The project’s outcomes have been very positive for both the community and the health system.
"In the future, our CDC will strive to coordinate with relevant units to sustain the achievements supported by the project and PATH.”
Nguyễn Hải Thượng, deputy director of PATH’s Primary Health Care Programme, noted that the project also faced some difficulties.
“Geographic conditions in some areas affect access to health services," he said.
"Integration of cardiometabolic diseases management and care into provincial health programmes has so far been implemented in only 10 out of 92 communes, so the ripple effect remains limited.”
The data management system initially supports continuous patient monitoring across different levels, but still needs to be standardised and its usage capacity strengthened to ensure interoperability and effectiveness.
This shows that the key factors for the model’s success are synchronous, continuous implementation with supervisory support and the use of data in management, he said.
Residents are gradually changing the way they care for their health. As a result, healthcare no longer starts at hospitals, but in every household.
What is happening here is a scalable health model, in which primary healthcare is equipped with tools to proactively manage community health earlier, remotely and more sustainably. — VNS

title: समस्याग्रस्तका पाँच सहकारीका १३५ बचतकर्ताको रकम फिर्ता
content:
काठमाडौं। समस्याग्रस्त सहकारी व्यवस्थापन समितिले पाँच समस्याग्रस्त सहकारीको बचत फिर्ता गरेको छ। समितिका अनुसार शिवशिखरका ५७, कान्तिपुरका ५२, ओरिन्टल को अपरेटिभका आठ, तुलसी बहुमुखीका नौ र आइडियल यमुना सहकारीका नौ जना साना बचतकर्ताको रकम फिर्ता गरिएको हो।
सरकारले समस्याग्रस्त सहकारीको ऋण असुलीबाट प्राप्त रकम पीडित बचतकर्तालाई फिर्ता गरिएको स्पष्ट पारेको छ। पहिलो चरणमा थोरै बचत रकम भएका बचतकर्तालाई बचत रकम फिर्ता गरिएको समितिले जनाएको छ। यसैगरी क्रमशः बचतकर्ताको रकमका आधारमा वर्गीकरण गरेर रकम फिर्ता गरिने छ।
समस्याग्रस्त सहकारी संस्थाहरुबाट ऋण असुली र सम्पत्ति व्यवस्थापनबाट प्राप्त रकमबाट सम्बन्धित सहकारीका बचतकर्तालाई बचत फिर्ता गर्ने कार्य प्रचलित कानुनी व्यवस्थाबमोजिम निरन्तर रूपमा सञ्चालन भइरहेको छ।

title: 5 British schoolgirls, 14-15, build firebreak robot, represent UK globally
content:
Five schoolgirls from Kent, aged between 14 and 15, have built a robot with five-metre folding arms to help fight wildfires. Their work has earned them the chance to represent Great Britain at an international robotics competition in South Korea. The team from The Folkestone School for Girls, known as Team Meglabyte, designed the robot to clear dry plants and create paths that remove fuel from the spread of fires. The school's robotics club was only founded in 2024, but it has now been chosen to represent Great Britain at the FIRST Global Challenge in Incheon.
Designing a solution to growing wildfire risks
The international competition brings together student teams from more than 190 countries to work on major environmental and technology problems. This year's challenge focuses on preventing, controlling and recovering from wildfires in a warming world. For the competition, the Folkestone students designed an autonomous vehicle with long, folding arms that can clear paths up to five metres wide through dry vegetation. The system removes plants and other surface material that can fuel a fire, creating natural firebreaks that can slow the spread of flames without putting firefighters directly in danger.
According to a statement on the official website of The Folkestone School for Girls, the students have been working to improve the robot before the global competition: "The Folkestone School for Girls robotics team, Team Meglabyte, are thrilled to be representing Great Britain at the First Global Challenge in South Korea."
Working with local firefighters
The five students worked with professional firefighters to make sure their design could deal with the real conditions faced during wildfires. According to a report by Kent news outlet Shepway Vox, the students spoke with Kent Fire and Rescue Service during the early stages of the project. The firefighters helped them understand how wildfires spread across difficult terrain. Their advice led the team to focus on building a lightweight and stable robot that could extend its arms across uneven ground without tipping over. The students also used standard parts supplied by the competition organisers to program the robot's autonomous driving system. The software allows the machine to avoid obstacles, clear debris and work on its own in areas where thick smoke could make remote control difficult.
National selection and fundraising
The team's success comes only two years after the school's robotics program was created. Despite having less experience than some international teams, the Kent students won the national selection process and secured Great Britain's single place in the competition. To help pay for their trip to Incheon and the materials needed to build their robot, the team launched a public crowdfunding campaign. On their official Crowdfunder page, the students explained their goal of representing Britain and encouraging more girls to study science and technology: "Our aim is to inspire young girls across GB into STEM and globally raise awareness about this year's competition theme of wildfires. Each year a single robotics team from a school in Great Britain is sent to compete in a robotics competition on the global stage. This year, five girls from the all-girls state school Folkestone School for Girls have been selected to represent the nation in South Korea to compete with their robot. The girls need your help to get them to the competition!" The students are also using the opportunity to create outreach programs for primary schools. These projects will give younger pupils basic coding kits and lesson plans showing how engineering can be used to solve real environmental problems. The FIRST Global Challenge will take place in Incheon, South Korea, where the five Folkestone students will put their robot to the test against teams from countries around the world.

title: AI and robots drive administrative reform in Đồng Nai Province
content:
ĐỒNG NAI — The Đồng Xoài Ward Public Administrative Service Centre in Đồng Nai City has introduced a reception robot and a multichannel artificial intelligence system, including chatbots and voicebots, as part of efforts to accelerate administrative reform and build a digital government.
Capable of automatically welcoming visitors, recognising faces and providing spoken guidance and advice on administrative procedures, the new technology not only eases the workload of frontline officials but also improves the public’s experience.
Technology improves public services
People visiting the centre are now assisted by an intelligent reception robot.
Ngô Hoàng Lãng, a resident of Residential Area 2 in Đồng Xoài Ward, said he was surprised by the changes in administrative services when he visited the centre.
In the past, he often worried about complicated procedures and lengthy waiting times whenever he needed to complete paperwork. Since the ward stepped up its digital transformation and introduced AI and robots, administrative procedures have become simpler and more convenient.
The robot provides detailed guidance in a clear voice and directs visitors to the correct service counters. Meanwhile, the AI system available on mobile phones allows residents to access and look up information anytime and anywhere, without having to make repeated visits to the centre.
“Modern technology gives people access to more useful information about policies and application procedures in a transparent and clear manner,” Lãng said.
“These changes not only save time and effort but also make the service feel more accessible and welcoming. People are genuinely satisfied with and appreciative of the local administration’s commitment to serving them.”
Nguyễn Trọng Phát, a resident of Residential Area 1, also praised the convenience offered by the new technology.
He said administrative procedures were now much quicker and more convenient than before. What impressed him most was the detailed advice and guidance provided through AI applications.
In addition to explaining application procedures, the AI system answers questions and provides useful information about new policies and regulations that residents may not yet know about.
The introduction of AI and robots has enabled people to take a more active role in looking up information and completing administrative procedures, while creating a more open and transparent administrative environment. These technological services have helped residents feel more confident and satisfied when dealing with local authorities.
With its friendly appearance, the robot welcomes visitors, directs them to the appropriate specialist offices and gives spoken answers to common questions. Facial-recognition technology has also been integrated to meet modern management needs.
Residents who do not visit the centre in person can still check the status of their applications or quickly submit feedback through AI-powered chatbots and voicebots on the centre’s website and social media platforms.
Trần Anh Mỹ, Director of the Đồng Xoài Ward Public Administrative Service Centre, said the introduction of administrative guidance and reception robots, along with a multichannel AI system, marked a new step in the locality’s administrative reform efforts.
At the centre, the robots welcome visitors, provide guidance and answer questions about procedures and application status. AI tools, including chatbots and voicebots on the website and social media platforms, are available around the clock to help users look up information and submit feedback.
The technology not only reduces pressure on officials working at service counters but, more importantly, also improves service quality, he said.
It is also an important milestone demonstrating Đồng Xoài Ward’s determination to build a modern, transparent and people-friendly administration.
AI supports internal management
Đồng Xoài Ward is also expanding the use of artificial intelligence in its internal management.
In addition to an AI chatbot integrated into its online information portal to help residents quickly look up administrative procedures, the ward has incorporated tools such as Smart AI and a key performance indicator tracking system into its operations.
These tools enable officials and civil servants to use data, handle tasks and monitor progress more effectively.
Expanding AI from public services to internal management is a strategic step towards building a comprehensive digital government.
Nguyễn Thị Bích Thuần, Vice Chairwoman of the Đồng Xoài Ward People’s Council, said applying artificial intelligence to management was a key measure to improve the performance of the local administrative apparatus.
To achieve this goal, ward leaders have asked every official and civil servant to actively improve their digital skills and flexibly apply new technology to their professional duties. The ultimate aim is to build a modern and transparent administration dedicated to serving residents and businesses.
During the first nine months of 2026, the Đồng Xoài Ward Public Administrative Service Centre maintained the stable and lawful processing of administrative procedures.
From January 1 to September 15, the centre received more than 9,500 applications, all of which were submitted online.
It processed more than 9,300 applications, equivalent to over 98.5 per cent, while the remainder were still within the permitted processing period.
Notably, all completed applications were processed either on time or ahead of schedule, with none overdue.
These results lifted the ward’s public and business service index to 97.56 points, placing it ninth among Đồng Nai City’s 95 communes and wards.
The achievement also resulted from proactive communication and direct public support.
During the first nine months of the year, the centre helped organise 20 face-to-face guidance sessions in residential areas, attended by more than 9,000 people. It also provided information through multiple channels, including its website, public loudspeaker system and community Zalo groups.
Mỹ said the co-ordinated measures had reduced the number of applications requiring repeated additions and increased the proportion submitted online.
They have also gradually encouraged people to use digital public services, helping improve service quality and advance administrative reform in the locality.
To effectively implement Project 06 during the 2026–30 period and advance digital transformation, the centre will continue diversifying its communication activities and strengthening face-to-face guidance to help residents and businesses make effective use of digital technology.
It considers public satisfaction the key measure of its performance and will conduct regular monitoring and evaluations to maintain a 100 per cent satisfaction rate, while building an image of dedicated and professional officials and civil servants.
After more than five months, the use of AI and reception robots at the centre has proved to be a technological breakthrough that has improved the quality of public services.
By combining modern digital infrastructure, stronger internal governance and public support, Đồng Xoài Ward has demonstrated the practical effectiveness of its digital government model.
Its strong record of processing applications on time, together with high levels of public satisfaction, reflects progress towards a modern and transparent administration centred on the needs of residents and businesses. — VNS

title: Deputy Prime Minister wishes children a joyful, safe Mid-Autumn Festival
content:
HÀ NỘI — Deputy Prime Minister Phạm Thị Thanh Trà wished the children a joyful, safe and meaningful Mid-Autumn Festival, and encouraged them to stay healthy, behave well and study hard.
Trà made the request on Sunday afternoon during a visit by her delegation to Trung Môn Kindergarten’s Kim Phú campus in Minh Xuân Ward, the northern mountainous province of Tuyên Quang, where she presented gifts to teachers and children on the occasion of Mid-Autumn Festival.
She has called on the province to continue improving the learning environment, facilities, equipment and other essential conditions for educational institutions.
Teachers should devote their love, dedication and sense of responsibility to their pupils so that “every day at school is a happy day” and every lesson is genuinely useful and meaningful, she said.
This should be a key task for the province’s education sector in the 2026-27 academic year and the years ahead.
She also stressed that the Party and State always pay special attention to children and seek to create the best possible conditions for them to study, play, receive care and grow up surrounded by the love of their families, schools and society.
In recent years, child protection, care and education have received increasingly comprehensive attention, ranging from investment in facilities and improving teaching quality to creating safe and friendly educational environments, she said.
On the occasion, Trà and the delegation presented Mid-Autumn gifts to the children and a television to the kindergarten to help improve equipment for childcare, nurturing and education.
The delegation also presented 30 computer sets to six communes – Đồng Yên, Tiên Yên, Liên Hiệp, Nhữ Khê, Phú Lương and Trường Sinh – with five sets for each commune.
The equipment is expected to improve working conditions at grassroots level, enhance the local authorities’ capacity to apply information technology and meet requirements for handling work in the course of performing their duties.
Spreading love
Also on Sunday, the People’s Committee of the southern province of Tây Ninh organised a provincial-level Mid-Autumn Festival camp themed “A Loving Moon” for children in An Tịnh Ward, providing a space for fun, social interaction and meaningful experiences while demonstrating the care and attention given to children by authorities, sectors and society as a whole.
The camp brought together 10 teams and 100 children representing more than 10,801 children in An Tịnh Ward.
Amid the festive atmosphere of the eighth lunar month, the children took part in a range of fun and experiential activities, including decorating their camp areas, making lanterns and playing games such as “Keeping the Loving Moon”, “Bringing the Moon to the Team” and “Mid-Autumn Picture Puzzle”.
Cultural performances and lion dances also created a lively, warm and colourful atmosphere for the festival.
Nguyễn Hoàng Uyên, Deputy Director of the provincial Department of Health and head of the camp’s organising committee, said the event aimed to provide children with a joyful, healthy and useful playground while giving them opportunities to interact, gain experience and develop their sense of solidarity, creativity, confidence and individual talents.
The health sector considers childcare to go beyond ensuring physical health, nutrition and disease prevention, she said, stressing the need to pay attention to children’s mental health, living environment and comprehensive development.
In recent years, authorities, sectors and localities across the province have organised numerous activities to visit and present gifts to children and provide them with care, particularly those facing exceptionally difficult circumstances or at risk of falling into such circumstances.
These efforts have helped give children greater strength and encouragement to overcome difficulties and continue attending school, studying and developing themselves. — VNS

title: De las lágrimas del novio a las palabras de Paz Padilla: la boda de ensueño de Anna Ferrer y Mario Cristóbal
content:
De las lágrimas del novio a las palabras de Paz Padilla: la boda de ensueño de Anna Ferrer y Mario Cristóbal
Enlace
La celebración ha reunido emoción, humor y tradición andaluza, con una charanga, una caseta de feria y numerosos detalles elegidos por los novios
Haber tenido una boda de ensueño era uno de los grandes deseos de Anna Ferrer y Mario Cristóbal, y la pareja lo ha cumplido rodeada de las personas más importantes de su vida. Después de cuatro años de relación, ambos se han dado el ‘sí, quiero’ este sábado en una ceremonia civil celebrada en el Trafalgar Polo Club, en El Palmar de Vejer, Cádiz. Un enlace que llegaba después de una preboda en Zahara de los Atunes y que ha puesto el broche a dos días de celebraciones marcados por la emoción, el humor y algunos detalles alejados de los convencionalismos habituales.
Uno de ellos se ha producido precisamente en la llegada de la novia. Anna ya había adelantado que no quería seguir algunas de las tradiciones más arraigadas y finalmente ha sido su madre, Paz Padilla, quien la ha acompañado hasta encontrarse con Mario. Madre e hija han hecho su entrada al ritmo de My Way, de Frank Sinatra, interpretada al piano, ante la mirada de un novio que no ha podido contener las lágrimas al ver aparecer a Anna.
Paz tampoco ha escondido la emoción. Horas antes, mientras ambas se preparaban para la ceremonia, ya había anticipado entre bromas lo difícil que sería contener las lágrimas. “¿Me habrás puesto rímel waterproof? Porque nada más que de pensar, ya estoy llorando”, comentaba mientras se peinaban y maquillaban. Una emoción que terminó aflorando durante el enlace, especialmente cuando llegó el momento de dirigirse a su hija.
Fiel a su sentido del humor, la presentadora comenzó su intervención riéndose de sí misma y de las bromas que habían acompañado los preparativos sobre sus supuestas ganas de acaparar protagonismo. “Que yo, que yo, será que yo no iba a estar en tu boda, yo que soy Paz Padilla, escritora, actora, presentadora, humorista”, arrancó antes de imaginar su propia entrada sobre un elefante, entre fuegos artificiales, un coro de góspel y hasta una avioneta surcando el cielo. “Porque soy muy protagonista. Mira, me tienen que matar”, remató.
Después llegó la parte más emotiva de sus palabras. “Como dicen las madres, siempre estaré cuidándote. He aprendido que ser padre significa soltar, que no hemos criado un águila para que viva en un corral”, explicó. Paz reflexionó entonces sobre la necesidad de dejar volar a los hijos y confiar en que estén preparados para construir su propio camino. También dedicó unas palabras a Mario. “Yo soy feliz porque tú quieres a Mario, hoy lo hemos visto todo, estáis tremendamente enamorados, todo lo que esté en tu corazón tiene un hueco en el mío”. Y terminó expresando un último deseo para ambos. “Solo te deseo que seas muy feliz”.
Para uno de los días más importantes de su vida, Anna apostó por el diseño español. Durante la ceremonia llevó su primer vestido acompañado de velo y un moño desenfadado, mientras que para la fiesta cambió por una creación de Claudia Llagostera. Este segundo diseño, confeccionado en tul sedoso bordado artesanalmente en algodón sobre una base de satén, incorporaba godets de georgette de seda, escote recto, tirantes finos, espalda abierta en V y una capa al cuello. Una mariposa bordada a mano completaba el vestido, que combinó con el cabello suelto y ondulado.
La personalidad de los novios también estuvo muy presente en la decoración. Las mesas incorporaron elementos relacionados con la gastronomía y con el universo de NoNiNá, la firma de Anna, entre ellos grandes velas con forma de sardina. Pimientos convertidos en portavelas y centros elaborados con patatas completaron una puesta en escena acompañada por una vajilla de inspiración andaluza, con estampados en tonos azules y tierra.
La gastronomía fue otro de los aspectos que Anna y Mario cuidaron especialmente. La pareja llegó a probar hasta 24 propuestas antes de decidir el menú definitivo y seleccionó 18 aperitivos para el cóctel. Entre los platos escogidos figuraba el solomillo acompañado de patatas rústicas.
Con la llegada de la noche, la celebración adquirió un ambiente todavía más festivo. Las velas repartidas por el recinto y las guirnaldas de luces iluminaron el espacio mientras los invitados disfrutaban de una charanga y de una caseta de feria en la que tampoco faltó un bingo. Los asistentes recibieron además distintos detalles, entre ellos pañuelos preparados especialmente para la ocasión.

title: Antonio Jesús, con inteligencia límite, prepara su segunda oposición: "Con apoyo podemos lograr cosas"
content:
Antonio Jesús, con inteligencia límite, prepara su segunda oposición: "Con apoyo, podemos conseguir grandes cosas"
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
Con los apoyos necesarios, Antonio Jesús ha logrado llevar una vida bastante autónoma. Trabaja, vive en un piso tutelado y se está preparando una oposición.
Aunque se calcula que el porcentaje es mucho mayor, 1% de la población está diagnosticada con inteligencia límite, un tipo de discapacidad intelectual leve -el CI de estas personas está entre 70 y 85- que es tan frecuente como desconocida e invisible.
Y es que personas como Antonio Jesús, no tienen ningún rasgo físico aparente, pero pueden presentan características como dificultades en el aprendizaje, desfase entre su edad cronológica y su edad mental o déficit en la psicomotricidad, en el lenguaje o en las habilidades sociales, entre otras cosas.
Se trata de características que pueden llegar a limitarles mucho, pero que no impiden que puedan alcanzar un alto grado de autonomía si cuentan con los apoyos y la comprensión adecuados. De lo contrario, como denuncian desde organizaciones como la Fundación Magdalena Moriche, se encuentran ‘en tierra de nadie’.
Eso es lo que le pasó a Antonio Jesús durante años, que encontró mucha incomprensión, sobre todo durante su etapa educativa.
Natural de un pequeño pueblo de Badajoz, Fuente del Maestre, en ese entorno no encontró lo que necesitaba, más bien lo contrario. "En el colegio lo pasé bastante mal, sufrí bullying, acoso… y la verdad es que por parte de los profesores, mucha ayuda no tuve, todo lo contrario. Casi no me adaptaban las asignaturas y yo lo pasaba mal, iba sacando las cosas como podía. Si no llega a ser por el apoyo que tuve de mi familia y más tarde de la asociación, no sé qué habría hecho".
La importancia de contar con apoyo especializado
Gracias al apoyo de la Fundación Magdalena Moriche años después, su vida cambió radicalmente. Allí no solo encontró comprensión y empatía, también todos los apoyos que le hacían falta para alcanzar todo su potencial. "No pude terminar la ESO por falta de apoyo y porque tuve una lesión en la rodilla, pero seguí estudiando gracias a la asociación, me preparé oposiciones y la aprobé, aunque no saqué plaza y me saqué el carnet de conducir. Y todo lo logré gracias a este apoyo, para mí fue un cambio radical. Allí encontré el apoyo que necesitaba y a nivel social fue tremendo, desde entonces tengo muchos amigos, cosa que en el pueblo no tenía", recuerda agradecido.
Sólo pido salud y tener una vida normal, como la de cualquiera
En la actualidad, Antonio Jesús tiene 28 años, vive en un piso tutelado con siete compañeros más y un monitor de la fundación y tiene una vida completamente autónoma y plena. Atrás quedaron los años de sufrimiento y de sentirse distinto. "Mi vida ahora es completamente diferente, para bien. En el piso nos organizamos muy bien, compartimos tareas y somos como una familia. Además, estoy trabajando de reponedor y hago un montón de actividades".
Entre sus favoritas, practicar deporte, sobre todo el judo y boxeo. "Mi ídolo ahora mismo es Ilia Topuria, me encantaría conocerlo", cuenta emocionado. Aunque si hay algo que le emociona aún más son los coches deportivos. "¡Me encantan! Como veis en la foto. El coche no es mío, ¿eh?, ya me gustaría, pero al menos lo pude conducir. ¡Menuda experiencia!", comparte, feliz.
Aprobar una oposición y más apoyo para la inteligencia límite
Como sabe lo que es sentirse distinto e incomprendido durante años, a Antonio Jesús le gustaría evitar más chicos pasarán por lo que él ha pasado. "La gente todavía no sabe lo que es la inteligencia límite, es muy desconocida y somos muchos. Y se tiene que conocer, porque, con los apoyos adecuados, como ha sido mi caso desde que entré en la fundación, las personas con inteligencia límite, podemos conseguir muchas cosas. Las personas con inteligencia límite y con discapacidad intelectual somos iguales que el resto y podemos hacer grandes cosas. Espero que poco a poco se vaya conociendo", insiste. "Y a los padres les diría que acepten lo que tienen sus hijos, porque hay familias a las que les cuesta verlo y así es muy complicado que encuentren el apoyo que necesiten sus hijos, y ellos sufren mucho. Por ese lado yo no he tenido problema, pero sé que hay gente que le pasa".
Él, desde luego, no se pone límites y seguirá luchando para mejorar su vida. "En mi trabajo estoy muy bien, mis compañeros me quieren mucho… pero mi próximo objetivo es aprobar una oposición y tener plaza. Y a nivel más personal, no pido mucho, sólo salud y tener una vida normal, como la de cualquiera".
